provenance: Private collection, California. | Thence by descent to the present owner. | | | | In the late 1950s, California-born artist Miyoko Ito began developing an impressive dexterity with oil painting while retaining the sensibilities of her education in the Berkeley School of Watercolor. This went hand in hand with the evolution of her unique take on organic abstraction, characterized by long, tubular and ovoid forms undulating in fields of earthy hues. The titles of her paintings during this period, including the present lot entitled The Sea, refer back to the natural and physical world, but the works themselves make no literal representations. Instead, her strength and precision in evoking a certain energy or mood without any reliance on figurative representation emerges. Deeply inspired by the work of Pierre Bonnard, Ito adopted his technique of underpainting in red and cool tones, with which she conveyed a sense of intentionality and intrinsic harmony in her use of color. Beyond just technical influence, there are echoes of Bonnard's slender-limbed nudes and tightly packed, flattened interiors in The Sea. | | The solid patches of deep colors, delineated by hard edges of this period gradually gave way to delicate gradients and more variable spatial dimensionality. Through further experimentation along the boundaries of abstraction, Ito entered the subsequent era of her work for which she is best known. The warm glowing palettes and vaguely architectural, liminal environments she constructed in this later era of her career are highly regarded as her finest work. The mystery and magic of her mature work also subtly reveal the impact of Surrealism, which Ito inevitably gleaned from her peers during the 1960s in Chicago. | | When asked in a 1978 interview whether, as a student, she tried to emulate the work of such giants of the canon, Ito explained that "Picasso and Cezanne gave [her] understanding" ("Oral History Interview With Myoko Ito at The Oxbow Summer School Of Painting, Saugatuck, Michigan, July 20, 1978", Archives of American Art, Smithsonian Institution, Online). This attitude is illustrative of her singular approach to artmaking and the conviction in her vision. Her work reflects a diverse education, from her early schooling in Japan, to her formative years in Berkeley and later the School of Art Institute of Chicago. For Ito, painting was a way of life that carried her through one upheaval after the other, beginning with the nervous breakdown she suffered as a child in Yokohama followed by her experience of the Japanese American internment in the United States during World War II. Miyoko Ito: Heart of Hearts, the first major monograph dedicated to Ito's life and work was published in 2024 by Pre-Echo Press and Jordan Stein. And despite her untimely death over 40 years ago, international acclaim for the artist is greater than ever.

provenance: The Collection of Timothy Egert, Maryland (acquired by 1991). | | Literature | The Martin Wong Foundation, Martin Wong Catalogue Raisonné, online (illustrated). | | | A towering edifice that rises toward golden skies of wingless skaters resembling the Putti of Giotto's frescoes, Martin Wong's Houston Street & Avenue B is a triumph of his late painting. Filled with allegory and personal inflection, this recently rediscovered work boasts an abundance of motifs and symbols that speak to Wong's centrality in the Downtown scene of the 1980s and 1990s, his Graffiti collaborators, the architecture of the Lower East Side, and his tapestried heritage. From his late lover Miguel Piñero, pictured at its base, to the stern, masonry visage of Lady Liberty, Houston Street & Avenue B paints a story of love and death, freedom and detention, New York City and the American Dream. Few artists of the Postmodern period have achieved such poetry and sincerity; fewer still have come to represent an authentic voice in such pivotal decades. Whilst Jean-Michel Basquiat synthesized abstraction, Graffiti and the energy of the Downtown scene to the toast of art world royalty, Martin Wong took no liberties in illustrating the same milieu with lucidity, ambition, and painterly prowess. | | A third-generation Chinese-American, Wong was raised in the Chinatown district of San Francisco, becoming an active member of the Bay Area art scene. After college, he worked as a performance artist and portraitist, later journeying across Asia, collecting and selling the antiques amassed throughout his travels. By the late 1970s, Wong's creative output had turned exclusively to painting, and, in 1978, he found himself in New York, inescapably drawn to the city's gritty, wild and vivid atmosphere. Moving from the desolate, foggy shores of Northern California to the allure of Manhattan, Wong found inspiration in the firefighters, b-boys and skateboarders running the city. This was Wong's new life, one where he "dressed like a rodeo cowboy and ran with graffiti artists who were tagging the neighborhood" (H. Cotter, "Martin Wong, an Urban Visionary With a Hungry Eye," The New York Times, November 19, 2015, Online). | | Upon his arrival in New York, Wong found and rented an empty apartment at 141 Ridge Street from 1982 to 1994, settling himself in the heart of the Lower East Side. Graffiti lined the entryway, mirroring the landscape of his new neighborhood. The apartment, a 1920s tenement building, engulfed the artist in a sea of brick, the view from his room that of a similarly faced building, covered in crumbling red bricks and lined with identically sized windows. It was within this apartment, and the decrepit motel room the artist inhabited beforehand, that Wong first incorporated bricks into his paintings, imagery that would become a central motif within his artistic oeuvre. Wong understood the materiality of the city, having graduated years before with a degree in ceramics. He used the bare brick walls of the surrounding buildings as his subject matter, a single object functioning as a metaphor for the urban landscape, embodying themes of spatial containment and psychological entrapment. | | It is just four blocks from Wong's Ridge Street apartment that Houston Street & Avenue B takes its title. Amid a bustling intersection at the very bottom of Alphabet City, Houston Street & Avenue B features a tall chain linked fence topped with swaths of barbed wire and a fiery golden sky dotted with skateboard riding figures. In the foreground stands Miguel Piñero, a poet and playwright, and Wong's longtime creative and romantic partner. Hair held back by a striped cap, Piñero tilts his head back, gulping down the contents of a dark bottle. The entirety of this scene unfolds against a backdrop of brick, swirling together to form the face of the Statue of Liberty, a symbolic source of inspiration for artists since her unveiling in 1886. | | For Wong, the Statue of Liberty was one of his most potent, recurring motifs. If Lady Liberty was once the emblem of the nation's ideal of freedom – and of welcome to those émigrés deboarding at Ellis Island in the preceding century – Wong recasts it here as the fortress of exclusion. His characters nonetheless transcend the architecture of control. In this sense, Houston Street & Avenue B articulates an alternative American sublime, one measured not by monumental progress but by the ascendence of those who move through its ruins. | | | A Lower Eastside Poem (excerpt) | Miguel Piñero | | Just once before I die | I want to climb up on | a tenement sky | to dream my lungs out till | I cry | then scatter my ashes thru | the Lower East Side. | | So let me sing my song tonight | let me feel out of sight | and let all eyes be dry | when they scatter my ashes thru | the Lower East Side. | | | The Lower East side of the 1980s, known as Loisaida by its black and Latino residents, attracted swarms of artists with its gritty charm. A vibrant, defiant community, immersed in the sounds of hardcore, punk, and hip hop. With bands like The Clash, the Misfits, and the Beastie Boys as its soundtrack, the Lower East Side stood in stark opposition to the rising tide of Reagan-era gentrification, becoming a sanctuary for outcasts and a powerful space for self-expression. Wong drew inspiration from these very sources to craft works that were passionate, poetic, and precisely executed, defying conventional expectations around ethnicity, culture, and sexuality. | | A remarkable and visionary artist of the late 20th Century, one who represents the authentic voice of the New York new wave, Martin Wong's work can be found in the permanent collections of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York; the Whitney Museum of American Art, New York; the Art Institute of Chicago; the de Young Museum, Los Angeles; the Museum of Modern Art, New York; and the New York Historical Society. Retrospectives of his work took place at New York's New Museum in 1998 and the Bronx Museum, New York, in 2015. | | Rediscovered after decades in private hands, the painting stands today as one of Wong's most profound meditations on the paradoxes of freedom. It transforms the vernacular of downtown life into a lasting parable of hope, mourning, and transcendence; a monument not to power, but to the poetry of survival.

Raphael, Von Monet zu Picasso, Grundzüge einer Ästhetik und Entwicklung der modernen Malerei, Munich, 1913, no. 22 (illustrated; titled 'Kopf'). | R. Schacht, Künstler der Gegenwart, Vol. IV, Henri Matisse, Dresden, 1922, p. 60 (illustrated; titled 'Kopf'). | A. Fried, 'A Blend of Legends in Historic Art Show,' in San Francisco Examiner, September 10, 1971, p. 28 (illustrated). | J.C. Bishop, C. Debray & R.A. Rabinow (eds.), The Steins Collect, Matisse, Picasso and the Parisian Avant-Garde, exh. cat., San Francisco Museum of Art, San Francisco, 2011, no. 99 (illustrated pp. 386 & 408). | | | La femme aux cheveux noirs, painted circa 1901, hails from a crucial moment in the artistic career of a founding father of modern art. Created on the cusp of his radical and defining Fauve epoch, the work's layered brushwork, bold delineation, and Cezanne-esque tonal construction offer the viewer a rare glimpse into Matisse's earliest development as a modern artist, rejecting the academic formalities of an anachronistic turn-of-the-century Europe. Contrary to the brazen Fauve canvases Matisse would first exhibit in 1905, the initially austere palette and direct, confrontational gaze of La femme aux cheveux noirs is a striking exemplar of the artist's early portraiture. While the reserved nudes, greys, and black hues of La femme aux cheveux noirs are present, we see the subtle foreshadowing to the later Fauvist style weaved within; flecks of blue on the collarbone, a richness to the pinks, bright greens and yellows developing as one's gaze lengthens. This delicate variation offering a clear visual trajectory in the artist's development towards 'pure color'. | | In the early 1900s, Matisse was a struggling, relatively unknown artist. According to fellow artist Maurice Boudot-Lamotte, he even reportedly accepted five francs from the owner of a junk-stall on Boulevard Raspail for three of his paintings. In dire financial straits and with a family to consider, Matisse felt caught between his intrinsic need to push the boundaries of traditional representation, and the obligation to appease collectors and generate revenue to support his family. It was during this time that Matisse began to explore different ways of rendering the world around him. The present work presciently anticipates some of the most radical, iconic aspects of his oeuvre, such as the intensity and concentration of color in his Fauve pictures, manifested here in the emphatically worked flesh and assured sense of line. | | The sitter's graceful visage is formed through thick, lavish brushstrokes applied with a heavy impasto, creating a strong delineation of subject and background, and a powerfully expressive contrast of a subtle multitude of colors that creates the impression of space opening in depth. Rare in its intimate scale and stark background, the black tonal contrast enhances the chromatic effervescence of the sitter's bare skin and offers an intimate study of great psychological power. Whilst completed earlier than Amedeo Modigliani's iconic nudes and portraiture of the 1910s, there is a handling, emotion, and expression in La femme aux cheveux noirs that forces a comparison and possible influence between the artists at this pivotal juncture. | | Before 1900, Matisse had produced very few figural studies. Following his renewed interest in the human form, however, portraiture became a renowned fixture throughout his prolific oeuvre. He wrote in 1908: "What interests me most is neither still life nor landscape, but the human figure. It is that which best permits me to express my so-to-speak religious attitude toward life" (H. Matisse, 'Notes of a Painter', in La Grande Review, December 25, 1908). In the present work, Matisse depicts his subject with an honest simplicity, forgoing anatomical exactitude and identifying details in favor of capturing the essential qualities that: "suggest the deep gravity which persists in every human being [...] Expression, for me, does not reside in passions flaring up in a human face or manifested by violent movement. The entire arrangement of my picture is expressive . . ." (ibid). Here, the jutting prow of the figure's collarbone and shoulders commands space within the composition, while the rest of her body contorts and almost recedes into the background of the canvas. | | Whilst the exact identity of the sitter of La femme aux cheveux noirs is unknown, records of correspondence in 1970 between Margaret Potter, Associate Curator at the Museum of Modern Art, and the family of the present owners revealed that Matisse's daughter, Marguerite Duthuit Faure, confirmed the sitter was a model frequently used by Matisse at the time. Rarely working from his imagination, the burgeoning artist hired countless models for periods both long and short throughout his career, often with the sitters themselves becoming iconic within modern canon. Matisse preferred paid models to sitters or patrons because he thought them to be much more malleable, offering him more artistic freedom and experimentation. As a paid 'employee', his models' identity and characterization could be manipulated in service of his artistic needs, whereas with portraits for patrons, friends, and family, he often felt beholden to preserve their individuality and remain accountable to social or professional interdependence. As such, the figure in the present work is rendered with generalized features that maintain little individuality: capturing the model's innate being is not the primary object of Matisse's representation, it is an experiment of medium and feeling. | | When referring to the model in La femme aux cheveux noirs, Duthuit also noted the use of the very same model in 1900 for a sculpture entitled Buste Ancien. Given the distinctive pictorial composition, and its relation to Buste Ancien, the present work was most likely realized in conjunction with a group of sculptural studies Matisse created between 1900 and 1903. As he began to create figural studies with greater frequency, he became preoccupied with the challenge of rendering a figure's arms in a manner so as to avoid interference with the silhouette of the torso. Ever the innovator, Matisse would often experiment with other mediums as a means of working through pictorial challenges that emerged in his painting. As such, there are numerous sculptures, paintings, and drawings from the turn of the century through which he experimented with different contrapposto stances, and the subsequent effect this had on the figure's torso and upper chest. | | An important and rare example of Matisse's Pre-Fauvist work, La femme aux cheveux noirs is also distinguished by its exceptional provenance. Purchased in Paris in 1909, this work remained in the personal collection of Sarah and Michael Stein for decades. These American collectors would arguably go on to become some of Matisse's most important patrons and promoters. In 1903 when Michael Stein and his wife Sarah moved to Paris from San Francisco, at the urging of his siblings Leo and Gertrude Stein, they swiftly immersed themselves within the cultural and social milieu of the Parisian avant-garde. As with Michael's siblings, this meant filling their 58 rue Madame apartment with their latest acquisitions; generally all exquisite examples of modern art. While Michael and Sarah's early collection included the names of Cézanne, Renoir, and Picasso, from 1905 it was soon to be dominated by the striking work of Henri Matisse. In a circa 1911-1914 photograph, taken in the apartment, La femme aux cheveux noirs can be seen on the wall behind the seated Sarah Stein and her friend, alongside a sculpture of the same model. | | The apartment, now filled with Matisse paintings, was the setting for an open house every Saturday evening, and their salon of modern art soon became the fashionable gathering place for connoisseurs and dilettantes alike. For most who attended Sarah and Michael's weekend salons, the work of Matisse would have been unfamiliar, and, to some, even savagely offensive. Slowly but surely, however, those who entered the Stein's apartment, mesmerized by Sarah's intelligence and eloquence, began to begrudgingly accept Matisse as the brilliant artist he was. Recounting his many nights spent as a guest at the Stein's, famed art dealer Ambroise Vollard wrote: "beautifully gowned in original costumes, antique jewelry... Sarah sat on the couch in the corner explaining to everybody the greatness of Matisse. People listened to her, unconvinced, but overwhelmed by her enthusiasm and authority" (Vollard, Recollections of a Picture Dealer, London, 1936, p. 137). Frequently taking their Matisse paintings back with them to show friends in America, Michael and Sarah Stein played a pivotal role in promoting Matisse's art within the United States, and are often lauded with carrying the artist's name outside of France. | | In addition to patron, Matisse also came to view Sarah Stein as a close confidante and friend. According to Therese Jelenko, friend and frequent guest of the Stein's, Matisse would regularly come to the Rue Madame carrying bundles of his pictures, and Sarah would: "tell him what she thought of things, sometimes rather bluntly. He'd seem to always listen and always argue about it" (ibid). Annette Rosenshine further recounted that: "I recall seeing Matisse in the Steins' apartment when he was in the throes of struggling with a new creative expression. There he found solace in unburdening his latest problems and uncertainties to Sarah Stein, knowing that he would receive sensitive, sympathetic understanding. The talk and friendship were valuable to him" (A. Rosenshine, Life's Not a Paragraph). Matisse valued Sarah's opinion and would often seek out her guidance when met with a particularly difficult artistic problem, once stating that: "she (Sarah) knows more about my paintings than I do" (Matisse quoted in Pollack, The Collectors: Dr. Claribel and Miss Etta Cone, New York, 1962, p. 270). | | The Stein's collection of Matisse works, while vast in size and breadth, is particularly notable for the way in which it acutely captured the artist's creative spirit. As one of the last Matisse works the Steins would buy due to limited space and the artist's steadily increasing prices, La femme aux cheveux noirs' inclusion in such a prominent collection speaks to the work's emblematic significance amongst Matisse's tremendous and coveted artistic output. | | Acquired by Michael and Sarah Stein at its last presentation at auction over a century ago, La femme aux cheveux noirs was later included in the seminal 1970 exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art that sought to regather the exceptional collections of this trailblazing family of collectors. Returning to auction with a history and pedigree only the finest works can boast, the present work remains a preeminent testament to a key artist-patron relationship in art history - a seminal masterpiece.

Mesens (ed.), London Bulletin, no. 4-5, July 1938 (illustrated p. 30). | P. Matisse & K. Sage (eds.), Yves Tanguy, Un Recueil de ses oeuvres, New York, 1963, no. 218 (illustrated p. 108). | P. Waldberg, Yves Tanguy, Brussels, 1977 (illustrated p. 85). | L. Riou, Ma vie blanche et noire, Notes sur Yves Tanguy, Baye, 1996, pp. 10 & 28. | | | "Yves Tanguy, the painter of terrible aerial, subterranean, and maritime elegances, the man in whom I see the moral adornment of our time: my adorable friend" | | - Andre Breton, 'Yves Tanguy', in London Bulletin alongside an illustration of the present work, no. 4-5, London, July 1938, p. 32). | | Though Yves Tanguy received no formal artistic training, his meticulous draftsmanship and inventive vision resulted in a highly refined, iconic personal style that transformed the boundaries of Modernist painting and helped to establish Surrealism as a major artistic movement. Bridging the gap between abstraction and figuration, landscape and still-life, Surrealist dreamscape and automatic form, Yves Tanguy's utterly unique artistry came to epitomize the surrealist movement and has inspired generations. | | While surrounded by the arts, literature, and culture from an early age, it wasn't until 1923, when passing a Giorgio de Chirico painting in the windows of Paul Guillaume's gallery, that Yves Tanguy decided that he, too, would become a painter. Struck by the enigmatic, metaphysical imagery of de Chirico's painting, Tanguy soon became interested in the Surrealist movement and was introduced to André Breton, the movement's protagonist and founding leader, in 1925. By 1926, the June issue of La Révolution surréaliste had featured a reproduction of Tanguy's early work, resulting in his recognition as an 'official' Surrealist artist. In the following year of 1927, Tanguy's mature style developed with an astonishing abruptness, and he exhibited his first one-man show at the Galerie Surréaliste in Paris. It is in this mature style that Tanguy's iconic dreamscapes of amorphous forms, as seen in the present work, emerge. | | This new, highly personal pictorial language was heavily influenced by the childhood summers Tanguy spent off the coast of Brittany, France. The prehistoric rock formations observed by Tanguy in his youth would later be subconsciously reimagined into the nebulous forms that occupy the sparse, vast expanses of his painted 'inscapes' of the mind. The haunting imagery of Tanguy's work, like so many of the Surrealists', was also heavily informed by the rubble, dilapidated ruins, and barren towns Tanguy encountered while growing up in WWI-era France. Equally important was his trip to North Africa in 1930, where he observed natural geological structures and stratifications, which were to appear as abstracted motifs in his paintings. While Tanguy felt deeply inspired by the work of de Chirico and also influenced by Hieronymus Bosch's mythical imagery, he seldom discussed personal influences from his private life that informed the imagery within his own works. | | Painted in 1938, Je tourne la tête vers moi (I Turn My Head Toward Myself) encapsulates a pivotal time in both Tanguy's art and life. As tensions began to escalate across Europe and the world, Tanguy was the first Surrealist artist to flee Europe for America in November of 1939, marking 1938 as what was to be his last year in the City of Light. His final years in Paris proved to be a time of great artistic development for Tanguy, as he worked towards achieving a completely ambiguous, horizonless space. This new pictorial development in the artist's mature work called for an intuitive, largely subliminal approach to painting, further cementing his works as a wholly unique, sacred poetry of the inner mind. Writing in admiration of this new-found, meditative approach to Tanguy's work, André Breton lauded that: | | "There are no landscapes. There is not even a horizon [...] There is only, physically speaking, our immense suspicion which surrounds everything [...] Where most observers would see only a favourite setting for obscure and magnificent metamorphoses, there is actually presented the first survey – achieved without the aid of legends – of a considerable extent of the mental world which is not in its Genesis" (A. Breton, 'At an Equal Distance', in Yves Tanguy par André Breton, New York, 1946). | | The rich swaths of hazy greys and modulating hues of blue present in Je tourne la tête vers moi form an ambivalent fusion of land into sky, an enigmatic vista of the mind in which space is both continuous and fluidly ephemeral. Upon first delineating this vast, weightless landscape of blue and grey swells, Tanguy would instinctively begin to populate the composition with spontaneously generated forms. Each new motif suggested its subsequent counterpart, until a dreamscape of delicate equilibrium became fully realized, each element held in place by a mysterious force of internal gravity. | | Tanguy found it most freeing when he relied solely on intuition and creative imagination, noting that: "I found that if I planned a picture beforehand, it never surprised me, and surprises are pleasure in painting" (Tanguy quoted in Yves Tanguy, exh. cat. New York, 1955, p. 17). When reflecting on his creative process shortly before his premature death in 1955, Yves Tanguy insisted that the "element of surprise in the creation of a work of art is, for me, the most important thing" (Y. Tanguy, 'The Creative Process', in Art Digest, Vol. 28, no. 8, New York, January 1954, p. 14). His unique worlds, while subconsciously conjured, were not, however, automatically articulated like the scribbled 'automatic drawings' of his Surrealist colleagues. Neatness and precision were deeply ingrained attributes of Tanguy's mind and personality, and he infused his surreal visions with an ultra-precise realism. Je tourne la tête vers moi offers viewers a curious glimpse into the dichotomous nature of Tanguy's surreal dreamworld, conjured through a scrupulous technique of hyper-realism. As a result of Tanguy's reverential attention to detail, the present work's array of nebulous forms punctuate the hazy, modulated backdrop with stunning sense of alacrity. Cacti-like forms and geometric structures resembling the scientific model of a module are interconnected through a constellation of taut, gossamer-like threads that stretch into the composition's deep perspective. The present work's amalgamation of disparate, elemental forms and innate sensations conjures the enigmatic inner world of Yves Tanguy's creative genius and presents a primitive, yet unprecedented version of reality- a hallucinatory myth of his time. | | Tanguy's intimate psychological landscapes, infused with an inscrutable mystery that is fully realized in the present work, were extolled by front-runners of the Surrealist movement, Andre Breton and the Belgian artist-turned-publisher E.L.T. Mesens. Je tourne la tête vers moi is one of only three illustrated paintings by Tanguy in the April 1938 edition of the London Bulletin, the highly influential Surrealist periodical Mesens edited and published, perfectly illustrating the high regard it was held in by Tanguy's contemporaries. Alongside this illustration, the London Bulletin included two texts by André Breton and Paul Eluard, commending the artist and his influence on surrealism. The present work was subsequently exhibited in the corresponding 1938 Tanguy Exhibition at the Guggenheim Jeune Gallery on 30 Cork Street on an hors-catalogue basis – possibly due to its only recent creation. Whilst not listed in the exhibition guide, this inclusion was confirmed by the artist's wife, Kay Sage, in a letter to the San Franciscan owners in 1957. Leaving for the United States after the London exhibition, yet not included in Pierre Matisse Gallery's October 1939 Tanguy show organized by Sage, it was only after Charlotte Mack, friend of the family and one of the original owners of Kandinsky's Lila (Lot 10A), notified the artist's wife of the location of Je tourne la tête vers moi, that anyone knew of its whereabouts in the US. This resulted in an intimate series of correspondence between the artist's wife and the family, ultimately reuniting her with the piece and ensuring it was included in the vital Tanguy literature, published in 1963. | | The acquisition of the work from California-based Stendahl Galleries, circa 1949-1950, by the family demonstrated a clairvoyant appreciation for the bold, cutting-edge output of the French modernists. Privately selling Je tourne la tête vers moi for a brief time in the 1970s, only to buy the work back in 1980 after finding it impossible to live without, demonstrates the true appreciation the owners had for this stunning painting on an art historical level and, more importantly, a deeply sentimental one. | | A scrupulous, reverential craftsman working in his spotless studio, Tanguy only painted when the spirit moved him, and resented the idea of painting out of necessity, or changing one's style to fit within a certain mold. As such, Tanguy's canvases are uniquely original, highly coveted, and rarely seen at auction. The provenance of this work underscores the inventive spirit and unconventional freedom at the heart of Yves Tanguy's artistic practice and, serving as an exquisite manifesto of surrealist aesthetics with great purity of execution, Bonhams is honored to platform Je tourne la tête vers moi's auction debut.

Barnett, Kandinsky, Watercolours, Catalogue Raisonné, Vol. II, 1922-1944, New York, 1994, no. 876 (illustration of the artist's sketch in the handlist p. 223). | | | For Wassily Kandinsky, art was always invention. His exacting artistic practice, particularly bolstered during his time at the Bauhaus (1922-1932) in Germany, was wholly in service of the realization of a 'science of art'. This theory, informed by psychological study and structural exactitude, was grounded in his belief that energy, movement, and rhythm enlivened one's perception of fundamental pictorial elements, thus triggering an inner resonance or spiritual vibration that could evoke an innately powerful emotional response. Lila, executed in 1928, masterfully illustrates the apogee of Kandinsky's realization of a universal order of harmony. Bold in its radiant coloring and rhythmic interplay of forms, this highly finished work on paper is a stunning exemplar of the transcendent elegance and explosive dynamism characteristic of Kandinsky's Bauhaus years. | | While Kandinsky created watercolor works throughout his career, it was only in later years that the medium began to assume a more prominent role in the artist's oeuvre. Previously used as preliminary studies considered supplemental to his paintings, it was not until his time at the Bauhaus that Kandinsky, feeling empowered to expand upon his means of expression, began to consider watercolors as individual works in their own right. From 1924 onwards, his watercolors were all assigned unique titles, no longer simply 'Entwurf zu' (Study of) or 'Projekt für' (Project for), these works now became 'Aglow' and 'Now Upwards!', giving them elevated status amongst his output. Accordingly, Kandinsky's use of the watercolor medium steadily increased throughout the decade; compared to the only twenty-five oil paintings created in 1928, he produced over a hundred watercolors, illustrating a voracious appetite for the medium. Elevated in their degrees of explicitness and elaboration, Kandinsky transcended the material limitations of oil in favor of the elusive qualities inherent in watercolor. | | The soft tonal shifts and slight gradations in coloration across the fine violet mist of the present work's compositional surface speak to Kandinsky's use of the 'Spritztechnik,' an airbrush-esque technique the artist first used in 1927 after it was introduced to him by friend and Bauhaus neighbor Paul Klee. An iconic component of his handling in many of works on paper from 1928-1930, Kandinsky's Spritztechnik created delicate transparencies that imbued his compositions with a more cosmic dimension, reflecting a newfound layer of atmospheric depth within the space as geometric elements hover and glide atop the surface. The present work's bold lilac coloring, pulsating with energy, has been understood as a distant memory of Kandinsky's Russian origins and the colors of Eastern cultures. The soft, sprayed application of modulated color in Lila collides abruptly with the precise geometric elements and boldly rendered lines: manipulating a continuous interplay between the spontaneous and the controlled. | | The present work's abstract arrangement of geometric forms is brimming with pictorial significance. Kandinsky, who believed in the expressive response evoked by the tension, contrasts, and consonance of forms, sought to create a world of heightened differentiation. It was his belief that the combination of circle and triangle created the most evocative juxtaposition, as it exemplified the power of abstract forms and their symphonic expression. He assigned profound spiritual and emotional meaning to the triangle, viewing it not merely as a geometric form, but as a visionary symbol of humanity's ascendent spiritual movement. In relation to the triangle, charged in the center of the pictorial space with connotations of significance, the present work's composition contains an extraordinary series of interactions between smaller triangles and circles, rectilinear shapes, and reverberating clusters of lines. The angular, zig-zagging lines piercing through the assemblage of circles, triangles, and curvilinear forms in Lila resemble jagged bolts of lightning – a visual link to the cosmos, symbolic of a higher order, power, and divine punishment. A carefully selected theater of opposing forces, the present work's dramatic contrasts and bold forms dominate the composition: a tour de force of Kandinsky's abstract language. | | Lila, brimming with explosive tension and a taut dynamism, presents the culmination of Kandinsky's pictorial achievement, attesting to the unique creative vision and innovative spirit of this seminal artist of the modern era. Kandinsky's faith in the power of line, color, and form is intuited through the profound lyricism of the work, fulfilling the artist's oft-stated desire for his compositions to become complete worlds in and of themselves. Through symbolism, these worlds express a newer, truer reality than is familiar to us. The individual forms, lines, and colors in Lila do not deign to have a direct association with figurative reality, but, when combined, their abstract forms are endowed with a pictorial significance that conveys an underlying energy and universal order of harmony. | | Lila was acquired by the esteemed art collector and dealer Emilie Esther Scheyer - commonly referred to by the moniker 'Galka' - shortly after its execution, in July 1928. Appearing in the opening provenance of some of the century's finest examples of European modernism, Scheyer was a tireless promoter of the genre and played an integral role in the American reception of the artist group 'The Blue Four', which comprised Lyonel Feininger, Paul Klee, Alexej von Jawlensky, and Wassily Kandinsky himself. A major factor in Scheyer's development of the group's success in the States were the travelling exhibitions that she organized, which began in the late 1920s. The present work was included in some of these opening exhibitions before ultimately being acquired by Charlotte Mack in 1931. Acquired from her by the family of the present owner and known only to Vivian Endicott Barnett from the artist's handlist illustration, Lila has not been seen in public since 1931 and comes to auction for the very first time. |

Sale, Germany. | Private collection, Germany. | Sale: Phillips de Pury & Company, New York, Contemporary Art I, May 12, 2005, Lot 45. | Private collection, US. | Acquired from the above by the present owner. | | Exhibited | Paris, Galerie Thaddaeus Ropac, Andy Warhol: The Statue of Liberty, March 6 - April 7, 1999, no. 25 (exh. cat., illustrated n.p.). | | | Painted the year before his death, Andy Warhol's Statue of Liberty marks one of the last great declarations of the master Pop artist's career. This synthetic polymer and acrylic painting is one in a larger series that captures a pivotal moment of renewal, turning his brush to one of the great American symbols in a swan song moment. An icon of American liberty and its vainglorious place amongst the global community, there are fewer images that conjure the American spirit as intensely as the visage of Lady Liberty. Warhol's rendition, emerging through an energetic script of verdigris and inky black, provides us with an unfinished monument; an examination of a national-cultural symbol. | | In the mid-1980s, Warhol had returned to creating entirely hand-painted canvases, a process reminiscent of his early years, while continuing a parallel practice of his signature silkscreen technique. His revived interest in a more manual approach coincided with a broader resurgence of gestural easel painting in the booming New York art scene. It was during that period that Swiss dealer Bruno Bischofberger initiated a high-profile collaboration between Warhol and two of the era's rising stars, Jean-Michel Basquiat and Francesco Clemente. The partnership proved especially fruitful between Warhol and Basquiat, inspiring a refreshed painterly energy in Warhol's solo production. The younger artist introduced him to the oil stick, prompting his embrace of expressive, hand-drawn elements, visible here in the loose handling of paint. | | As a former graphic artist, Warhol immediately understood the power of a distinctive visual symbol that spoke to larger cultural mores, from the Hollywood celebrity to Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper to the dollar sign. The Statue of Liberty—which fit very well in this category—was not a new subject for Warhol. He had first explored it in 1962, basing a series of prints on a postcard image of the monument. The fact that it made a return to his oeuvre in 1986 should not be surprising, considering the statue's omnipresence in the public imagination exactly one hundred years after the statue's arrival in New York from France as a diplomatic gift. Recently restored to celebrate its centennial, new color photographs of the statue proliferated in print magazines, newspapers, and tourist memorabilia. The incessant press coverage fit perfectly with one of the artist's trademark fascinations. Warhol was deeply invested in the social effects of this kind of media saturation, particularly the way that the repeated mechanical reproduction of an image—of a person or a symbol—changes our understanding of that very subject as something degraded and disconnected from its original source. | | One such place where Lady Liberty's face appeared was on a commemorative tin of Fabis brand French cookies that inspired this painting's composition. At the lower left, Warhol painted the word "Fabis" in bubble letters, and above it, the tagline "les bons biscuits" ("the good cookies"). The American and French flags that appeared behind the logo of the souvenir tin allude to the statue's origin and remind the public of the values of freedom and democracy shared between the two nations. | | The origins of this image in such a mass culture product perfectly align with the artist's lifelong preoccupation with the rampant commercialism of twentieth century capitalist society and its connection to symbolic abstractions of American moral principles. In many ways, this late work can be seen as a bookend to his career, evoking the hand-painted process and use of a brand logo that featured in his breakthrough 1962 Ferus Gallery show of 32 Campbell's Soup Cans in Los Angeles. Warhol's choice of a greenish hue, recalling the oxidized copper of the original monument sets it apart from other versions in this series, including silkscreens in varied palettes and camouflage motifs. Other examples from this late series are held in major public collections, including The Broad in Los Angeles and The Andy Warhol Museum in Pittsburgh.

provenance: Private collection, US (acquired directly from the artist). | Acquired from the above by the present owner. | | | | Few artists have mapped the mythology of American aspiration with as much wit and profundity as Richard Prince. In Mustang Painting (2014–2016), the artist revisits one of the country's most enduring emblems of freedom and desire: the muscle car. Suspended over a saturated violet ground, the car – an iconic and rare Shelby Mustang GT350 - appears to hover between motion and stillness, its wheels dancing lightly on their tread. At once an image and an apparition, it crystallizes Prince's fascination with the promises and delusions that animate the American dream. | | Prince's career has long been entwined with the visual rhetoric of advertising and desire. Beginning in the late 1970s with his now-canonical Cowboys and Girlfriends series, he appropriated mass-media imagery to expose the coded fantasies underpinning masculinity, sexuality, and success. The muscle car entered his iconography as a natural extension of these themes: a fetish object of autonomy and performance, and a proxy for identity itself. In Mustang Painting, Prince reanimates that motif not through direct quotation from an advertisement, but through an image already mediated by the screen and the printer. The result is both painterly and mechanical, a composition whose digital inkjet underlayer is inflected with visceral streaks of acrylic paint, bridging the distance between the seductive gloss of commerce and the expressive force of painting. | | The Mustang, of course, bears its own cultural meaning. Launched in 1964 as the sports car for a newly mobile middle class, it was designed to embody youth, rebellion, and self-invention. Here, it menaces with an unnatural intensity, rendered in the synthetic hues of a dream sequence. Yellows and electric blues that dissolve into the royal violet of the background. The car is less an object than an attitude, an avatar of speed and seduction suspended in painterly limbo. | | Prince's hybrid process reflects his ongoing dialogue with the traditions of Pop. Like Warhol before him, he understands that the image is never neutral; yet unlike Warhol, Prince allows the image to reassert the hand of the artist amid the mechanics of reproduction. The inkjet transfer and Prince's overpainting blurs authorship and authenticity. | | Occupying a commanding scale that recalls the monumental proportions of roadside billboards, its single, central subject radiates an almost devotional focus. The Mustang here is not merely an icon of mid-century Americana but a mirror for the spectator's own projections of power and freedom. Prince's art has always courted this ambiguity, the fine line between critique and complicity, between desire and disillusion. | | Mustang Painting stands as a late meditation on the mirage of freedom that defines the American image world. It is a painting about velocity and stasis. Within its vivid field of color and glare, Prince distills half a century of American dreaming into a single, dazzling pause.

In the lineage of Duchamp, who famously remarked that the viewer completes the work of art, Gonzalez-Torres work invites the viewer into an individualized experience with art, one in which they actively participate in his works' meanings. "Untitled" (Last Light) is a hallmark piece within one of the artist's most recognizable and captivating bodies of work, the light strings. These works can be installed in different configurations by the owner or exhibitor each time they are shown; their choices of configuration complete the work. Whenever a bulb burns out, it must be promptly replaced, perhaps instilling a potential for continual renewal that is both actual and metaphorical. (The work can also be exhibited with all the bulbs turned off.) Though the work resembles standard and widely available string lights, to experience Gonzalez-Torres' light strings is an emotive experience that can elicit a wide range of associations and interpretations. | | The first work that utilized light bulbs as a material, "Untitled" (March 5th) #2 (1991), was made the same year that Gonzalez-Torres lost his partner, Ross Laycock, to HIV/AIDS, and the parenthetical portion of this work's title references Laycock's birthday. In considering the late artist's personal memory, the utilization of light bulbs as a material could be an allusion to the practice of lighting a candle in remembrance of a lost one. Andrea Rosen, Gonzalez-Torres' longtime gallerist, has remarked on the importance of political and social theories, philosophical and psychological writings, the history of artistic and conceptual movements, as well as the artist's own experience – including his childhood in Cuba in the development of his visual index. Mentioning stories Gonzalez-Torres would recount to her of how the doorways to small stores were lined with strings of light." ('"Untitled" The Neverending Portrait', Felix Gonzalez-Torres, Ostfildern-Ruit, 1997, p. 58). Yet as memories can be nonlinear and accumulate into a palimpsest of experiences, the light string works also evoke travel and the artist's memories of spending time in Paris – the city of lights. | | Assembled from prefabricated everyday materials, the replaceability of the material in Gonzalez-Torres' work expresses an idea central to Conceptual art practices: with a devaluation of the material qualities of the work it is not the materiality of the object itself but rather the meanings behind the work which gives it value. Composed of twenty-four light bulbs, with bulbs placed at six-inch intervals, on twenty-four-foot-long cords,"Untitled" (Last Light) is one of twenty-four light string works the artist made, and one of only two examples from the series which are editioned pieces. "Untitled" (Last Light) is in an edition of twenty-four with 6 Artist Proofs. | | Numbers appear throughout Gonzalez-Torres' works; as the artist himself remarks in an interview with Tim Rollins: "I do like uncanny numbers. Things happen to me around certain numbers: 5, 24, 12... If the piece is about something that is very distant to me, then numbers like 17, 35, and 21 sound perfect because they are numbers that I would never use for anything except for a piece that is very uncomfortable" (the artist in Bill Bartman, ed., Felix Gonzalez-Torres, New York, 1993, p. 8). Despite wanting the viewer to create meaning for themselves, unlike the Minimalists Gonzalez-Torres did not deny the subjectiveness of experience as well as how the context in which a work is exhibited inevitably has an effect on the work. As the artist explains in the same interview with Tim Rollins, "Forms gather meaning from the historical moment.....But after twenty years of feminist discourse and feminist theory we have come to realize that "just looking" is not just looking but that looking is invested with identity: gender, socioeconomic status, race, sexual orientation... Looking is invested with lots of other texts"(ibid.). | | Time is a recurring theme within Gonzalez-Torres' oeuvre. Here, the twenty-four bulbs may represent each hour of the day. . This work operates similarly to his iconic 1987-1990 work, "Untitled" (Perfect Lovers) —where two identical commercial clocks are installed side by side, initially set to the same time, yet will invariably fall out of sync. In the light strings works, sooner or later a bulb will burn out which must promptly be replaced. Both of these works can function on a similar metaphorical apparatus, whereby the work could alludes to the cycle of life and death, day and night, temporality and loss, celebration and mourning. But perhaps most crucially, rebirth and renewal, as the owner or installer must actively replace any bulb that burns out. | | Like Dan Flavin, Gonzalez-Torres chose for almost all his works to be "Untitled" – specifically enclosed in quotation marks reflecting the hierarchies embedded in language, broadening the work's interpretive possibilities. Also like in Dan Flavin's work, many of Gonzalez-Torres' works (including most of the light string works ) carry a parenthetical title. In looking at the parenthetical text chosen for this piece, "Last Light" may reference twilight, suggesting that while daylight is still present the night will soon come. In this way, "Untitled" (Last Light) — which when interpreted as the nineteenth work in the series, or 7pm if one is interpreting it within the twenty-four hours in a day— may also be a reference to or acknowledgement of mortality, perhaps of oneself, a friend or loved one, or of Gonzalez-Torres. Having watched his own partner succumb to HIV/AIDS and he would also pass away due to complications relating to the disease three years later. | | Yet despite the prevalence of death, degradation, and endings in his work, they nonetheless also hold an utter optimism in the potential to make something of remaining time, and a hopefulness that exists with the possibility for rebirth. As an edition, carrying the concept of, multiplicity, perhaps "Untitled" (Last Light) also alludes to a sense of infinity, the sunrise and the sunset, or the cycle of life where life and death are infinitely connected. With this cycle, time becomes infinite again. | | As Rosen explains, "In confronting Ross' death, Felix was also confronting his own, and with the full extent of his desire for life... It is extremely clear that Felix focused on creating systems to ensure that the works did not disappear permanently... What emerges is that the work is less about the self-aggrandizing implications of immortality than the desire for the continuation of life... The idea of life lived to its fullest propelled Felix" (Ibid., p. 44). If the nature of all art is, as González-Torres believed, fundamentally political, then his political stance was to render agency back to the viewer or installer as a symbol for the agency they can take to construct meaning in their own lives or the world around them. "So, in his gentle and generous way" Rosen goes on, "Felix created structures that subtly but actively lead the viewer, and more particularly, the owner through the revelatory process of freedom of choice and possibility of influence through choice" (Ibid., p. 57). | | With seven of the twenty-four editions held in prestigious museum collections worldwide, including the Art Institute of Chicago; the Centre Pompidou in Paris; Harvard Art Museums, Cambridge; the Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles; The Israel Museum, Jerusalem; the Walker Art Museum, Minneapolis and The National Museum of Art, Osaka, it is no question that "Untitled" (Last Light) is recognized as a defining work of contemporary art.

Herkenhoff, et al., Cildo Meireles, London, 1999 (illustrated p. 18). | | | "For me the art object must, despite everything else, be instantly seductive; it cannot work without that seductive involvement... If something has sufficient poetic power to be considered as an art object, it should be comprehensible to anyone, without the provision of extra information. This is why I try to make art which has that level of communication and immediacy." | - Cildo Meireles | | | Bridging Brazil's Neo-Concretist and Conceptual art practices, Cildo Meireles is one of the most respected Latin American artists of the latter half of the twentieth century. Known for his ambitious and extraordinarily diverse practice, which comprises drawing, sculpture, installation and performance via a wide array of media, Meireles sought to challenge the concepts and structures we assume and take for granted. With a philosophical and sometimes political modus operandi, his questions range from the metaphysical to the social, emphasizing themes that includes space and time, the art object, as well as economic, social and hierarchical systems and beliefs. As Brazilian curator Paulo Herkenhoff writes, "throughout the work of Cildo Meireles, there is a constant manifestation of tension and torsion––whether in the realms of aesthetics, perception, science or economics. Centering on our experience of these different branches of knowledge, his art aims to generate new meaning through recognition of the limits and fallibility of these systems of understanding." (Paulo Herkenhoff, "A Labyrinthine Ghetto: The Work of Cildo Meireles," Cildo Meireles, London, 1999, p. 38). | | Inmensa encompasses Meireles' aim of creating work that proposes reflection and questioning in the viewer both through a poetic-artistic language and an economy of means. Comprising the work is a combination of simple domestic objects, specifically five wooden tables and three wooden chairs. These everyday objects are subverted from their everyday functionality, in this transformation becoming an impractical and illogical structure. Combined, this assemblage becomes a quasi–architectural form –– heightening the arbitrary nature of the structure that could have been arranged in myriad ways. For Meireles, the use of everyday objects as material was key to achieving art which manages to interrogate many ideas at once while remaining accessible and therefore more powerful. "What interested me was the double character... one object could simultaneously engage on two levels, both within and outside an art-historical definition of the art object," Meireles says in an interview with curator Gerardo Mosquera. (Ibid., p. 13). | | Most notably, however, it is a construction in which the smallest tables and smallest chair support the largest, eliciting a poignant visual metaphor for a social structure where the working class sustains the power and weight of the ruling elite. Executed in 1982, Inmensa was created in the wake of Meireles' most political period and served as a discreet response to the dynamics of power that played out during the Brazilian military dictatorship of 1964-1985. The regime was known for its oppressive human rights abuses which included censorship, torture, and forced disappearances, and was supported by conservative sectors such as the Catholic Church and anti-communist sectors of the middle and upper classes. Many artists––including some from the famed Neo-Concretism movement, including Lygia Clark and Helio Oiticica––could not avoid making art in response to such urgency. Meireles himself has remarked on artmaking during the period, saying: "some Brazilians felt obliged to make compromising political work at that time, even if their actual artistic and intellectual interests were apolitical, as mine were" (Ibid., p.15) | | In Latin, in mensa means "over the table," while in various modern languages, it either directly signifies or is close to the word "immense." This can also be read to describe the sense of overwhelming weight these larger components subject the smaller ones to, and their corresponding significance in real world hierarchies. Though Inmensa's components are firmly constructed together and thus appear challenging to move or theoretically deconstruct, his chosen composition keeps their apparent modularity at the forefront. It is this which conjures possibility and alternative modes of thinking in the viewer, and which the work universally appealing. As curator and writer Maaretta Jaukkuri writes of Meireles' practice, "today, we know better than ever that the banality of cruelty is no local issue. There [Meireles'] works share the quality of wishing to go beyond the metaphor in order to participate in real life processes... His means of expression... are at the same time local and global, timely and untimely, and their target is a sense of commonality, the beauty and pain of being a human being both at this specific time, and in the continuum of memories and history" (M. Jaukkuri, "To be curved with the eyes," Cildo Meireles, London, 2008, p. 36).

S.2393 (another cast illustrated p. 162; marble version illustrated p. 163). | C. Farge, B. Garnier & I. Jenkins, Rodin and the Art of Ancient Greece, exh. cat., The British Museum, London, 2018, no. 40 (marble version illustrated on p. 105). | | | Among the pantheon of Auguste Rodin's masterpieces, Le Baiser (The Kiss) stands as one of the most celebrated icons of modern sculpture, its fame rivalled only by that of Le Penseur (The Thinker). A consummate embodiment of sensuality and emotional truth, Le Baiser captures love at its inception; an instant suspended between innocence and abandon. The work's timeless appeal lies in its duality: at once tender and erotic, idealized and modern, it crystallizes Rodin's unrivalled ability to sculpt passion in motion. | | The story that inspired this immortal embrace originates in Canto V of Dante Alighieri's Inferno (c. 1321), which recounts the tragic tale of Francesca da Rimini and her husband's brother, Paolo Malatesta. While reading the romance of Guinevere and Lancelot together, the pair realize their own forbidden love; their first kiss, born of literary temptation, seals their fate. Discovered by Francesca's husband Gianciotto, they are murdered mid-embrace and condemned to the second circle of Hell, reserved for sins of the flesh. It was this fatal union—where passion and damnation meet—that first stirred Rodin's imagination. | | Rodin initially conceived Le Baiser as part of La Porte de l'Enfer (The Gates of Hell), the monumental bronze portal commissioned by the French government in 1880 as a sculptural interpretation of Dante's Inferno. The lovers appeared on the lower left panel of Rodin's third and final terracotta maquette, described by critic Octave Mirbeau in La France (1885). Modelled in the round and later attached to the plaster panels, their embrace was, however, deemed too tender for the cataclysmic drama of La Porte. Around 1887 Rodin removed them, replacing the group with a more tormented version, Paolo et Francesca. Yet rather than abandon the figures, he recognized their independent power and developed the composition into a freestanding sculpture—exhibited in plaster at the Brussels Salon of 1887 and later that year in bronze at Galerie Georges Petit, Paris—under the title Le Baiser. | | The original Le Baiser measured approximately 85 centimeters in height, but following its critical success in Brussels and Paris, the French state commissioned a monumental marble version in 1888, enlarged to roughly 190 centimeters. Rodin labored on this marble for a decade; unveiled at the Paris Salon of 1898, it caused a sensation. Viewers were captivated, even shocked, by the idealization and sensuality of the intertwined nudes. As contemporary critics observed, the sculpture's frank eroticism and palpable humanity signalled a break from classical restraint. Romantic love and sexuality—central to Rodin's oeuvre—were here presented without moral filter, elevated instead to the realm of the eternal. | | While Le Baiser shares thematic kinship with Rodin's other explorations of the embrace, such as L'Éternel Idole and L'Éternel Printemps, no other work so perfectly captures the dawning of desire. In Dante's text, Paolo initiates the kiss; in Rodin's re-imagining, Francesca rises toward him, her body alive with agency and anticipation. Her right leg drapes over his, a gesture of confident surrender, as she draws his head gently toward her own. Paolo, by contrast, hesitates, his left hand still cradling the book that has slipped open upon his knee, the page bent beneath the weight of their union. His other hand rests delicately upon Francesca's thigh, the fingertips expressing both passion and restraint. Their lips barely touch; the moment is one heartbeat before consummation, frozen forever at the precipice of love. | | Art historian Albert Elsen observed, "The whole impression ... is one of Paolo's slowly eroding resolve and awakening desire" (A. Elsen, Rodin's Art, Oxford, 2003, p. 211). Indeed, Rodin achieves here what few sculptors before him dared: the rendering of psychological and physical awakening in marble and bronze. Every curve and surface radiates emotion; flesh breathes, stone trembles. | | In 1898, to meet the mounting demand from collectors worldwide, Rodin authorized the celebrated Barbédienne foundry to produce bronze editions of Le Baiser in four reductions, 25 cm, 38 cm, 60 cm and 73 cm, retaining for himself the right to cast the full-scale version. The present example, cast between circa 1914 and 1918 by Gustave Leblanc-Barbédienne, belongs to the second reduction, the larger of the two 60 cm domestic-scale casts. This size, with its commanding yet intimate presence, is widely considered the most balanced and harmonious of the reductions, preserving the expressive force of the original while allowing it to inhabit the refined spaces of the modern interior. | | The bronze's surface, softly modelled and alive with Rodin's tactile energy, invites the viewer's gaze to linger. Light glides across the forms as if caressing skin, animating every subtle shift of muscle and curve. The composition's modernity lies not only in its realism but in its psychological immediacy: Rodin transforms myth into human truth, passion into permanence. | | When Le Baiser first appeared in marble, critics' responses oscillated between awe and scandal. To some, the lovers' nakedness seemed audacious; to others, it revealed a new ideal of beauty freed from academic constraint. In this tension, between propriety and passion, Rodin's genius resides. As with Antonio Canova's Psyche Revived by Cupid's Kiss (1787-1793) - held in the Louvre museum since 1824 - which had enchanted early-nineteenth-century audiences, Le Baiser reignited the Romantic fascination with love's divine folly. Yet where Canova offered mythic idealisation, Rodin presented carnal truth. His lovers are not gods but mortals, their joy and doom inseparable, their kiss both sacred and profane. | | Originally conceived as a tragedy within The Gates of Hell, the scene might once have been read as a warning against desire; an allegory of impulsive sin. Yet Rodin's reimagining transforms the narrative entirely. By extracting Paolo and Francesca from the infernal context and enlarging their moment of passion into a self-contained work, he suspends judgment itself. The lovers are no longer punished; they are redeemed through the eternalization of their love. Rodin solidifies not their doom but their joy, capturing a rapture that transcends consequence. | | Today, Le Baiser endures as an emblem of Romantic love, of beauty, resilience, and hope. The 60 cm second reduction encapsulates the essence of Rodin's achievement: a sculpture at once monumental in spirit and intimate in scale, capable of expressing universal desire within a domestic setting. In its presence, time seems to halt; the lovers remain forever poised at the brink of union, untouched by the tragedy that awaits them beyond the moment. | | Through Le Baiser, Rodin distilled the very essence of passion: raw yet refined, temporal yet eternal. It is a triumph of modernity and emotion, where love, unburdened by fate, exists purely for itself: an eternal present in bronze.

provenance: Estate of the artist. | Robert Miller Gallery, New York. | Acquired from the above by the present owner. | | Exhibited | New York, Robert Miller Gallery, March 11 - April 12, 1997 (exh. cat., illustrated p. 74). | Washington D.C., National Museum of Women in the Arts, Alice Neel's Women, October 28 - January 15, 2006, pl. 17 (exh. cat., illustrated p. 40). | | | | "I do not pose my sitters. I do not deliberate and then concoct... Before painting, when I talk to the person, they unconsciously assume their most characteristic pose, which in a way involves all their character and social standing - what the world has done to them and their retaliation." | – Alice Neel | | | Executed in 1930, Fanya is a powerful and intimate early portrait by Alice Neel and notably one of the earliest canvas portraits by the artist ever to appear at auction. The painting depicts Fanya Foss, a close friend of Neel's and a figure who would go on to have a celebrated career as a Hollywood screenwriter active between the 1940s and 1960s. The two women met in 1927, when Neel had just arrived in the city after her studies at the Philadelphia School of Design for Women. Searching for stability, Neel took a job at Foss's Greenwich Village bookstore, and their bond soon became an important part of the artist's early New York life. Their friendship was one of mutual admiration and intellectual exchange. Foss, a politically engaged writer with literary ambitions, encouraged Neel's growing sense of artistic and feminist independence. "Foss typified the intellectuals to whom Neel was attracted...In her two portraits of Foss, Neel expresses both admiration and annoyance...In the painting, her friend poses in a demure, unassuming manner" (C. Carr, Alice Neel: Woman, New York, 2002, p. 6). | | The sitter's composed yet emotionally charged presence is emblematic of Neel's extraordinary ability to fuse psychological depth with painterly directness. Foss sits in a soft lounge chair, an elemental motif that recurs throughout her oeuvre, functioning as both a stage and a silent witness to the lives she portrayed. Underscoring the formal and symbolic importance of this device within her practice, the chair serves as not merely a seat but a psychological anchor - a space of containment and endurance. Its iconography would follow Neel throughout her career, culminating decades later in Dr. Finger's Waiting Room, the empty chair painting that now holds her auction record, | | The year 1930 was one of profound personal crisis for Neel as it was the year her husband, Cuban painter Carlos Enríquez, left for Havana with their young daughter. This loss marked Neel deeply and that summer she threw herself into painting before suffering a devastating mental breakdown leading to a period of hospitalization. The emotional weight of this moment; grief, abandonment, and inner turmoil is palpable in Fanya. The sitter's distant, almost guarded gaze and the quiet tension of her pose mirror the artist's own psychological state during this pivotal year. Her teal dress forms a rhythmic cascade of curves that contrasts with the strength of her posture while the gesture of her hands conveys both composure and unease. The sorrow and dislocation of that period seep into Fanya in her quiet restraint, the melancholy color palette, and the air of suspension all seem to mirror the artist's own fragile state of mind. "Fanya in 1930 holds a slim hand against her chest and stares at the viewer, as if to say, 'Why am I myself? And why do you look at me?' Repose and denial of the sitter: Fanya will next say, 'No, you don't mean 'me.' I am not entirely or only myself.' And yet notice how regally – with what sublime sufferance -- she permits the viewer to doom her to portraitures apparatus" (W. Koestenbaum, Alice Neel: Paintings from the Thirties, Robert Miller 1997, p. 3). | | Fanya Foss would remain a resonant figure in Neel's imagination. She reappears in The Intellectual (1930), a related work on paper that was featured in the recent traveling retrospective organized by The Metropolitan Museum of Art in 2021, underscoring the significance of this early subject in Neel's portraiture. Together, these two works encapsulate Neel's fascination with women of intellect and conviction who, like herself, challenged the confines of gender and social expectation. Fanya not only captures a formative friendship but also embodies the raw, searching quality that defined Neel's most affecting works. | | With emotional depth, compositional clarity, and profound biographical resonance, Fanya stands as a landmark in Neel's early development, offering a deeply personal window into Neel's artistic and emotional landscape at a critical juncture in her life. It reveals the artist at a moment of personal upheaval yet remarkable creative clarity, transforming private struggle into enduring her practice- a powerful precursor to the fearless, incisive portraiture that would cement her place as one of the most important American painters of the 20th century.

A trailblazer in her field with countless professional accomplishments, Tucker was also a staunch supporter of the Civil Rights and Women's movements. Amongst her many notable accolades, including holding two Ph.Ds. (one in Education and one in Professional Psychology) Tucker served as the commissioner of several city departments and was the president of the California Psychology Association. Moreover, she helped found the Los Angeles Black Women's Forum and was on the board of the Westside Women's Clinic. Tucker was an active, passionate, and beloved contributor to her community, much like Ernie Barnes who was a close friend of hers. | | The present work portrays an intimate moment that is both grand and quiet. The house in the background, an iconic motif of Barnes' most successful basketball paintings, pays homage to his upbringing in North Carolina. At a time when minimalism and pure abstraction prevailed, Rothenberg reintroduced the figure - specifically, the horse - as a vehicle for exploring the relationship between image, gesture, and form. Rendered in a simple palette and characterized by rough, expressive brushwork, these monumental compositions balance the formal concerns of abstraction with the immediacy of figuration. The horse, abstracted and removed from narrative context, functions less as a literal subject than as an emblem of energy and presence - an exploration of motion through the medium of paint. By combining material intensity with symbolic depth, Rothenberg brought new vitality to painting, uniting the clarity of conceptual art with the emotional force of expressive gesture. Mares and Foals revisits the iconic imagery that established Rothenberg's reputation, recontextualizing it within the landscape and rhythms of her later life in New Mexico. | | In the early 1990s, Susan Rothenberg relocated from New York to a ranch in Galisteo, New Mexico, marking a new chapter in both her life and artistic practice. "It felt like a completely different situation—the light, the space of the landscape. Everything was different. It seemed like I needed to make a new start," she later reflected (quoted in M. Auping, Susan Rothenberg: Moving In Place, Fort Worth, 2009, p. 19). Although several aspects of her work evolved - most notably her expanded use of color and the integration of human figures into her works - the fundamental character of her paintings remained. Life in New Mexico merged the restlessness of Rothenberg's inner world with the unpredictability of rural experience, particularly the spirited behavior of the animals surrounding her studio. This environment inspired an extended series of works depicting rabbits, horses, dogs, goats, and snakes. The dynamic, rotating spatial compositions she had long cultivated proved ideally suited to portraying scenes of movement and interaction among multiple figures. | | Rothenberg's years in New Mexico revitalized her artistic practice, prompting her to once again draw on her enduring ability to challenge and expand painterly conventions through her distinctive approach to pictorial space and her nuanced exploration of light, color, form, and movement. Mares and Foals, which portrays a tender moment between mother and child, revisits the bold color and monumental scale of her early horse paintings, filtered through a more introspective and personal lens. The work reflects on the fragility of life, serving as a meditation on memory, stillness, and the threshold between worlds. | | "It was important that I was painting something that was alive. I didn't want to paint something inanimate. It needed to have flesh and spirit. I guess I wanted to paint the kind of energy you find in the real world rather than the abstract world" (quoted in Ibid., p. 13).

Wiener, Walton Ford: Pancha Tantra, Cologne, 2015 (illustrated pp. 76-77). | | | | Celebrated for his timeless and elegant draftsmanship, Walton Ford's Chingado is a provocative and monumental watercolor that blurs the lines between realism and fantasy, past and present, beauty and violence. Ford is a contemporary master of the natural history painting genre, drawing on traditional animal subjects in allegorical dramas to reveal the impact of humans and globalization on the natural world. Widely exhibited and often cited, Chingado is a quintessential example of Ford's compelling subversion of the visual language of natural history painting. | | Ten years after its creation, Ford described the Chingado as a disturbed scene from the imagination of a "delirious Audubon...or Akeley" (quoted in F. Hirsch, 'King of the Beasts [Walton Ford]', Art in America, Volume 96, Issue 9, October 2008). In the early 1990s, he began incorporating the imagery of nineteenth-century naturalists John James Audubon and Carl Akeley, whose paintings and dioramas remain important sources of inspiration. Ford skillfully leverages the life-size scale, lush landscapes, and meticulous details of the natural history painting genre, appropriating its visual appeal with a critical eye that reveals its layered historical and intellectual context. | | It is evident in his naturalistic treatment of animals and dynamic compositional framing that Ford pulls from an array of art historical references from the Old Masters to French Romanticism, channeling classical scenes of warfare or hunting such as Sir Peter Paul Rubens' The Tiger Hunt. One among a series of hunting scenes Rubens painted between 1614-1616, this work depicts a vicious power struggle between man and beast in a swirling storm of chaos. | | Ford distills Rubens' complex web of focal lines down to the two key visual elements of Chingado in a compelling energetic arrangement. In Rubens' example, the composition explodes in all directions with animal and human limbs bisecting each other. The tiger overtakes a defenseless man on horseback, its claws and powerful jaws sinking into the man's flesh, while shielding a tigress and her young cubs. In a strikingly similar pose, Ford's jaguar clamps its jaws around the bull's jugular, drawing ruby droplets of blood with its claws. The visual and thematic resonance between these works underscore the eternal and cyclical nature of the conflicts that lie at the bedrock of humanity: man versus man, man versus earth, and man versus beast. | | The work's title translates to fucked in common Mexican vernacular. A contemporary spin on a painting overflowing with historical flare, Ford weaves a complex web of meaning into the present work, illustrating the furious wresting of power from the jaguar, indigenous to the American continent, by the bull imported by Spanish conquistadors. "They're coupling to create Mexico," Ford later reflected (quoted in C. Tomkins, "Man and Beast: The Narrative Art of Walton Ford", The New Yorker, January 2009). | | A complex interrogation of Mexico's founding myths, Chingado excavates layers of conflict between Spanish settlers and Indigenous peoples, collapsing time in this striking metaphor. Through calligraphic texts interspersed in the margins, Ford explicitly asserts continuity between the historical Spanish Conquest of Tenochtitlan and the contemporary Zapatista rebellion in Chiapas. Other stylized inscriptions exemplify Ford's impressive use of diverse sources and sardonic political humor to articulate analogies between the past and present. Passages from the Popol Vuh, the sacred cosmological epic of the Kʼicheʼ Maya people, trace the origins of man. Mayan glyphs correspond to cycles of life and warfare, the latter of which is branded on the bull's flank. An excerpt from historian Enrique Krauze's introduction to Mexico: Biography of Power (1996) conveys the intent behind this perverse allegory: | | It is the beginning of a long history | I undertake to relate to you. | Register it all of you, and let your memory | never permit it to be forgotten. | | Chingado is not only a technical masterpiece of Ford's impressive use of watercolor, but a multilayered and rigorous investigation of colonialism, neoimperialism, and environmental devastation. It encapsulates the artist's breadth of historical knowledge, sharp critical eye, and strength in allegory, reflecting a defining moment in his career when these values came into focus to form the foundation of his ongoing practice. The present lot was included in Ford's Tigers of Wrath: Watercolors by Walton Ford, a midcareer survey presented in 2006 at the Brooklyn Museum, New York and Bestiarium at the Hamburger Bahnhof–Museum für Gegenwart, Berlin in 2010, the artist's first institutional exhibition in Europe. More recently, the Morgan Library & Museum in New York held an exhibition in 2024 in celebration of the artist's gift of 63 sketches and studies to the museum, displayed alongside larger-scale watercolors and selection of works hand-picked by the artist from the permanent collection including prints and drawings by Rembrandt, Dorothea Maria Gsell, Eugène Delacroix, Antoine-Louis Barye, and John James Audubon.
