Adler & Lillian Adler Collection, Cincinnati (acquired from the above on January 3, 1950). | Emma Margaret Goldman Collection, Cincinnati (by descent from the above). | Thence by descent to the present owner. | | | Marc Chagall's Les amoureux is a radiant celebration of one of the artist's most enduring themes: the triumph of love as the ultimate human experience. Executed circa 1938, this romantic composition encapsulates the painter's conviction that love was not merely a subject but the very essence of art itself. As Chagall would later reflect: 'In it lies the true Art: from it comes my technique, my religion... Art, without Love... would open the wrong door' (the artist, quoted in J. Baal-Teshuva (ed.), Chagall: A Retrospective, Westport, 1995, p. 179). Nowhere is this credo more poignantly expressed than in the tender embrace of the figures at the heart of this work, who embody both personal devotion and universal harmony. | | The composition presents a pair of lovers seated on a rustic wooden bench; their forms united in a gesture of profound intimacy. The male figure, rendered in glowing red tones, leans protectively toward his companion, who is enveloped in the serene coolness of blue. The chromatic contrast of their garments - fiery passion tempered by tranquil devotion - creates a visual metaphor for balance within unity. Their faces, softly illuminated and delicately modeled, radiate a serenity that transcends the earthly moment, suggesting that the embrace captures not a fleeting instant but an eternal state of communion. Hovering in the upper left of the composition, an angelic figure reaches forward with an olive branch, blessing the couple with both divine sanction and symbolic peace. The motif recalls biblical messengers and the longstanding artistic tradition of the olive branch as an emblem of hope and reconciliation. Here, the celestial gesture elevates the earthly embrace, transforming a private moment into a vision of universal love. Chagall, who frequently combined personal imagery with spiritual symbolism, succeeds in making his own life's passion - his devotion to his wife Bella - an emblem of love in its most transcendent form. | | The dreamlike palette, dominated by radiant blues and verdant greens, envelops the scene in an atmosphere of otherworldly calm. Although grounded by the bench and the grassy knoll, the figures seem suspended within a realm outside of time. This balance between earthly intimacy and ethereal detachment is characteristic of Chagall's oeuvre, in which lovers soar over rooftops, float among village squares, or, as in Les amoureux, inhabit a serene landscape infused with memory and longing. | | The poignancy of this work is heightened when considered in relation to the circumstances of its creation. Executed in the late 1930s, Les amoureux emerged at a moment of escalating turmoil in Europe. Having been granted French citizenship in 1937, Chagall and his wife Bella settled in the countryside, first in St. Dyé-sur-Loire and later in Gordes, Provence. Yet the world around them was rapidly destabilizing. In May 1940, Germany invaded Belgium and Holland; by June, Paris had fallen. While many contemporaries fled, Chagall hesitated, immersing himself in his work even as the threat to Jewish artists grew dire. It was only through the intervention of Varian Fry and the Emergency Rescue Committee in 1941 that the Chagalls escaped to New York, carrying with them the memory of a Europe they were uncertain to see again. | | In this context, Les amoureux assumes a dual resonance. It is, on one level, a deeply personal tribute to Bella, whose presence animated Chagall's imagination throughout his career. Yet it is also a symbolic refuge, a declaration of love's permanence in the face of dislocation and uncertainty. While war consumed Europe, Chagall's composition affirmed the resilience of human connection. The painting thus embodies both private devotion and a universal message: that love endures, unassailable, even against the backdrop of history's darkest upheavals. | | Chagall's Les amoureux stands as a testament to his singular vision, one in which the intimate and the eternal, the personal and the universal, are seamlessly intertwined. With its vivid colors, poetic symbolism, and profound emotional resonance, the work captures the essence of the artist's lifelong pursuit: to transform memory and emotion into timeless images of love, hope, and transcendence.

Grosz had befriended Craven in the late 1930s, and he made several portrait studies of him. Craven was also very fond of Grosz and included him in his esteemed bestseller A Treasury of Art Masterpieces. From the Renaissance to the Present Day (New York, Simon & Schuster, 1939). Craven selected a watercolor by Grosz from the year 1928 to be reproduced in the book Ein Mann von Überzeugung/Ein Hakenkreuzritter (A Man of Opinion), which today is in the Collection of the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, D.C. | | Thomas Craven, who also promoted other American artists like Thomas Hart Benton, John Stuart Curry and Grant Wood, was, however, a vehement critic of the Paris School. Grosz did not agree with him about this crusade. With fine cynical insinuation, without being offensive, Grosz portrayed Craven in his Christmas card as a fearless dragon-slayer, dressed in medieval costume with his initials 'Th.Cr.' on his doublet. Craven fights the French Dragon, a legendary dragon-like mythological hybrid from Provence in Southern France, but in this case, without any doubt, represents the School of Paris. | | Excerpted text by Ralph Jentsch.

provenance: The artist. | With Kanst Gallery, Los Angeles. | | | Exhibited | Oakland, The Oakland Art Museum, Granville Redmond, 3 December 1988 - 29 January 1989. | Laguna Beach, Laguna Art Museum, Granville Redmond, 9 March - 30 April 1989. | Washington D.C., Gallaudet University, Granville Redmond, July 1989. | | Literature | Alma May Cook, 'Paintings on Show at the Galleries,' Los Angeles Evening Express, 24 August 1907, p. 7. | The Oakland Museum, Granville Redmond, Oakland, pp. 56, 96, no. 21, illustrated. | | Granville Redmond was born in Philadelphia and contracted scarlet fever which robbed him of his hearing before his third birthday. Soon after, his parents moved to San Jose, California, and sent him to a specialized school, the California School for the Education of the Deaf and Dumb, and the Blind, Berkeley, California. This was the first school to nurture his love of art and here he would meet two long term advocates Theophilus Hope d'Estrella and Douglas Tilden. | | Redmond went on to study at the San Francisco School of Design. Counted among his early teachers were Arthur Mathews and Amédée Joullin, both of whom often painted in a similar tonalist style. While training as a painter, Redmond became acquainted with many other artists including Gottardo Piazzoni and Giuseppe Cadenasso. Although Redmond was deaf, it did not hamper his relationships with his fellow artists; his lifelong friend Piazzoni even learned sign language. | | Redmond distinguished himself as an art student and won the W.E. Brown medal of excellence. In 1893 he was awarded a grant from the California School of the Deaf which enabled him to study at the Académie Julian in Paris under Jean Paul Laurens and Benjamin Constant. While in Paris, Redmond quickly distinguished himself once again when his large tonalist canvas, "Matin d'Hiver", was accepted for the Paris Salon in 1895. Unfortunately, his success was not sustained and his subsequent submissions to the Salon were rejected. | | Redmond's artistic vision was expanded in France through formal instruction as well as traveling and painting with fellow artists. Faced with financial distress, he moved in with fellow Californian and friend Gottardo Piazzoni in 1897. The two artists much admired the work of the Barbizon painters, particularly Theodore Rousseau. The Californians painted near Fontainebleau some 70 years after the Barbizon artists made the locale so famous. Rousseau's love of trees and the reverential way he painted trees, like a portrait, resonated with the young Californians. They took his philosophy to heart – quoting to each other Rousseau's phrase: "let us make a man breathe, a tree really vegetate." 1 | | With his goal to earn a medal in the Salon thwarted and a significant amount of debt, Redmond returned to California in 1898 and settled in Los Angeles. His old art teacher Theophilus d'Estrella visited Redmond in Los Angeles in 1899 and wrote about the difficulty Redmond was having in advancing his artistic career. Following d'Estrella's criticisms of Los Angeles as an art market, he went on to compliment Redmond: "He has a fine eye for the beautiful even in homely bits of landscape which might escape the eyes of most persons." 2 Redmond found his life partner and married Carrie Robinson in 1899 and in the ensuing few years finally began to find real success in his career. He was selling paintings, and his reputation was growing. In 1902 d'Estrella -ever Redmond's advocate - wrote that "Finally Fortune had begun to smile." And by June of 1905 Redmond was described by d'Estrella as the "foremost artist of Southern California." | | Following an unsuccessful show in 1907 at Steckel gallery, perhaps due in part to the gallery not being of sufficient size for Redmond's larger scale paintings, Redmond moved his work to the Kanst Art Gallery in Los Angeles. Of the painting "California" on offer, in the Los Angeles Express, Saturday, August 24, 1907, Alma May Cook wrote: "Granville Redmond has recently completed his largest landscape painting which he simply calls a California landscape. It is a scene taken in the arroyo near Pasadena, with "Old Baldy" in the distance. In the middle distance a patch of warm sunshine shows the foreground being in half shadow. The painting is hung in the Kanst gallery." | | To the right of center on the horizon, as Alma points out, is the snowcapped peak of Mt. Baldy standing at 10,064 ft., it is the highest point in Los Angeles. For Redmond it is background to the easily missed drama of contrasting tones on display. The trees on view at the center of the horizon provide the chromatic pop that Redmond would later exploit in his depictions of blooming wildflowers. He relies on the less flashy golden yellows, burnt oranges and bright greens of the foliage to provide the contrast with the green and brown grasses and the sandy tones of the arroyo. | | At the center of the painting is the path across the hill. The path is Redmond's only oblique acknowledgement of humankind in the picture. Like his antecedent Rousseau, Redmond found the trees more fascinating than people. Tellingly, the path leads diagonally toward the compositional center of the painting which contains the commanding presence of a single tree overlooking the landscape. Redmond invests this sentinel with an individual and meditative presence. On the left side stands a grove of trees as a subtle counterweight to the power of the tree on the right – like a large family looking with pride on the prodigal child that has struck out to make their way in the world. | | California shows Redmond obsessing over every inch of the massive canvas. There is a detailed and nuanced attention lavished on the sky. A gradual tonal shift takes place from the upper left to upper right corners across the width of the canvas like a gradual echo of the shaded and brightly lit areas in the landscape. The breadth of sky is such that the viewer almost expects the weather to be different from one side of the painting to the other and Redmond does not disappoint. In addition to the tonal changes, the brushwork in the sky is exceptionally varied. The upper right is largely composed of agitated broad blocks of lighter blue interspersed with small contrasting angled dabs of white. The brush strokes gradually decrease in size, contrasting angles and chromatic variance as the landscape meets the sky in the center and along the left side of the painting. On the right edge of the sky, emphasizing the changing weather, the brush strokes are still quite choppy and diverse with the background color quite visible as the spacing is broader as well. This treatment in the sky acts as yet another device to bring the viewer's eyes to the central figure of the tree. | | Redmond's skill as a colorist and his awe at the beauty of California's landscape are on extravagant display in this painting. The artist evokes a sense of quiet through his restrained use of color. This painting, like a Cathedral, encourages soft voices and contemplation. He did not paint out of instinct alone. He enumerated his philosophy, in part, in the Los Angeles Times in 1906: "Artist is colorblind if they pay too much attention to drawing at color's expense." 3. In a 1929 letter Redmond wrote: "Art after all is useful as well as beautiful. One can use it in life as something very tangible. From it I have learned to observe life and nature—a great teacher if one cares to adapt its teachings." 4. Granville Redmond absorbed the lessons and with this masterful work he teaches the rest of us. | | 1.Scott Shields and Mildred Albronda, Granville Redmond: The Eloquent Palette, Portland Oregon, Pomegranate, 2020, p. 43. | 2. ibid p. 4. | 3. ibid p. 51. | 4. ibid p. 35.

provenance: Private collection, Sebastopol, California. | Private collection, Berkeley, California. | Bonhams, Los Angeles, 25 November 2013, lot 43.  | Acquired by the present owner from the above.  |  |  | Beginning in 1903, Arthur Putnam was commissioned by Edward Willis Scripps to produce a series of large outdoor sculptures in bronze for his Miramar Ranch north of San Diego. Putnam did not work on the commission continuously, as he took a lengthy trip to Europe in 1905. Visits to Rome and Paris, as well as a move to San Francisco, delayed the work. But Putnam again took up the commission in 1907. A number of models were made and a handful of full-size figures were cast. Putnam created two life-size puma casts for Mrs. Scripps. The Scripps family bronzes, Puma with Cub and Puma, were cast in 1911 and 1910 respectively. Each is 38 inches tall with a base that measures 20 x 50 inches. These works are still held by the Scripps family. |  | The works in this lot: Puma with Cub and Puma are comparable works and are of identical subject matter. While the bases are of smaller size (17 x 45 inches) the Pumas themselves are of very similar scale. These bronzes have the best elements of Putnam's work: a deft anatomically accurate depiction of the languid but powerful big cats. As Rose Berry wrote in The American Magazine of Art, May 1929, Putnam's work has an impressionistic looseness; he casts aside all haggling detail, leaving in its place something irresistible, something so full of life, movement and the traits and instincts which make life that his work, once seen, is not to be forgotten (p. 280).

'I tried to put your face on her, but couldn't trust myself to draw the line between reality and imagination.' His affection for Miss Klauber never diminished, for a letter from Grace Storey Putnam to Miss Klauber in 1909 indicates that while finances were at low ebb, Arthur was 'turning out some good things.' In fact, she notes: 'He has just finished a Mermaid (Sphinx) with great lines in it - and the most beautiful swing of muscles I have seen him do yet. The face reminds me a little of you.'" | | "On this minimal evidence, it is presumptuous to assume that this is meant as anything more than a compliment and lasting token, to their friendship. Arthur Brown, one of the architects of the San Francisco Panama-Pacific International Exposition, 1915, used The Mermaid, in the great fountain on the fairgrounds. From a 1915 visit to the San Francisco Exposition, Miss Klauber makes no comment other than mentioning the work in a list of sculptures and their artists that she saw. 'The damned thing disturbs me by thrusting his individual peculiarity between my conception and the work I am doing.' His conceptions were to some degree formed by tradition, and this is particularly true of his sculptures of the human figure. For example, Flying Messenger, ca. 1906 (California Palace Legion of Honor), is borrowed from Rodin's Fugitive Love, 1880-82, while his Mermaid, 1910 (The Oakland Museum), seems directly related to Rodin's Torso of a Woman, 1909. Shields, Armin Hansen, The Artful Voyage, Pasadena Museum of California Art, 2015, p. 169, illustrated. | | The son of prominent 19th Century Western artist Herman Wendleborg Hansen, Armin Hansen was an accomplished painter, etcher and draftsman in his own right. Rather than follow in the Western tradition of his father, the younger Hansen's oeuvre largely focuses on maritime scenes marked by rain-soaked decks, turbulent seas, and weathered fishermen. Yet, allusions to the frontier era remain at the forefront of this work with overlapping themes of hard labor taking place beyond the boundary of civilization. The present lot highlights both the physical and mental rigors of seafaring life that are immediately confronted when crossing the safety of the sand bar into the vast unknown of the open sea. | | Hansen first became acquainted with seafaring culture in his early twenties when he was working aboard a trawler in the North Sea off the Belgian Coast. Scenes from this earlier period in his career are much more tonalist in palette, reminiscent of both the Barbizon School and his contemporaries from his native San Francisco, Xavier Martinez and Gottardo Piazzoni. In these earlier works, gray and brown hues make up overcast skies above Belgian port towns like Nieuwpoort and Ostend. Hansen would spend four years working as a deck hand before returning to Northern California where he settled just south of San Francisco in Monterey. Later Monterey works like the present lot use bolder colors. Here deep shades of indigo are broken up by the stark patches of white in the foaming aerated water. Hansen adds intensity of the blues by incorporating dabs of orange to the lone figure and his boat. | | Hansen arrived in Monterey at a time when commercial fishing was beginning to take off. During this next evolution of his style, he brought visibility to the livelihood of Monterey's fisherman while elevating them as worthy of artistic expression. He chose to depict it as it was, reflecting the diversity of its workers, the bustle of a growing commercial fishing port, and modern advancements to the trade. Hansen would often depict close-up views of fisherfolk with strained brows and rolled up sleeves emphasizing the physical toil of the job. While Hansen is best known for his maritime scenes from this period, he does have examples of Western works in his oeuvre (see Salinas Rodeo sold in April 2018 and Cowboy Sport sold in August 2018). In these, cowboys command a horse like a captain commands his ship, each a careful balancing act unsure which way bronco or boat will tilt next. | | The present lot puts less focus on the figure itself and more emphasis on the sea and what lies beyond. With no visible landmarks in the vast scene and only a sliver of sky appearing along the upper edge of the composition, crossing the bar is akin to crossing the frontier – a taxing and isolating endeavor on both the body and the mind. In a poem by Alfred Tennyson of the same name, Crossing the Bar refers to the afterlife or a peaceful transition from safety into the unknown. This perspective of calm amongst the chaos gives the painting a narrative quality wherein the figure has relinquished his fate to the sea. In a review of Hansen's work one critic even wrote "the artist has told a complete story, a complete history, of seafaring in this one canvas."1 | | With its extensive exhibition history including the Biltmore Salon, the National Academy of Design and the California State Fair, Crossing the Bar is an institutional quality work that balances the romance and reality not only of the sea but the final frontier. | | 1Scott A. Shields, Armin Hansen: The Artful Voyage, Portland, Pomegranate Communications, Inc., 2015, p. 146.

He was particularly fond of the Spanish beach community of Valencia where he met and worked with the Spanish Impressionist Joaquin Sorolla. Sorolla was known to drag large canvases down to the Valencia beaches, tie them down to weather the winds, and paint images on the spot of everyday life along the coast; scenes of fishing boats coming and going, children playing and swimming. Rider, along with other important American impressionist painters, worked side by side with Sorolla painting similar compositions and gleaning as much inspiration from the Spanish master as possible. | | Painted a few years after Sorolla's death, Against the Light is an homage to the Spaniard's influence on Rider and his mastery of Mediterranean light. Here a lone fisherman dons a straw hat to shade himself from the glimmer of the sea as he drags his boat ashore. Light catches the crests of gentle waves and filters through a billowing sail to the point of translucency. In an otherwise cloudless sky, Rider has transformed the sail into a puffy cumulus form. Beyond the shore break, sea and sky blend together with horizontal bands of turquoise and blue. | | Rider went on to exhibit the present lot back home in his native Chicago at the 30th annual exhibition at the Art Institute. Rider continued to be drawn to coastal artist's colonies and ultimately relocated to Laguna Beach in 1931.

provenance: From the Estate of Marion Dodge Harris (1905-1998), widow of the artist. | Property sold to benefit animal rescue through Harris Art Works. | | Exhibited | Pasadena, Who Was Sam? The Art of Sam Hyde Harris (1889-1977), Pasadena Museum of History, 24 January - 29 April 2007. | San Clemente, Casa Romantica, Sam Hyde Harris, Seeing the Unusual, 21 November 2021 – 27 February 2022. | Pasadena, 100 Years - 100 Images: Pasadena Society of Artists (PSA) Centennial Anniversary Exhibition, Pasadena Museum of History, 2025. | | The work has been authenticated by Maurine St. Gaudens, administrator of the Marion Dodge Harris Estate. | | A limited-edition copy of the first printing of Sam Hyde Harris, 1889-1977: A Retrospective: A Pictorial Biography of His Life and Work, edited by Maurine St. Gaudens with Essays by Marian Yoshiki-Kovinick, and Gary Lang, featuring the present work on the cover of the dust jacket, accompanies the lot. | | Sam Hyde Harris was the among the second generation of Southern California plein air painters that carried on the legacy set by trailblazers such as William Wendt, Guy Rose, and Franz Bischoff. His contemporaries included Edgar Payne, Jack Wilkinson Smith and Hanson Puthuff, and they remained committed to capturing the phenomenon of the natural world against encroaching industrialism and modernist trends in art. | | Harris was a professional artist from the age of fourteen, working for the art department of a photo-engraving firm in London. He emigrated with his family to America in 1903, arriving in Los Angeles via New York. Harris pursued work as a sign painter and founded his own commercial studio in 1914. 1 | | Harris ran a successful commercial studio from the 1920s to the mid-1950s, producing advertising signage and travel posters for such regional and national companies as Van de Kamp's Bakery, Gilmore Oil Company, Atchison, Topeka, and Santa Fe, Union Pacific, and countless others. In this context, he worked adeptly with tempera on board to produce vibrant and eye-catching imagery for reproduction. | | The present work in tempera was painted and made as a tripartite fire screen for Marion Dodge Harris, the artist's second wife and love of his life. Sam and Marion married in 1945, and in 1946, they moved from Los Angeles to an artist enclave in Alhambra, California. 2 The screen remained beloved in their Alhambra home for over five decades, throughout Marion's lifetime. | | 1 Maurine St. Gaudens, ed., Sam Hyde Harris, 1889-1977: A Retrospective: A Pictorial Biography of His Life and Work, Atglen, Schiffer Publishing, 2006, pp. 17, 236. | | 2 Ibid, p. 20.

It caused his move to the temperate San Diego. As a teenager Horde attended classes at the San Diego Evening High School where Anna Valentine, a Cincinnati artist who studied with Rodin, sparked a lifelong pursuit of sculpture. | | Donal Hord's diverse influences ranged from T'ang Dynasty earthenware to Olmec and Zapotec art. Numerous examples of his public work can be found in and around San Diego including: Spring Stirring, 1947-48 at the Scripps Institute of Oceanography, Guardian of Water, 1939 outside the San Diego County Administration Center, Aztec, C. 1936, (nicknamed Montezuma) at San Diego State University, and Morning, 1951-1956 at Marina Park near Seaport Village. | | The present lot Descending Sun demonstrated Hord's mastery of the figure and the spiritual nature of his vision. As Bruce Kamerling wrote: | | "As Hord reached the maturity of his style, his subjects became less literal, tending more toward abstract concepts and symbolic imagery. Titles such as Descending Sun, Desert Night Wind, and Summer Rain are indicative of his attempts to interpret nature's forms, moods, and forces through idealized figures." 1 | | 1.The Journal of San Diego History, San Diego Historical Society Quarterly, Summer 1985, Vol.31, No.3. provenance: William A. Karges Fine Art, Los Angeles. | J. Mark Sublette, Medicine Man Gallery, Inc., Santa Fe and Tucson. | Private collection, Pacific Northwest, acquired from the above. | | Born in the vast flatlands of the San Joaquin Valley in 1875, Maynard Dixon was afflicted with asthma from an early age. Because of his illness, Dixon led a quiet childhood sketching and listening to the tall tales of Native Americans and cowboys told by his paternal grandfather and six uncles. These stories inspired in Dixon a lifelong fascination with the lives of the settlers of the American West, Native Americans and the landscape of the West. | | Dixon's artistic skill was recognized early in his life, however, living in rural California provided little access to formal art instruction. Dixon turned to the engravings in periodicals such as Scribner's and Harper's Weekly to improve his technique. Through these publications, Dixon became familiar with the work of contemporary artists illustrating the American West, chief amongst them Frederic Remington. Remington's dramatic and technical depictions left an indelible impression on young Dixon, and at age 16, Dixon sent two sketch books to Remington for criticism and advice. On September 3, 1891, Remington responded with support, enthusiasm and the instruction to 'draw, draw, draw'. | | Encouraged by Remington's response, Dixon enrolled at the School of Design in San Francisco. He quickly found formal training to be stifling and left before the end of the year. The peripatetic artist spent the ensuing decades building a career as a magazine illustrator--depicting his extensive travel throughout the United States. In the early 1920s Dixon shifted his energy to focus on painting murals. The large surface area of mural painting taught him to distill his painting style into simple but powerful compositions with hard horizon lines and vivid colors. He continued to develop and distill these insights and applied them to his easel paintings. | | Point of Rocks has Dixon's signature clarity of vision. Arthur Millier summarized his abilities writing in 1945: "His technical equipment included fluent, robust draftsmanship, a fine taste in color ... the ability to organize the abstract elements of painting into dramatic and coherent structures. The clear pattern, clearly defined forms and architectural compositions so typical of his pictures reflected the natural choice of the artist's independent mind full as much as the character of the country he painted." 1 | | Maynard Dixon in 1936 possessed the vision and skill to render a simple group of rocks into something monumental and at the same time imbued with an almost human presence. He accomplishes this through palette and line. The intensely saturated blue sky stands as a dramatic background for the focus of the picture which is the Point of Rocks. They are delineated with clean planes via a subdued palette of salmon and sand tones. The structure is the same that Dixon used depicting robed figures. | | 1.Arthur Millier, Maynard Dixon: Painter of the West, Tucson, Arizona, 1945, copyright 1967 by Edith Hamlin.

provenance: Private collection, Pacific Northwest by family descent. | | Exhibited | Los Angeles, The Biltmore Hotel, Biltmore Salon, 1935, no. 13. | | We wish to thank Melissa Webster Speidel for her kind assistance in cataloging this lot. This painting is included in the catalogue raisonné database Melissa Webster Speidel is compiling of the artist's oil paintings. | | At the height of Frank Tenney Johnson's career as a cowboy-artist, he built a log cabin and studio in Wyoming on Rim Rock Ranch. The land, owned by his cousin Mildred and her husband Earl Martin, was located near the East gate of Yellowstone Park on the North fork of the Shoshone River.1 While Johnson's primary studio and residence at the time remained in Alhambra, California, he would go on to spend almost every summer from 1931 until his untimely death in 1939 painting and hiking around this beloved second home. Painted during the infamous Rim Rock years, A Wyoming Night Herder depicts one of Frank Tenney Johnson's most celebrated subjects, a moment of stillness between a cowboy and his horse set against a starlit night. | | While the Rim Rock years are now synonymous with Johnson's mature career, the artist had a fascination with the American West from an early age. Johnson settled in Wyoming by way of Iowa, where he was born on a humble prairie farm a stone's throw from the historic Overland Trail. Watching the stagecoaches pass by the farm first sparked his imagination and fueled his curiosity about the frontier. By age 14 Johnson and his family had relocated to Milwaukee where visits to the city's first public museum, the Layton Art Gallery, prompted him to become an artist. Johnson went on to apprentice under two German expatriate artists followed by further training at the Art Students League in New York under John Henry Twachtman (1853-1902) and National Academicians Robert Henri (1865-1929) and William Merritt Chase (1849-1916). It wasn't until a 1903 commission with Field & Stream magazine however, that Johnson was finally able to travel extensively throughout the West. On this seminal trip, Johnson visited cattle ranches in Colorado where he observed and developed the heroic cowboy archetype that would become his trademark during the Rim Rock years. | | In A Wyoming Night Herder a cowboy mounted on his Palomino horse pauses for a well-earned cigarette after the day's duties. While the faint glow of the match brightens the figure's face and the rim of his hat, it is moonlight that illuminates the scene. From the figure's crisp white shirt to the metallic on his spurs, the moon shines bright enough to cast shadows on the unmarked trail despite a clouded indigo sky. Seated side-saddle with one leg outstretched and the other hiked up, the figure holds the reins slack in his hands signaling complete trust in his steed. The horse, possibly Tejon, a model Johnson frequently used during this period, gazes into the distance at the rocky outcroppings and the valley beyond. 2 Together the figural vignette represents Johnson's years of experience and observation on the western range revealing a mature style now known as the Rim Rock years. | | 1.Harold McCracken, The Frank Tenney Johnson Book: A Master Painter of The Old West, New York, 1974, p. 123. | 2. ibid, p. 189.

provenance: Carolina Nitsch Contemporary Art, New York. | Acquired from the above by the present owner. | | Executed in 2005, Black Arcs/Untitled (Black) belongs to the extraordinarily fertile final chapter of Louise Bourgeois's career, when she turned to drawing and printmaking as acts of meditation, introspection, and release. Working from her Chelsea townhouse studio until her passing in 2010, Bourgeois collaborated with Benjamin Shiff of the Osiris imprint to produce a series of complex, experimental works on paper that rearticulated her lifelong preoccupations including memory, trauma, motherhood, and the fragile balance between control and chaos. For an artist who once declared, "To create is an act of liberation and every day this need for liberation comes back to me," these late works reveal a distilled, essential form of self-expression. (P. Herkenhoff, Louise Bourgeois, Phaidon, 2003, p. 19)  | | In Black Arcs/Untitled (Black), Bourgeois employs etching, watercolor, and gouache to create an elegant rhythm of interlocking oval forms, rendered with both delicacy and tension. The repeated, almost pulsating patterns recall her Spiral series of the same period, where looping, vortex-like motifs symbolized psychological cycles of repression, rage, and renewal. The spiral was, for Bourgeois, a metaphor drawn from her childhood: she remembered watching workers twist and wring soaked tapestries in the River Bièvre near her family's restoration workshop — a gesture that embodied both care and violence. "The spiral is an attempt at controlling the chaos," she once said, "beginning at the outside is the fear of losing control; winding in is a retreating, a compacting to the point of disappearance." ('The Art of Louise Bourgeois', Tate, June 2016) In the present work, the curved lines verge on abstraction but retain an unmistakable corporeal charge, echoing the curving limbs and coiling forms of her monumental Spider sculptures — icons of maternity, resilience, and entrapment.  | | While Bourgeois is celebrated primarily for her large-scale sculptures, drawing was the medium through which her ideas were first conceived and continually reworked. As a child, she had filled in missing motifs on the tapestries her parents restored — an early act of image-making that marked the beginning of her artistic vocation and her lifelong dialogue between memory and creation. In the last decade of her life, she returned to these instincts with renewed urgency. Works such as Black Arcs/Untitled (Black) reveal the artist in full command of her expressive language in which she transforms fragility into structure, pain into rhythm, and the personal into the universal. The interlacing forms, hovering between tension and release, become visual metaphors for the endurance of the human psyche. Both intimate and monumental in feeling, the work embodies Bourgeois's lifelong negotiation between memory and healing and further stands as a testament to her enduring relevance as one of the most psychologically profound artists of the twentieth century.

King-Nero, eds., The Andy Warhol Catalogue Raisonné: Paintings and Sculptures 1970-1974, Volume 3, New York, 2014, pl. 2749-2750, illustrated pp. 413-414. | | "Andy, in my mind, was fundamentally a voyeur. He had to go out and see and do and be seen to have the energy for his work." | - Robert Denison | | Robert J. Denison, a longtime friend and advisor to Andy Warhol, was first introduced to the art world by Dorothy and Roy Lichtenstein, his neighbors on Long Island. As chairman of the investment firm First Security Management, Denison counseled Warhol to establish the Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts in Pittsburgh and was instrumental to the financial security of the Warhol legacy. In addition to advising Warhol, Denison also advised artists such as Roy Lichtenstein and Robert Rauschenberg, forever impacting the way artists capitalized on their artistic star power and secured their legacies. Warhol created these two silkscreen portraits, both of unique size, along with two additional portraits of his friend Denison, now held in the Andy Warhol Museum. Never before offered for sale, these two portraits have been in Denison's collection since their creation.   | | Denison's work in finance and advice to Warhol inspired both Warhol's 1980s  Dollar Sign and Gems series as well as his broader reflections on money. Warhol once remarked, "I'm convinced that if you can spell things out very simply and say everything clearly right away, you'll be a success in business. Like Bob Denison can do that." Denison's identity as a "money man" aligned perfectly with Warhol's portraiture practice from the early 1970s onward—one that critics have often discussed as reinventing the humanist genre through its engagement with the commodity form.  | | This pair of acrylic and silkscreen portraits of Denison belongs to Warhol's extensive series of society portraits begun in the 1970s, which defined the second half of his career. Warhol photographed his subjects using a Polaroid camera, transferring the instant print to an acetate to create a silkscreen stencil. Having started with photobooth reels in the 1960s, by the 1970s Warhol had adopted the Polaroid as his preferred tool. The transfer process allowed him to exercise artistic license—removing blemishes, altering hair color, and heightening contrast. Many portraits were commissions, and Warhol often chose color schemes that reflected the sitter's personality.  | | Drawing on his background as a 1950s commercial illustrator, Warhol skillfully employed mass-reproductive techniques and vivid color to command attention. The same strategies that informed his iconic portraits of Marilyn Monroe, Elvis Presley, and Elizabeth Taylor are evident in his society portrait series. Here, too, Bob Denison is distilled to his essence: cigarette in hand, his expression cool and detached. In a distinctly Warholian way, he performs his own identity.  | | At the time, curator Robert Rosenblum dubbed Warhol the "Court Painter of the '70s," likening his work in the portrait genre to John Singer Sargent and his late-nineteenth-century portrayals of the wealthy elite. Warhol's portraits, however, suited the "Me Generation," shaped by Watergate disillusionment and disco-era glamour. Sleeker and glossier than his 1960s celebrity silkscreens, these works echoed the polished aesthetics of Vogue and Vanity Fair. Among those immortalized alongside Denison were Debbie Harry, Liza Minnelli, and Gianni Versace. The Denison portraits, among the earlier examples in the series, feature the expressive, hand-painted acrylic details also found in Warhol's Chairman Mao works—a technique he had recently revived in the late 1960s and would abandon again by the end of the following decade.

Wiener, Walton Ford: Pancha Tantra, Cologne, 2015 (illustrated p. 175). | | | Born in 1960 and growing up in the Hudson Valley of New York, Walton Ford has always had a strong connection with the natural world. Ford graduated from the Rhode Island School of Design in 1982 and soon established his reputation in traditional natural history illustration through his early depictions of indigenous birds throughout the 1990s. Ford expands on this tradition by incorporating a broader narrative often as commentary on the legacy of human impact to the environment.   | | The present work, El Poeta, completed in 2004, appears to be a continuation of his indigenous birds series which he began in the 1990s during a visit to India. The work depicts the Cuban Red Macaw, a now-extinct species of macaw that was native to Cuba and the Cuban Parrot. The central Macaw dominating the composition is ensnared in a trap while the Cuban Parrots below appeared to have walked into a baited snare. The inscriptions and title suggest a critique on the fate of the indigenous birds of North America whose demise is extrinsically linked to colonialism and western expansion.   | | Ford's work is included in a number of private and public collections, including the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art, Bentonville; the Detroit Institute of Arts, Detroit; the Minneapolis Institute of Art, Minneapolis; the Museum of Modern Art, New York; the Princeton University Art Museum, Princeton; the Smithsonian American Art Museum, Washington, D.C.; the Wadsworth Atheneum Museum of Art, Hartford; and the Whitney Museum of American Art, New York amongst many others.

provenance: Estate of the artist. | Baumgartner Galleries, Inc., Washington, D.C. | Acquired from the above by the present owner. | | Exhibited | New York, The Museum of Modern Art, The Art of the Real: USA 1948-1968, July 3-September 8, 1968 (exh. cat., p.30, illustrated p. 31). | | Alphecca: the brightest star in the Corona Borealis and the jewel in its northern crown. Paul Feeley was an artist deeply attuned to the harmonies of cosmic order and the richness of Classical art and the age of Enlightenment. In the present work, we glimpse an almost hieroglyphic translation of a universal system. Rediscovered from long term ownership and presented at auction for the first time, Alphecca belongs to Feeley's celebrated series of 'jacks,' the radiant, cruciform compositions that are the signature of his mature style. Alphecca wonderfully embodies the austere resolve that enabled Feeley to produce some of the most visually arresting images of post-war abstraction. An artist, educator and curator who was deeply embedded in the Abstract Expressionist movement – famously Helen Frankenthaler's tutor at Bennington College, and collaborator with Clement Greenberg on multiple group exhibitions – his tragically curtailed career has left an enduring mark on twentieth century art history, holding an almost unique position as part of, but distinct from, Color Field and Hard-Edge painting. | | Across an unprimed canvas, five vivid red 'jacks' radiate in poised equilibrium, their rounded limbs echoing one another in a visual fugue of repetition and pause. Feeley's compositional rigor is underscored by his restraint: each form hand-drawn and rendered with calculated precision. The raw canvas ground creates an open field in which the geometry of Feeley's system operates, emphasizing the painting's architecture rather than its imagistic quality. The scarlet red 'jacks' of Alphecca sit firmly against the picture plane, giving an intense feeling of depth. It is a masterclass of abstract painting that deals as much with the phenomenological effects of technique as with the formal issues that weighed heavy on Abstract Expressionist and Minimalist practitioners. | | Included in the landmark exhibition The Art of the Real: USA 1948–1968 at the Museum of Modern Art in New York, Feeley's disciplined compositions stand apart from the declarative gestures of Abstract Expressionism and the impersonality of Minimalism. His work occupies a middle ground, intensely composed yet organic and tactile. Writing in the exhibition catalogue accompanying the 1968 show, E.C. Goossen notes that "the new attitude has been turning art inside out: instead of perceptual experience being accepted as the means to an end, it has become the end in itself. The Renaissance artist labored over perspective in order to create an illusion of space within which he could make believable the religious and philosophical ideals of his time; the contemporary artist labors to make art itself believable" (E.C. Goossen, The Art of the Real: USA 1948-1968, New York, 1968, p. 11). In this regard, we experience Feeley's 'jacks' literally as well as illusionistically. Like the star after which the present work is titled, there is a corollary relationship: we experience the real, enormous celestial bodies of our night sky as single flares of light amongst groups; our relationship to them is entirely abstract. Feeley's 'jacks' provide no more information to the spectator than their simple form amongst others, yet the magnitude of their presence lingers as a known unknown. | | Feeley's premature death in 1966 marked the loss of an artist of great sincerity and depth. Alphecca stands as proof of his quiet radicalism. His 'jacks' exemplify a vision of abstraction stripped of grandiosity yet charged with power and play. In its serene luminosity, Alphecca affirms Feeley's belief that painting could be both intellectual and corporeal; speak to cosmic order as readily as personal experience. The present work offers an opportunity to acquire one of the finest examples of Feeley's late works with exceptional period history, included in a seminal exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art that signaled the very best of post-war American painting.

Miami Herald, June 19, 2005, (illustrated p. 3M). | | Felix Gonzalez-Torress "Untitled" (1990) embodies a characteristic restraint and sensitivity, distilling profound emotional and conceptual resonance within the simplest of forms. Comprising a stack of pristine white sheets each embossed with a ring of dolphins, the work merges the visual language of Minimalism with intimate symbolism. The delicate circular impression—visible only when light grazes the surface—suggests continuity, motion, and infinity, while the dolphin introduces a gentle lyricism into the work's otherwise austere materiality.A recurring motif in his oeuvre, the dolphin holds layered symbolic weight within Gonzalez-Torres's visual lexicon. Often associated with intelligence, companionship, freedom and migration, it can be read as a metaphor for the artist's own life as an émigré from Cuba, navigating between cultures and identities. The circular formation of the animals evokes both the cyclical nature of return and the longing inherent in displacement—an emblem of community and exile, distance and reunion.Unlike his well-known participatory stacks, whose parameters allow viewers to choose to take sheets which can be replenished, "Untitled" complicates this interactive aspect of the work. Most other stack works are unique and can be manifested in more than one place at a time, and sheets can be endlessly replenished, however, "Untitled" is an editioned work whose sheets are finite and can never be replenished if they are taken, and as such, the owner may opt not to allow viewers to take from the work. By changing the stakes of physical engagement, the work may prompt questioning around generosity, value, and permanence.

provenance: Galeria Thomas Cohn, São Paulo. | Acquired from the above by the present owner. | | Exhibited | Madrid, Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía, Guillermo Kuitca: Obras 1982/2002, 2003 (later traveled to Buenos Aires, Museo de Arte Latinoamericano de Buenos Aires MALBA) (exh. cat., illustrated p. 122). | | Painted in 1988, L'Enfance du Christ stands as a haunting synthesis of Guillermo Kuitca's core themes: displacement, theater, architecture, and religion. Created during a pivotal period in the artist's career, the work transforms a domestic interior into a suspended, dreamlike stage. Rendered in rich gradations of red, black, and white, the scene unfolds like an aerial blueprint of a private home- its roof removed, walls exposed, and furniture frozen in quiet disarray.  | | The work's title references Hector Berlioz's 1854 oratorio L'Enfance du Christ, recounting the Holy Family's flight into Egypt. Kuitca reinterprets this sacred story through the lens of Argentina's post-dictatorship reality, embedding within it a meditation on exile, fear, and survival. The Holy Family's journey becomes an allegory for the artist's family history of migration and his generation, who came of age amid political violence and social dislocation. Born in Buenos Aires in 1961, Kuitca was a teenager during the years of military rule (1976–1983), a period marked by censorship, forced disappearances, and mass migration. The resulting sense of rupture and diaspora, both national and personal, pervades his imagery.  | | Visually, L'Enfance du Christ reveals Kuitca's fascination with the intersection between painting and theater. The composition recalls a theatrical set viewed from a bird's-eye perspective, an approach that denies architectural closure and complicates the viewer's position. By stripping away the roof and doors, Kuitca invites the viewer into an exposed, voyeuristic gaze, in turn granting access to a private world that is simultaneously abandoned and alive. The recurring absence of human figures heightens this tension: chairs, curtains, and a vase of flowers suggest human presence, yet their emptiness speaks to departure and loss.  | | The deep crimson tones that dominate the canvas convey a sense of corporeal intensity and emotional volatility. The light source emerging from the upper left corner imbues the scene with a theatrical glow, evoking both divine illumination and psychological unease. Kuitca's controlled palette reinforces the sensation of turbulence contained within silence, of history distilled into architectural form.  | | Religion and theatricality converge in this composition. After encountering Frida Kahlo's work in Madrid in the early 1980s, Kuitca began integrating Catholic and Latin American symbolism into his practice, despite his own Jewish upbringing. The sacred subject matter of L'Enfance du Christ thus marks an act of transgression and reconciliation—an attempt to bridge inherited faith and lived history through the visual language of theater.  | | Ultimately, L'Enfance du Christ embodies Kuitca's conviction that painting can serve as both mirror and stage for the human condition. It reflects the traumas of political exile, the fluidity of identity, and the enduring search for spiritual refuge. Through its haunting emptiness and architectural precision, the work offers not only a record of absence but also a profound meditation on the spaces where memory, belief, and loss intersect.

provenance: Property from a private collection, London; acquired from the artist circa 1960s, thence by descent; | Bonhams, Islamic & Indian Art, 25th October 2007, lot 311. | Property from a private collection, London; acquired from the above. | | "Renaissance painters painted men and women making them look like angels. I paint for angels, to show them what men and women really look like." - F.N. Souza, 1962. | | Painted in 1962, a period marking a pivotal shift in Souza's artistic development, this masterpiece, Untitled (Head), stands as a defining moment in his career, bridging the visual languages of his 1950s and 1960s periods. Created during his celebrated Gallery One years, the work embodies both an aesthetic breakthrough and a testament to Souza's rise as a leading figure in contemporary art. | | After leaving India for London in 1949, Souza endured several years of hardship before establishing himself as a vital voice within postwar British art. His perseverance culminated in widespread recognition by the late 1950s, notably with his first major solo exhibition at Gallery One in 1959. Organised by Victor Musgrave, this landmark show marked Souza's emergence on the international stage. Musgrave's vision proved instrumental in shaping the global recognition of modern Indian art. He was among the first to exhibit artists such as Sayed Haider Raza, Akbar Padamsee, Tyeb Mehta, Paritosh Sen, Avinash Chandra, Anwar Jalal Shemza, Ram Kumar, Laxman Pai, Maqbool Fida Husain, and Souza himself, an audacious and pioneering gesture that redefined the visibility of South Asian modernists abroad. | | Throughout his career, Souza sustained an unyielding commitment to experimentation. His portraits of the 1950s are distinguished by assertive cross-hatched lines, while by the early 1960s his approach had evolved toward radical distortion, transforming faces into complex, mutated forms. The present lot stands as a compelling testament to this evolution, an image where intensity, audacity, and emotion converge. | | "I have created a new kind of face... I have drawn the physiognomy way beyond Picasso, in completely new terms. And I am still a figurative painter... [Picasso] stumped them and the whole of the western world into shambles. When you examine the face, the morphology, I am the only artist who has taken it a step further." (F. N. Souza quoted in Y. Dalmia, 'A Passion for the Human Figure', The Making of Modern Indian Art: The Progressives, Oxford University Press, New Delhi, 2001, p. 94). | | As theatre director Ebrahim Alkazi, who lived with Souza in London during the 1950s, observed "Souza has despised artists who have merely played with the fire of art, warmed their hands over its embers. For he himself has stepped into the flames... His fundamental aim is to destroy art as it is commonly understood." (E. Alkazi, Souza's Seasons in Hell Art Heritage, Vol. 6, New Delhi, 1986–87, p. 76). | | Untitled (Head) captures Souza's artistic inferno. The painting channels his inner turmoil and relentless drive into a primal, distorted portrait, where exaggerated, disjointed features and heavy cross-hatching reject traditional aesthetics. Aggressive black lines and a stark palette transform the face into a grotesque icon, a visceral commentary on suffering and the raw physicality of existence. | | Here, Souza's exploration of the human condition reaches an uncompromising intensity. It conveys anguish and post-war existential anxiety while offering a critique of societal hypocrisy. The painting presents a profound inquiry into identity and offers a daring critique of the role and meaning of art.

His works are meditations on rhythm, movement, and light - each brushstroke animated by colour and motion. | | Trained initially as a portrait painter, Gulgee's early exposure to calligraphy, encouraged by his father, himself a skilled calligrapher, laid the foundation for his later experiments with tradition and innovation. In 1960, his encounter with an exhibition by the American abstract artist Elaine Hamilton in Karachi proved pivotal. Inspired by the dynamism of action painting, he began combining its spontaneity with the discipline of calligraphy, creating a new approach to modern South Asian art. | | As art historian Ijaz ul Hassan notes, 'Each part of the canvas is painted with loving care, each brushstroke is aware of itself, every impression is infused with light, which makes the picture surface vibrate with a transcendental glow. Gulgee, while painting, wants to carry the viewer along by appealing to his emotional and sensual faculties. (Painting in Pakistan, Lahore, 1991, pp. 119–120). | | In works such as the present lot, Untitled (Abstract), Gulgee's sweeping gestures and radiant colours embody both physical immediacy and spiritual contemplation, an enduring testament to his visionary approach and his profound contribution to the language of modern Islamic art.

Depicted without arms, Husain stands broad-shouldered and upright, partially enclosed within a rectangular outline suggestive of a mirror, a device that frames both reflection and self-confrontation. Painted almost entirely in modulations of white, with only the faintest breath of blue animating the surface, this monumental work demonstrates Husain's ability to create visual drama through restraint. The large horizontal composition stages a compelling tableau; on the left sits a regal figure, perhaps a swami or king, enthroned upon a raised takht, presiding over the ceremonial Ashvamedha, while six horses surge dynamically across the plane, embodying energy, vitality, and divine force. | | The Ashvamedha, an ancient Vedic ritual of royal consecration, was traditionally performed to assert a monarch's sovereignty and cosmic legitimacy. A sacred horse, representing the spirit of the king, was set free to wander for a year, followed by warriors who protected it. Upon its return, the horse was ritually sacrificed, symbolising renewal, dominion, and the cyclical power of life and death. Husain, ever attuned to the mythic and the allegorical, revisits this potent symbol not as literal narration but as an abstracted visual metaphor for creation, conquest, and spiritual release. | | The presence of six horses rather than one intensifies the drama of the composition. In Vedic and later Indian thought, the horse signifies strength, speed, and divine vitality, attributes associated with Surya, the sun god, whose chariot is drawn by seven horses, each representing a ray of light. Husain's choice of six may allude to the balance between motion and control, matter and spirit, the threshold between the earthly and the celestial. Educated initially in conventional academic painting, Abanindranath soon became dissatisfied with Western academic methods, seeking instead an art that would express Indian cultural identity, spiritual values, and indigenous aesthetic traditions. He drew inspiration from Mughal miniatures, Rajput painting, and folk art, synthesizing these into a style that was both nationalist in vision and deeply lyrical. | | Abanindranath was also profoundly influenced by East Asian techniques, particularly Japanese brushwork and the morotai method, which emphasizes soft tonal washes and subtle gradations of colour. These techniques allowed him to create ethereal, atmospheric compositions that conveyed mood, spirituality, and narrative with economy of line and form. While Abanindranath inspired him to look inward toward Indian tradition, Bose brought a distinct sensibility shaped by close observation of nature and an interest in the emotional and spiritual resonance of ordinary subjects. | | Bose's early works reflect his mentor's influence in their use of ink, water-based media, and subtle tonal gradations, but he expanded these techniques to develop a personal vocabulary. provenance: Property from a private collection, India. | Acquired from the artist. | | Vaikuntam is a celebrated Indian artist whose works are held in major collections both nationally and internationally. Deeply rooted in Indian artistic traditions, his practice draws inspiration from the everyday life and cultural vibrancy of Telangana. Central to his oeuvre are striking portrayals of village women - figures of strength and sensuality. As A Visual History of Indian Modern Art notes, 'Bright primary colours evoking nature, rendered in fine brushstrokes, bring to life his sensuously rendered women, and their lustrous dark skin and sturdy bodies that are hardened by labour but also decorated in jewellery and flowers.' (Vol. 8, January – February 2015, New Delhi, p. 1759). | | Vaikuntam's distinctive palette, dominated by rich primary colours such as red, saffron, and orange, reflects his commitment to the natural, elemental tones of Indian life. As he notes, 'I like using rich primary colours... because these are essentially Indian colours. I don't like using colours that are a mix of two... they don't exist in our surroundings, in our everyday life' (Thota in Uma Nair, The Times of India, 11 February 2023). | | His artistic vision was also shaped by his years as an art teacher at Jawahar Bal Bhavan in Hyderabad, where the bold colours and uninhibited creativity of children left a lasting impression; the centre became a key source of inspiration, offering an environment untouched by academic constraints, where imagination flourished freely.

provenance: Property from a private collection, Sri Lanka. | Acquired from Ivan Peries wife, Veronica Peries in 2002. | | Painted in 1986, just two years before Peries's death, the present lot Standing Man and Seated Man comes from the final chapter of the leading 20th century Sri Lankan modernist artist. A founding member of the landmark '43 Group, Peries helped catalyse a decisive break from the academic naturalism of the Ceylon Society of Arts, establishing a new modernist language for Sri Lankan art. | | As art historian Jagath Weerasinghe noted, the '43 Group's key achievement was transforming European modernism into a distinctly Sri Lankan visual language, a synthesis Peries carried forward throughout his career. After receiving a government scholarship in 1948, he moved to London to study painting and later settled there permanently. Despite this distance, his work remained deeply tied to the culture, coastal landscapes, and village life of Sri Lanka, which continued to inform the emotional atmosphere of his art. | | The present pair of acrylics depicts a seated man and a standing man, rendered in the distilled, geometric language characteristic of Peries's style. Reduced to simplified modernist forms and rendered in restrained, neutral and warm palettes, the figures appear introspective, taking on a quiet, haunting lyricality. In these works, Peries demonstrates his enduring ability to evoke presence and emotion through essentialised forms, reinterpreting European modernist forms through a distinctly Sri Lankan lens. | | The present lot forms part of a cohesive series of related works executed by Peries during the 1980s. Significantly, the series has been the source of record-setting results for the artist on the secondary market. The Ivan – Tree Series, offered at Christie's in March 2025, established a then-record of USD 43,000, which was surpassed in the September auction by another work from the series achieving USD 63,000, the current world record for the artist. | | Institutional recognition of the importance of this body of work is likewise notable, the Victoria & Albert Museum, London, holds three examples from this series, and further related works are illustrated in plates 121–126 of Ivan Peries: Paintings 1938–88 by Senaka Bandaranayake and Manel Fonseka (1996).

provenance: Property from a private collection, UK. | | Brunner is a key figure in the twentieth-century story connecting European and Indian art. Born into a Hungarian family of artists, she developed within a European tradition. Like her compatriot Amrita Sher-Gil, who also navigated a Hungarian and Indian heritage, Brunner's practice evolved through her sustained engagement with India. Both artists drew on their Central European roots while responding closely to the people, landscapes, and ideas they encountered on the subcontinent. | | Brunner's life was marked early by a vision: at nineteen, she dreamed of a silver-haired man handing her an oil lamp and urging her to carry its light across the world. Her mother, the artist Elizabeth Sass-Brunner, interpreted the dream as a summons from Rabindranath Tagore, whose visit to Budapest had left an indelible impression on Hungarian intellectual life. Mother and daughter then embarked for India in 1930, and were among the Europeans who made their way to Asia in the years between the two World Wars. | | India became not simply a destination but a home. Santiniketan, the utopian environment nurtured by Tagore, offered a sanctuary that aligned with their spiritual aspirations and artistic ideals. From this base, the Brunners travelled widely across India, forming connections with its people, landscapes, and creative communities. They painted not only the prominent figures who shaped India's cultural life but also the everyday individuals who embodied its rhythms and spirit. | | Brunner's works pulse with a gentle humanism, marked by a quiet spirituality and an attentive empathy that transcends classical portraiture. The present work, Kashmir, captures a serene moment in one of Kashmir's characteristic landscapes. A lone figure stands at the water's edge, seen from behind; her elongated silhouette and draped clothing giving her a composed and almost statuesque like presence. Before her, a calm river stretches between tall poplars, while the snow-covered Himalayan peaks rise in the distance. | | The painting reflects Brunner's dual inheritance: the discipline and tonal restraint of her Central European training enriched by the luminosity and warmth she encountered in India. Combining lyrical sensitivity with a measured naturalism, Kashmir stands as a rare and strikingly beautiful testament to Brunner's place in Hungarian–Indian modernism and her deep connection to the region's people and landscapes.

Because most people cannot draw a line straight or otherwise' - Avinash Chandra | | Born in Shimla, Chandra forged a distinguished career between India and the United Kingdom. He studied at the Delhi Polytechnic Art School, where he later served as a professor. Among his students were notable artists such as Paramjit Singh, Arpita Singh, and Gopi Gajwani. In 1956, Chandra moved to London with his wife, marking the beginning of a defining phase in his artistic development. | | Chandra's work reflects the influence of European modernism, most notably Picasso and Paul Klee, while also drawing upon the expressive techniques and emotional intensity of Van Gogh and Soutine. Writing in The Guardian, art critic Eric Newton remarked that 'Chandra's nearest counterpart in Western art is to be found in the work of Paul Klee.' | | The female figure remained a central motif throughout Chandra's oeuvre. His early compositions featured refined linear studies that, by the 1960s and 1970s, evolved into works charged with sensual and erotic undertones. Writing in The Guardian, art critic George Butcher hailed Chandra as 'a new painter of great ability,' praising 'the glowing sensuality of his colour' and 'the symbolic sexual references drawn from Hindu imagery.' | | The present Untitled work exemplifies this pivotal transitional phase in Chandra's practice. Executed in soft watercolours, it balances delicacy with an underlying sense of tension. The female form becomes increasingly abstracted, fragmented, and suspended across the canvas, juxtaposed with a phallic form. Through this composition, Chandra examines the dynamic interplay between the feminine and the masculine, employing abstraction, form, and fluidity of line, while charging the work with a subtle yet striking sensuality.

provenance: Property from a private collection, India. | Acquired from the artist; | Acquired from the above. | | Renowned British–Indian sculptor, Kar was among the pioneers who redefined modern Indian sculpture in the mid-twentieth century. Initially trained in the academic and representational tradition of the Bengal School, his practice evolved toward a distinctly modern idiom following his studies in Paris in 1938. There, his encounter with European modernism and exposure to sculptural experimentation further liberated him from the constraints of strict formalism. As Kishore Singh observes, this period marked 'a freedom from rigid tradition so sculptors no longer conformed to popular taste but were driven by sculptural values. '(A Visual History of Indian Modern Art: The Making of Modern Sculpture in India, Delhi, p. 1753). | | In this bronze sculpture, Untitled (Lady), Kar presents a faceless, voluptuous female form, poised in quiet contemplation. The work's rounded volumes and self-contained form convey a meditative stillness, while the gentle rhythm of the lady's arms brings a lyrical grace to the figure. Though marked by European modernism in its stylised treatment, the work remains deeply rooted in local cultural traditions. Its tactile simplicity and sensuous form recall the sculptural language of South Asian folk and classical art. The absence of facial features universalises the figure, transforming it from individual portrait to timeless archetype, and affirming Kar's modernist pursuit of pure sculptural expression over narrative. | | Elected in 1947 as a member of the Royal Society of British Sculptors, the first and only Indian to receive this honour, Kar occupies a key position among the generation of artists who, from the 1930s onward, sought to reconcile modernist principles with an evolving postcolonial identity. Untitled (Lady) stands as a testament to this synthesis: at once rooted in Indian sensibility and alive with the expressive freedom of international modernism.

provenance: Property from the artist's collection. | | The Modern & Contemporary South Asian Art department at Bonhams and curator Vittoria Beltrame are pleased to present You Also Live in Someone's Eyes, an auction bringing together works by Amrit Singh Sandhu, Anjuli Rathod, Kavitha Balasingham, Anousha Payne, and artist duo Nina Mhach Durban and Athen Kardashian. | | This section of the auction takes its title from a verse by Mumbai-based writer and poet Sanober Khan, a line that captures the profound notion that each of us exists in the consciousness of others: through love, admiration, memory, or even pain. The phrase suggests that identity is never fixed or solitary - it is formed through shared experience and perception. | | Each of the artists in You Also Live in Someone's Eyes engages with questions of selfhood, belonging, and inheritance. Their practices explore what it means to articulate the complexity of diasporic identity and the ways in which memory, displacement, and cultural hybridity inform creative expression. Working across painting, sculpture, drawing and installation, these artists weave together fragments of lived experience and collective history to build visual languages that are at once personal and universal. | | Through their distinct material and conceptual approaches, the auction and view unfolds as a conversation about lineage and transformation: how emotion, memory, and familial tales are transmitted, altered, and reimagined across distance and time. In this shared space, the act of looking becomes reciprocal: to see is also to be seen, to hold and be held in the eyes of another. | | Kavitha Balasingham (b. 1994, Kent) | | Balasingham is an artist and educator whose practice explores the instability of meaning as it travels through distance, time, and technological mediation. She received her MFA from Goldsmiths (2022) and is currently a Lecturer in Fine Art at Norwich University of the Arts. Her work has been exhibited at Turner Contemporary, Palmer Gallery, and Bow Arts, among others, and she has received support from Arts Council England and the Gilbert Bayes Trust. | | Balasingham works across sculpture, drawing, and digital media, combining humour and speculative fiction to examine intimacy, translation, and miscommunication. As someone who maintains familial ties across continents through technology, she reflects on how emotion, memory, and language are altered through transmission: stretched, blurred, or refracted like light across space. Her forms occupy a state of partial arrival: neither message nor echo, but something suspended in between. In these quiet distortions, Balasingham locates tenderness, a recognition that even in misalignment, connection persists. | | About Vittoria Beltrame | | Vittoria Beltrame is a curator, writer, and advisor dedicated to championing artists whose creative vision and talent deserve global recognition. Her practice is guided by a deep fascination with transhistorical themes, which informs her appreciation for diverse art movements and the enduring forms of talent they embody. Through her curatorial work, Beltrame seeks to create lasting dialogues between artists and movements across time. | | She has curated exhibitions for galleries internationally, including Wilder Gallery, Tube Culture Hall and MyMA among others. Beyond her curatorial practice, Beltrame is an active writer, contributing to curatorial texts and various art publications. She also runs Art for Thought, a blog where she highlights standout exhibitions and artists each month. In addition, she has lectured at Christie's Education. | | Beltrame oversees the residency program founded and hosted by Soho Revue, which offers emerging artists complimentary studio space, mentorship, and opportunities to connect with institutions and present their work. Most recently, she founded Carta Magna, a nomadic art platform dedicated exclusively to showcasing works on paper. | | Beltrame holds an MSc in Art, Law, and Business from Christie's.

A graduate of the University of Sindh, Jamshoro, where he earned his Master of Fine Arts in Painting in 1993, Abbas has developed a practice deeply rooted in observation, empathy, and restraint. His works reveal not only technical mastery of watercolour, a notoriously demanding medium, but also a profound sensitivity to the lived realities and quiet dignity of rural life in Sindh. |  | Renowned for his People of Thar series, Abbas transforms everyday moments into meditations on endurance, solitude, and belonging. In the pair of paintings shown here, two women are portrayed separately, one cradling a child, the other turned away from the viewer, both rendered in traditional attire with delicately nuanced expression. The mood is contemplative, the palette subdued and atmospheric, with earthy tones and muted washes that evoke the arid vastness of the desert landscape.
subject_matter: two women, child, traditional attire, desert landscape, earthy tones, muted washes

provenance: Property from a private collection, India. | | The present lot is a compelling etching on paper with chemical treatment, rendered in dark, monochromatic brown tones. Its expressive brushwork and abstract forms exemplify Swaroop's experimental approach, inviting the viewer into a contemplative space where mystic forms resonate on an emotional level. | | Born in Jodhpur in 1939 into a family of modest means, Swaroop showed an early and unusual interest in art. Considered one of the trailblazers of modern art in Rajasthan, he worked in an international style at a time when few others did, revolutionising traditional art forms dominated by folk and miniature styles. Often compared to Souza in his time, Swaroop's work is marked by continual evolution - from dark, subdued watercolours and semi-figurative forms in his early period to later works featuring expansive colour fields, bold lines, and expressionistic use of colour, which have become hallmarks of his style. | | Described as a seeker of the void, Swaroop consistently explored the depths of his distinctive visual language, producing work that is at once avant-garde and deeply evocative. This present Untitled lot with its monochromatic abstraction and expressive rendition, stands as a striking example of his experimental and emotive oeuvre. | | To see other works from the artist see Bonhams, Modern and Contemporary South Asian Art Exhibition Jyoti Swaroop, 20th - 25th May 2022, https://www.bonhams.com/auction/27948/modern-and-contemporary-south-asian-art-exhibition-jyoti-swaroop/. | | To see works by the artist sold in these rooms see Bonhams, Modern & Contemporary South Asian Art Online, 4th - 14th July 2022, lot 21 and Modern & Contemporary South Asian Art Online, 20th February - 6th March 2023, lot 68.

provenance: Property from a private collection, UK; | Acquired from a local house clearance in 2024. |  | This striking oil on canvas presents a beautiful woman rendered with her head turned gently to the left, her breast exposed beneath the folds of a vivid red sari. Reminiscent of Prabha's iconic depictions of women, the painting moves fluidly between figuration and abstraction, offering just enough anatomical clarity to anchor the subject while allowing the surrounding forms to soften and dissolve. The background glows in a rich yellow, creating a warm, atmospheric field against which the figure emerges. Her skin, modelled in expressive tones of brownish green, heightens the work's emotional resonance and lends the composition an otherworldly presence. Though she appears to sit atop a surface, this too slips into abstraction, reinforcing the painting's dreamlike balance between the real and the imagined.

provenance: Property from a private collection, Germany. | Acquired in 2023/2024 from a Berlin household.  |  | This chromolithograph, depicting Kadambari, an epithet of Saraswati exemplifies Varma's ability to blend classical Indian iconography with the visual language of European realism. Printed at the Ravi Varma Press and later hand-embellished with applied details, the image captures the goddess seated serenely, adorned with jewels and drapery rendered in exquisite detail. Whether interpreted as the literary muse Kadambari or the goddess Saraswati, the composition reflects Varma's vision of divine femininity — graceful, learned, and luminous. |  | Chromolithographs such as this were instrumental in democratizing art in colonial India, making sacred imagery accessible to a wider public. The applied embellishments, likely added by hand after printing, enhance the work's devotional aura, transforming a mechanical reproduction into a cherished, almost sacred object. Today, such prints stand as testaments to Varma's pioneering role in shaping the visual culture of modern India, bridging courtly painting, popular art, and printmaking. |  |  |

R.170, under rejected attributions, as Circle of Alessandro Magnasco. | | Exhibited | Hartford, Wadsworth Atheneum Museum, Exhibition of Italian Painting of the Sei- and Settecento, 22 January- 5 February 1930, no. 20, as Alessandro Magnasco. | | New York, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Tiepolo and his Contemporaries, 14 March- 24 April 1938, no. 7, as Alessandro Magnasco. | | New York, Durlacher Brothers, A Loan Exhibition of Paintings by Alessandro Magnasco, 9 January- 3 February 1940, no. 16, as Alessandro Magnasco. | | N.B. | The present work was previously attributed to Alessandro Magnasco. Antonio Francesco Peruzzini and Magnasco have similar styles and indeed once collaborated while working in Florence under the patronage of Ferdinand de' Medici, with Peruzzini painting the paintings' landscapes and Magnasco painting the figures. | | The present painting is likely a fragment - perhaps the lower right corner - of a larger composition titled The Smugglers. In May 2025, Daniele de Sarno Prignano and Laura Muti revised their 1994 opinion and suggested a new identification for the work, on the basis of high-resolution color photographs, as a collaboration between Antonio Francesco Peruzzini and Alessandro Magnasco (for the figures). Some of the figural groups resemble ones in other known collaborations by Peruzzini and Magnasco. In particular, the woman being helped ashore by a man at left-center and the man yanking the boat ashore at center-right each appear in almost identical iterations in at least four other paintings.

De Troy depicted his female subjects as Venus disarming Cupid at least two other times: one of these portraits was sold at Sotheby's, London, May 8, 2019, lot 62, and the other was exhibited at the Musée Paul Dupuy in Toulouse in 1997. Both of these two works, which are very similar in composition, date to 1695-1700. | | When the present portrait was acquired in Paris in 1847, its subject was identified as Françoise-Athénaïse de Rochechouart de Mortemart, Marquise of Montespan (1640-1707), known as Madame de Montespan. Madame de Montespan was a highly influential mistress of Louis XIV who was known by some contemporaries as 'the true Queen of France'. She was one of the earliest patrons of François de Troy and a prominent client throughout his career; de Troy painted several known portraits of Madame de Montespan's children and relatives as well.
