He himself was a man of intense Christian faith, and the work in question is one of a group of religious paintings which are amongst his most personal and greatest achievements. | | The subject of The Good Shepherd | In Dyce's painting the robed figure of a shepherd leads a flock of sheep through an open gateway into a sunlit pasture. An ivy-clad fence runs away into the landscape, with a mountainous horizon. A tree stands beside the fence, with bare branches and a contorted stem, while in the far distance on the left stand further trees before a group of farm buildings. The ground across which the barefooted figure walks is stony, but the pasture into which he and his accompanying sheep enter offers the sustenance of fresh grass and water. The shepherd holds in his right hand a crook and looks downwards at the lamb which he holds in his left arm with clear awareness of the solemn duty of caring for his flock. | | When the painting was shown at the Royal Academy in the summer of 1859, and then again at the Liverpool Academy later in the same year, verse 11, Chapter 40, of the Book of Isaiah was attached in an abbreviated form: 'He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and shall gently lead those that are with young.' This text forms the opening of what is known as the 'Deutero-Isaiah', the oldest part of the Book of Isaiah and which was written by an anonymous author in the 6th century BCE at the time of the Babylonian exile. It describes how God determined to protect Jerusalem and that it was his intention to send a messiah to allow the Jewish people safe return to their city. The text pleads for the protection of the poor and dispossessed, but claims that righteousness comes not from Israel's Covenant with God but from God's essential holiness. | | In Dyce's painting, the sheepfold stands for the Promised Land; the sheep for the people of Israel and the shepherd for their Messiah. The Messiah is in turn a type of Jesus Christ, the Saviour. The painting is an exploration of typological symbolism – the parallels between events described in the Old and New Testaments and the links between types and antitypes – and of which study Victorian scholars were so preoccupied. In The Good Shepherd, Dyce created a universal symbol of loving care – which stands for the figure of Christ and of the Christian virtues. | | Images of the Good Shepherd as a type of Christ occur frequently in early Christian art, for example in wall paintings in the Roman catacombs, in sculpted sarcophagi, and in mosaics (as for example in the sixth-century Mausoleum of Galle Placidia in Ravenna), from a time before the conventions by which Christ was to be represented were established. Therefore, while on other occasions Dyce treated the figure of Christ following Biblical narrative, with The Good Shepherd he offered an image of a man like any other, performing a mundane duty, but who stands for the antitype of Christ and exemplifies his teaching. The work is therefore both absolutely immediate and direct in its message, treated as it is with scrupulous honesty and care, but also a highly sophisticated meditation on a particular type of Christian imagery. | | The precise date and likely setting of The Good Shepherd. | Although first exhibited in 1859, The Good Shepherd appears to have been painted two years earlier. In 1856 a cartoon or preparatory drawing apparently related to the same composition was shown amongst the drawings and miniatures at the Royal Academy summer exhibition (as mentioned by James Dafforne in his Art Journal article describing Dyce's work), while further evidence supporting a date of 1857 for the present painting is provided by the reference to it in a letter dated 10 September 1857 in which the painter listed his recent works: 'Here is my account of dispatch of business for the first part of this year [...] painted a picture of the Good Shepherd'. It seems likely that the physical setting of the subject was inspired by places Dyce had visited on the Isle of Arran on the west coast of Scotland, to which place he is known to have gone in or before 1856, or in Dumfriesshire and Galloway, where he had family friends who he was known on occasions to visit. The close observation of detail, as in for example, the circular feeding byre around the trunk of the dead tree at the upper left-hand corner of the composition, leaves no doubt but that this was an actual place. In the 1850s Dyce was committed to the principle of working out of doors so as to gain authentic representation of landscape and natural detail, as Jennifer Melville observed in 2006: 'Dyce imbues his paintings with an intensity of vision that come through direct observation of nature. He combines this with a spirituality that comes from his own deeply felt faith. This gives each work a personal dimension that is unique.' | | British artists working in the middle years of the nineteenth century occasionally provided landscape settings for their Old and New Testament subjects which were intended to represent or at least to suggest the topography of the Holy Land, whether treated from the imagination or on the basis of actual exploration and study. Alternatively, and as on this occasion, painters were content to represent Biblical subjects in landscape settings with which they themselves were immediately familiar. Debate about the appropriateness of Biblical subjects in settings other than those of a supposed Holy Land recurred. Of Dyce's subject The Man of Sorrows (National Gallery of Scotland, Edinburgh), which shows Christ seated on a glacially smoothed rock in a wider upland setting which probably represents Aberdeenshire, F.G. Stephens, writing in the Athenaeum, asked why the artist had not made a similar attempt: 'But why – with all this literalness – not be completely loyal, and paint Christ himself in the land where he really lived?' In fact, as Michaela Giebelhausen has observed, 'Stephens either failed to realise, or simply ignored, the fact that the jarring juxtaposition between figure and landscape [in The Man of Sorrows but the same response might apply to The Good Shepherd] was intentional and essential to the meaning of the painting [...] In the face of the doubt and anxiety characteristic of the age, Dyce offered an incongruous image of Christ and invited his viewer to make a leap of faith which demanded the acceptance of Christ's divinity notwithstanding such questioning.' In his later paintings of religious themes Dyce had no need for such motifs to lend authenticity to his religious subjects, so that The Good Shepherd (described by Marcia Pointon as 'aggressively contemporary') is striking for its verisimilitude and authenticity. | | The sincerity of Christian message radiates from every element of the composition and requires no elucidation while it is the actuality of the scene as a real place that is so compelling. Even the physiognomy of the figure of the shepherd and his beard and hair, which seems to have a reddish tinge, allows the spectator to feel himself in the presence of one who is recognisably Scottish rather than Semitic. Pointon elaborated on the painter's need to represent a religious subject as something entirely real: 'Dyce, as an extremely active and articulate High Churchman, believed in a contemporary Christ. His deliberate presentation of biblical characters as very human and existing in a physical environment described in concrete detail is essential to his theological interpretation of his subject and is not merely a means of evoking the ethos of an earlier style of art or of creating an anachronistic appeal.' | | Dyce and the Pre-Raphaelites | The point of intersection between Dyce and the Pre-Raphaelites (they themselves were approximately a generation younger than he) was in the creation of religious subjects which would inform, educate and instil faith. To paint carefully and according to the principle of 'truth to nature' was for him, as it was for William Holman Hunt, a way of honouring God, for he believed that – although the physical world might be explained in scientific terms – nonetheless the universe was a divine creation. In 1850 Dyce persuaded John Ruskin to look carefully at John Everett Millais's painting Christ in the House of his Parents (Tate), shown that year at the Royal Academy, and with the consequence that the critic took up the cause of Pre-Raphaelitism | with letters to The Times and the pamphlet Pre-Raphaelitism. Dyce visited Italy three times, and in fact had a larger knowledge of European art – and particularly early Italian schools of painting – than any member of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood. The interdependence of Dyce and the Pre-Raphaelites is partial but mutually important; as Allen Staley wrote of him: 'His work is not central to the movement, but with sobriety and discipline he built upon Pre-Raphaelitism to paint a handful of the most memorable pictures of the Victorian era.' | | Dyce the Christian polymath | Dyce was a man engaged with a multitude of different interests – spiritual and scientific – and in addition to his commitments as a painter and public servant. In all respects, he believed in the power of art to convey the Christian message. In 1839, he had been a founder member of the Society for the Promotion of Christian Knowledge (an organisation led by members of the Tractarian movement, the purpose of which was to return the Anglican Church to its pre-Reformation function to inspire Christian belief). In the early days of the Society there was discussion about how a projected book paraphrasing the Gospels of the New Testament should be illustrated, either with engravings after Old Masters, or – as advocated by Dyce – with images made by contemporary artists which he believed would be more clearly understood by a modern audience. In 1856, in a letter in which he reflected upon how churches might be decorated to encourage faith, he commented on the sixteenth-century text known as the 'King's Book' (1543), in which as he explained 'not only justifies but orders the erection of images of Christ [...] it also directs all curates to instruct their parishioners in the lessons taught by such images and pictures.' | | Ruskin and Dyce knew each other without ever becoming friends. At least twice they clashed openly, once in a dispute about how art should be taught (as explained by Lindsay Errington in her 1992 article 'Ascetics and sensualists, William Dyce's views on Christian art'), but before that when Dyce issued a contradiction of opinions expressed by Ruskin in his text Notes on the Construction of Sheepfolds (1851). In the early 1850s Ruskin was an Evangelical Protestant, virulently opposed to the extension of Roman Catholic influence in Britain at a time of the establishment of a Catholic church hierarchy. Dyce, by contrast, was a High Church Episcopalian Anglo-Catholic, and one who occasionally contemplated conversion (following the lead, as it would have been, of his friend John Henry Newman). Thus, Ruskin and Dyce differed on the principles of organisation, function and purpose of the Church. Ruskin's Notes on the Construction of Sheepfolds was intended as a supplement to his three-volume Stones of Venice, the sub-text of which was that the true expression of faith depended upon a personal freedom which might never be achieved by people living under the authority of the Roman Church. Dyce's response was to defend the role of the priesthood, trusting the church administration with responsibility to care for the people and their needs. As Emily Hope Thomson has explained, Dyce was the first to make 'a written and later a pictorial response' to Ruskin's text. The written response took the form of Notes on Shepherds and Sheep: A Letter to John Ruskin (1851); the pictorial response was The Good Shepherd. The argument between the two men hinged on whether the person of faith might believe that they were in direct communication with Christ, or whether it was accepted that an appointed priesthood might stand proxy for the Saviour. | | How The Good Shepherd was received | The Good Shepherd was met with huge enthusiasm when first seen in public in 1859. The Art Journal, in its review of the Royal Academy exhibition said of it: 'This is a literal presentation of the Saviour as the Shepherd; he gathers the sheep into the fold, bearing in his arms a lamb, and being followed by the sheep as he enters. [...] It is painted in the most perfect purity of feeling; it is, in truth, a work of the highest order, compelling not only reverence for the theme, but respect for the artist who could so well conceive, and so admirably picture it.' A year later, James Dafforne, in his Art Journal article describing Dyce's work, wrote: 'Neither have we forgotten "The Good Shepherd," exhibited in 1859 [...] The title sufficiently indicates the subject, which has been literally carried out, in a spirit and with a feeling that, viewed either artistically or devotionally, leaves nothing to be desired: it is altogether a work of the highest character.' The painting presumably remained unsold at the 1859 Academy exhibition and was shown again later in the year at the Liverpool Academy and where it was awarded the first prize. Although the figure in this case is standing, the paintings are similar in type and the same embroidered cloak is worn in both. In the bedroom of an ancient country house, a beautiful young woman kneels in a prayerful attitude beside a large brass-studded leather trunk, her arms resting on it as, lost in thoughts of her absent love, she gazes towards the light that filters through the casement window. Only two small panes are visible but these are sufficient to suggest that it is a frosty moonlit night. Inside, all is dark and shrouded. Her narrow bed stands against the wall, its frame adorned with Gothic finials. The padded headboard is embroidered with a pair of angels and the words 'Deus Magnificat', pointing to the pious nature of the household of which she is a member. The lute and bow traditionally signify the pleasures and happiness of love-making. Lying silent on the bed, they echo her lonely state and an emotional life as yet unfulfilled. | | The girl has gathered flowers while walking: the forget-me-nots which give the painting its title; the ox-eye daisies and red poppies. Ox-eye daisies signify patience and the poppies consolation, so that despite the present separation from her loved one, the omens are good. | | The picture centres on the feelings of the girl so clearly revealed in her earnest face and pleading eyes, and Hughes has created the perfect ambience for her. The room resonates with warm, sonorous colours: the dark crimson of the trunk and bed cover; the pale brown panelling and floor; the red and gold figures of the angels; all serve to enhance the luminous figure of the girl in her diaphanous gown and blue satin cloak. In the letter quoted above, Hughes' own itemising of the accessories underlines the importance he attached to them, and the results are patent. The solid painting, the meticulous attention to detail, and the lighting effects make this one of Hughes's most successful single figure compositions. | | The picture has been described as echoing Hughes' Pre-Raphaelite past1, and although the lighting and colour are more brilliant, in subject, composition and mood it is indeed reminiscent of examples like Millais' Mariana (1851, Tate Gallery). Hughes was only eighteen years old when he discovered the Pre-Raphaelites, and in the 1850s he made a major contribution to the movement in the form of works such as April Love and The Eve of St Agnes (both 1856, Tate Gallery) in which he combined realism and poetry in equal measure. His later work diversified to include illustration, landscape, and portraiture - some of the most successful of which were painted in the 'aesthetic' vein - as well as the figurative subject pictures which remained his chief ambition. Hughes outlived most of the artists of his generation, exhibiting regularly at the RA and elsewhere until the year of his death in 1915. | | 1 Quoted in Leonard Roberts, Arthur Hughes: His Life and Works, p. 235. | 2 Stephen Wildman, Arthur Hughes, Museum of Richmond, 1998, p. 6.

Carbonell. | | Tangier had long been a draw for European Orientalists, among the first visitors being Eugène Delacroix, John Frederick Lewis and David Roberts in the 1830s. Later visitors included Alfred Dehodencq and Mariano Fortuny, the latter's work 'helping to construct the myth of Oriental Tangier' according to Jordi Carbonell1. Benjamin-Constant first visited Tangier in 1870 then returned, at the behest of Charles Tissot, a friend of his father, in 1871, spending 18 months working in the city. As George Clairin, who met Benjamin- Constant during his first visit, later noted, 'his entire oeuvre was subjected to the fortunate and beneficial influence of Tangier; his entire Orient was Morocco ... he always carried with him this first impression of Tangier, white and bright.'2 | | During his sojourn in the early 1870s, Benjamin-Constant made numerous sketches of the city and its inhabitants, working them up into compositions back in his studio, with the many Islamic objects and artifacts he collected used as props. These would inform his output for the next ten years. | | Benjamin-Constant's meticulous attention to architectural and costume detail reflects both his fascination with the visual richness of Tangier and the broader European interest for the exotic. His use of vibrant colour, dramatic lighting, and carefully orchestrated figures conveys a sense of theatricality, while maintaining ethnographic precision in the depiction of dress, weaponry, and domestic objects. This combination of accuracy and artistic flourish helped solidify his reputation as a leading Orientalist painter of his generation. He was one of the founding members of the Société des Peintres Orientalistes Français in 1893, alongside artists such as Alphonse-Étienne Dinet. | | Compositionally, the present lot calls to mind The Pasha's Soldiers (circa 1880, Museum of Art, Rhode Island School of Design), with soldiers at rest among the ramparts of the 'White City', the sparkling Mediterranean sea beyond. Exhibited in the European Arts section at the Canadian National Exhibition in Toronto in 1910, the painting was shown alongside major works by Daniel Maclise, Harold Knight, Frank Holl, Frederic, Lord Leighton, George Clausen, William Holman Hunt, Stanhope Forbes, Gaston la Touche, Pascal Dagnan-Bouveret, William Bougereau, and Jean-Léon Gérôme . | | This work also exemplifies Benjamin-Constant's interest in combining leisure and military life, a recurring theme in his North African scenes. By presenting soldiers at rest, rather than in action, he captures a moment of calm and humanizes the figures, allowing viewers to engage with them on both a formal and narrative levels. Such compositional choices were influential among his contemporaries and contributed to the enduring appeal of his Moroccan subjects in European collections. | | Henry James Turner (1831-1924), who owned the present lot in the early 20th Century, was a successful industrialist, who assembled a large collection of art by contemporary British and continental artists. Turner also owned Dagnan-Bouveret's La Vaccination, included in the present auction (see lot 41). | | 1Jordi A. provenance: Anon. sale, Maitre Blache, Paris, 3 June 1981. | Private collection, UK. | | A founder of the Society for French Orientalist Painters, Alphonse-Étienne Dinet's love of North Africa and its people was so strong that he eventually converted to Islam in 1905, taking the name Nasrédine. His knowledge of the Arabic language allowed him access to remote locations and enabled him to capture a more intimate portrayal of the life of North Africa. | | Few Orientalist artists are remembered as national icons in the countries they depicted. Yet Dinet (1861-1929), a French-born and Paris-trained painter secured the posthumous reputation of 'master' in Algeria where he lived and worked for almost fifty years. The son of a prosperous lawyer, Dinet first completed his military service in Normandy before enrolling in the École des Beaux-Arts and the Galland atelier where he studied painting and anatomy, eventually moving onto the Académie Julian for the remainder of his education. His paintings received critical acclaim at the Salon des Artistes Français and afterward, in 1884, Dinet embarked on the first of many trips to Algeria with a team of entomologists. He returned the following year and completed his first two works inspired by the region, Les Terrasses de Laghouat and L'Oued M'sila après l'Orage. During his third trip in 1886, Dinet, along with thirteen other artists including Paul Leroy and Baron Arthur Chassériau, formed the Société des Peintres Orientalistes Français with Jean-Léon Gérôme and Benjamin-Constant as honorary presidents, and Léonce Bénédite, Conservator of the Musée du Luxembourg, as president. | | In 1888, Dinet took important steps to solidify his growing interest in North Africa: he enrolled in formal Arabic classes at the Oriental Language School in Paris and returned to Algeria for a fourth time, accompanied by the young guide, Sliman Ben Ibrahim, with whom Dinet was to eventually live and collaborate with for many years. Dinet's work was displayed in the Algerian pavilion at the Universal Exhibition of 1889, where he would also win the silver medal for painting, and following this surge of publicity, Dinet helped found the Société Nationale des Beaux-Arts along with thirteen other artists. In 1904, after spending many months of each year in Algeria, Dinet decided to create a more permanent base for himself in-country and bought a house in the southern Saharan city of Bou-Saada. | | Delving deeper into Orientalist themes with his work now spanning two continents, Dinet had a respected place among the desert culture from which he drew inspiration. Having rejected early representations of the Maghreb modelled after exotic scenes taken from Greek and Roman antiquity, Dinet was a stunning realist, focused more on the interactions between natives, representations of women and manifestations of the Muslim religion. Despite his numerous paintings of nude Algerian youths – he was, surprisingly, never wanting for indigenous models – Dinet's paintings lack the frank eroticism of his counterparts who illustrated an Orient full of reclining odalisques oozing sensuality. | | Employing the use of photography to capture the fleeting expressions of his models, Dinet's cinematic approach was far removed from the disengaged reserve of fin-de-siècle aesthetics which lent an air of theatricality. His landscapes lack exaggerated romanticism and his depictions of women, a favourite subject, hold no territorial claims over the eastern body seen through western eyes. With his conversion to Islam in 1908 and made formal in 1913, Dinet used his nudes to express a right to represent beauty as created by God, rather than the purely voyeuristic impressions of imagined, private moments. | | With such composites frequenting the canvases of his contemporaries, it is easy to criticize the Orientalist genre of painting Dinet came to define as perpetuating the mythology of an 'empire of the senses' free from the restraints of western civilization and encompassing a timeless zone of primitivism. Yet, this argument is precisely why Dinet is so important to the history and popularity of Orientalist art. With each brush stroke, Dinet penetrated the deeper themes of family, faith and survival unique to the Saharan life he shared with his subjects instead of skimming the surface decor of earlier Orientalist painters passing through the region. | | Never seeking out the exceptional or strange for subject matter, Dinet believed the mission of his art was to describe the souls of his models, express the essence of a people, and to celebrate his own adopted faith of Islam. With those tasks in mind, Dinet also collaborated with his friend, Ben Ibrahim, on translating and illustrating books about Algeria, such as Khadra, Danseurs des Ouled Nails and Tableaux de la vie Arabe, which became quintessential to foreign understanding and perceptions of North Africa. In the words of Léonce Bénédite, Dinet 'became an Arab, a cultured Arab, who clung desperately to the last vestiges of greatness of his race.' | | Shortly after making the Hajj pilgrimage to Mecca, Dinet died in his native France in 1929. Today in Bou-Saada, where he was eventually buried, The Nasreddine-Etienne Dinet Museum stands as a testament to Dinet's unique place in the history of Orientalist painters. Though later on in his career to be found behind the times by his peers, Dinet and his true understanding of Saharan life lend his works encapsulating the history and peoples of Algeria an authenticity rarely surpassed. The art critic Camille Mauclair predicted Dinet's staggering importance in the history of Orientalist painters: 'Later on, they (Dinet's canvases) will be incomparable references; they will have fixed without the coldness of archaeology a civilization and a race called upon to transform themselves to the point of travesty by the fatalities of a 'modernism' that is slowly killing the Orient.' By allowing his models to face forward rather than backward to suit the tastes of a time obsessed with antiquity, the work of Etienne Dinet acts as a rich cultural currency towards understanding a way of life now transformed yet far from forgotten.

Braun (see Wellcome Collection 17870i). | | | There are some artists of rare ability, of extreme sincerity, who are astonishing observers, far more conscientious than one can imagine, who spent enormous amounts of time and who lavish superior talent to give us just the emotion which might be produced by photography. M. Dagnan-Bouveret is one of these artists. | Le Siecle 1885. | | In the latter half of the 19th century, French society stood at the crossroads of tradition and modernisation. Nowhere is this tension more evident than in the work of Pascal Dagnan-Bouveret (1852–1929), a realist painter whose oeuvre captures the quiet transformation of rural France. The present work, painted in 1882, is a prime example of how art can reflect and support social progress. La Vaccination became part of a national narrative that celebrated science, health, and the expansion of modern values into rural life. | | Dagnan-Bouveret was a leading figure in Academic Realism, a style characterised by meticulous attention to detail, idealised yet naturalistic figures, and a focus on moral or social themes. Born in Paris, the son of a tailor, he entered the École des Beaux-Arts in 1869; among his tutors were Alexandre Cabanel and Jean-Léon Gérôme. During his studies he formed a close friendship with Gustave Courtois. His education was briefly stalled by the Franco-Prussian War and the Paris Commune; resuming in 1872 when he entered Gérôme's atelier. Dagnan-Bouveret was heavily influenced by both classical techniques and the emerging Naturalist movement. Uniquely, he was also one of the first French artists to integrate photography into his process, allowing for a level of precision and emotional nuance rarely seen in academic works of the time. | | Dagnan-Bouveret married Coutois' cousin Anne-Marie in 1879, the couple spending a great deal of time in Corre, a village in the Franche-Comté region of north-eastern France. The artist's Salon debut came in 1875, and he became a regular exhibitor there, as well as at the Salon de la Société Nationale des Beaux-Arts, the Exposition Universelle -winning major prizes in 1889 and 1900- and the Salon de Champ-de-Mars. He was elected to the Académie des Beaux-Arts of the Institut de France in 1900, one of the youngest painters to ever receive this honour. | | La Vaccination portrays a rural family gathered in a modest interior, probably a schoolroom, as a doctor administers a smallpox vaccine to a child. The setting is humble, the figures understated, yet deeply expressive. The mother, seated, gently restrains the child while others look on with solemn curiosity. The doctor, dressed in formal attire, appears calm and deliberate. The overall mood is one of quiet dignity, reflecting both the human vulnerability of the scene and the trust placed in modern medicine. Through its naturalistic lighting, soft colours, and photographic realism, Dagnan-Bouveret elevates what might seem a mundane act into a moment of profound emotional and cultural significance. The painting captures a transitional moment: the encroachment of scientific rationalism into the realm of rural tradition, handled not with drama but with empathy. | | The early history of the work is well recorded; it is listed in the stock books of Goupil & Cie, Paris, for 1882: '16415, Vaccine, 20-12-82, Londres @ H. Turner Esq, Dagnan Bouveret avec portage de Benefice [with profit sharing], 14-4-83'. Founded in 1850 by Auguste Goupil (1806-1893), Goupil & Cie were a central force in the French art market. Dealing in art works by the major academic, realist, romantic and Barbizon painters of the day, and also licencing and distributing reproduction prints, at their zenith, the business had offices in Paris, New York, London (established by Ernest Gambart), Brussels and The Hague. In 1884 the business was succeeded by Boussod, Valadon & Co. and continued until 1919. | | According to Goupil's records, the painting was sold to H. Turner, who is the listed lender when the work was exhibited in 1883. It is likely that Goupil's purchaser was Henry James Turner (1831-1924), a successful industrialist, who assembled a large collection of art by contemporary British and continental artists (Turner was also the owner of On the Roofs by Benjamin-Constant, which is featured in the current sale, see lot 25). Following Turner's purchase of the work, it was exhibited at the Paris Salon in 1883, the Royal Academy in 1884 -the artist's only submission to the famous London exhibition- and the Exposition Universelle in Paris in 1889. | | The 1889 Exposition Universelle was one of the most ambitious world's fairs of the 19th century. It celebrated the centenary of the French Revolution and served as a platform to project France's industrial, scientific, and artistic achievements. Among its most iconic symbols was the unveiling of the Eiffel Tower, itself a triumph of modern engineering. With this backdrop, La Vaccination was exhibited in the Palais des Beaux-Arts, part of the fair's Fine Arts Pavilion. Its inclusion speaks to the painting's alignment with the fair's themes: progress, health, and the moral duty of the state to modernise and educate its population. By depicting vaccination - a then-controversial practice in many rural areas - the painting subtly endorsed France's growing public health initiatives and reinforced a sense of national unity through shared scientific progress. | | Dagnan-Bouveret's technique is crucial to the painting's impact. His use of photographic references allowed for subtle facial expressions, delicate skin tones, and lifelike body language. These details lend credibility and intimacy to the scene. The balanced composition—with figures arranged in a semicircle around the doctor—creates a sense of shared focus and emotional weight. His method anticipated modern realism, even as he remained rooted in academic traditions. The inclusion of the work at the 1889 Exposition Universelle cemented Dagnan-Bouveret's reputation as a socially aware artist who could translate complex themes into accessible imagery. But this is more than a depiction of a medical procedure; it is a celebration of science and progress aimed to reassure a nation facing change. Through his technical skill and emotional insight, Dagnan-Bouveret has captured this moment of quiet revolution. | | We are grateful to the late Professor Gabriel P. Weisberg for confirming the authenticity of the present lot on the basis of photographs.

provenance: Anon. sale, Waddington's, Toronto, circa 1980. | Private collection, North America. | | Léon Bazile Perrault was a leading figure of late 19th century French painting, admired for his technique and his sensitive portrayals of childhood and mythological subject matter. Born in Poitiers in 1832, he trained in Paris under François-Édouard Picot and later worked closely with William Adolphe Bouguereau, absorbing the classical discipline and luminous surface finish that characterise the academic tradition. Through them, Perrault also inherited an admiration for the 18th century masters Jean-Antoine Watteau and François Boucher, whose spirit of grace and refinement he carried forward into his own work. | | Perrault began exhibiting at the Paris Salon in 1861 and quickly established a successful career during the Second Empire, a period in which the bourgeois public increasingly developed an interest in art that offered visual pleasure and emotional escape. His compositions, from mythological idylls and allegories to genre scenes and portraits, responded perfectly to this demand. He received several Salon distinctions, including an honourable mention in 1864, a second-class medal in 1876, and in 1887 he was appointed Chevalier de la Légion d'Honneur. | | Although he mastered many academic genres, Perrault is especially celebrated for his images of children, which he portrayed with extraordinary delicacy. These works reflect the 19th century conception of childhood, presenting youth as a state of grace, vulnerability and charm. In the present work, Perrault depicts a moment of mourning, with a mother on a prie-dieu accompanied by her young children. This intimate scene reveals the vulnerability of the sitters and the quiet depth of their despair, while also demonstrating Perrault's ability to unite academic refinement with genuine emotional resonance. | | By the end of his career, he was hors concours at the Salon, exhibiting without jury approval, and his reputation had become firmly established in France and abroad. Perrault died in Royan in 1908. His paintings are today held in several museum collections including Bordeaux, Poitiers, La Rochelle and Stuttgart.

Ross, William Bouguereau: Catalogue Raisonné of his Painted Work, New York, 2010, p. 299, no. 1895/08, illustrated. | | In Fardeau agréable all Bouguereau's formidable prowess is distilled onto the canvas in two engaging young sisters and the pastoral idyll in which they exist; the result is an image of beauty at its purest in the mind of the artist. This is art for art's sake with Bouguereau giving all his attention to the flawless depiction of the figures, spurning any sense of narrative. The composition is dominated by the two sisters in an idealised image of their humble existence. Pastoral subjects such as this, almost always a single peasant girl or two sisters, became the subject matter for some of Bouguereau's most revered and popular works. | | While some French artists of the Realist movement such as Jean-François Millet and Léon Augustin Lhermitte sought to faithfully depict peasant life and its labours, Bouguereau romanticised it and here we see a serene, innocent scene unburdened by any trace of social or economic hardship. In striving to achieve a vision of idyllic rural youth he deliberately ignores the realities of political, industrial and urban life of 19th late century France. According to Alfred Nettement, a student at the Académie Julien, his teacher Bouguereau 'had an absolute horror of what we would call realism and he always said that reality is charming when it borrows a gleam of poetry from the imagination'1. | | The sisters are set before a landscape and sky which not only attest to Bouguereau's skill as a landscape painter but are redolent of late 19th century taste. The first half of the century saw the industrial revolution change pastoral landscapes in Europe and America for ever and as manufacturing increased and urban centres expanded, so did nostalgia for an unspoilt countryside and peasant life. In Fardeau agréable, as in nearly all of Bouguereau's work, the industrial age is not evident, no buildings mar the landscape, and no smoke clouds the skies of the imagined Arcadia. Bouguereau raises his figures above the harsh truth of day-to-day existence in the French peasant countryside and exalts the joy and tenderness of youth and the beauty of nature. | | The younger sister can be identified as Yvonne, one of Bouguereau's favourite models. Little biographical information is known about Yvonne and her two sisters, Jeanne and Marguerite, however they probably lived in La Rochelle as they came regularly to the Bouguereau household and were treated like family. They provided much inspiration for Bouguereau who was born in the area and spent his summers there in the 1890s to escape the social and professional pressures of Paris. The growth of Yvonne and her sisters is recorded in Bouguereau's work of the 1890s, from Yvonne's first appearance in Allant à la Fontaine in 1893 (J. B. Speed Museum, Louisville, Kentucky) at the age of perhaps five or six, we see her grow up as Bouguereau used her as a model until the end of his life. | | Often Bouguereau's figures appear contemplative or distracted, far away in a daydream, however here he seems intent on portraying Yvonne's character as well as her likeness. She gazes engagingly out of the canvas with the confidence and innocence of youth fixing the viewer with an expression full of emotion and intelligence. The elder sister stands on the cusp of womanhood and the dashes of colour Bouguereau has added in the form of wildflowers in the lower left, not only add colour to the composition but come to symbolise the flowering of youth, connotations which would not have been lost on his audience. Bouguereau has been lauded for his mastery of rendering the human figure and nowhere is this more evident than in Fardeau agréable. The sisters sit together in perfect balance and harmony, their movement natural as they pass through the landscape, briefly interrupted by the viewer. | | Great care and consideration are given to every passage and every detail and the execution of the interlocked hands is a perfect example of this meticulous attention. To achieve such authenticity in his figures Bouguereau became a master of the academic style. While working on an oil such as this he would produce many preparatory drawings paying close attention to each individual detail, working and reworking the important parts of the composition ensuring he had full freedom and confidence when setting paint to canvas. Unlike many of his contemporaries, he also preferred to use life models instead of adapting to use photographs as can be seen in fig. 1 which shows Bourguereau in the summer of 1898 working on Les deux soeurs, 1899 and features Yvonne three years after her appearance in Fardeau agréable. | | The latter period of Bouguereau's career from which Fardeau agréable dates followed the great successes of his classical, mythological and religious subjects of his earlier oeuvre and was ushered in by his association with the art dealer Durand-Ruel in the 1860s. To cater to the tastes of his patrons and particularly the international market, Bouguereau shifted his choice of subjects away from the historical and religious and towards the romanticised images of the pastoral, of the type we see here. This resulted in an appetite for Bouguereau's work in North America which neared insatiable in the later years of the 19th century fuelled by first by the French dealer Paul Durand-Ruel and then solidified by Durand-Ruel's foremost competitor, Adolphe Goupil. Between 1866 and 1887, Bouguereau would sell ten to twelve works per year to Goupil for an agreed upon sum, and Goupil then sold approximately nine out of every ten to dealers outside of France, mostly to Wallis in London and Knoedler in New York. In fact, only eight works painted during this period are recorded by Goupil as having been sold to collectors in France. | | The taste of these American patrons would lay the foundation for the collection of many American museums and as art critic and author Clarence Cook noted in his second volume of Art and Artists of Our Time, "Hardly any French painter can be named who is more widely popular in America than Bouguereau. His pictures always meet with a ready sale at large prices, and at the exhibitions they are sure of approval from the majority of the visitors, who would probably pass by Delacroix, Decamps, or Puvis de Chavannes, with small notice, or none at all"2. Fardeau agréable formed part of this tradition when it was acquired by Pittsburgh based financier and iron magnate Alexander McBurney Byers, directly from Knoedler just twenty-four days after it entered the galleries' inventory. | | 1A. Nettement, William Bouguereau, L'Académie Julien, January 1908, p. 3, as quoted in M. S. Walker, William Bouguereau, exh. cat., Montreal, 1984, p. 57. | 2As quoted in Fronia E. Wissman, Bouguereau, San Francisco, 1996, p. 108-9.

provenance: Private European collection. |  | The present lot is accompanied by an expertise certificate from Gianni Caffiero and Ivan Samarine dated February 2026 and is included in their numbered archive of the artist's work. |  | Aivazovsky, renowned worldwide for his marine paintings, was a virtuoso of the stormy sea. The artist possessed an astonishing ability to work rapidly, often completing a painting in a single session. It is this lightness and airiness of his brush that lends his works a special expressiveness and vibrancy. |  | The subject matter, the rendering of colour and light, the dramatic sea, and the small, staffage figures of the men - all this is the master's textbook language. The painting vividly expresses the desire to convey the power of nature, its superiority over the weakness of the small man, completely defenceless against the unbridled elements. |  | The sea on the canvas lives, breathes, and moves. The artist masterfully depicts it in numerous shades of blue, from an almost blackish blue in the depths to a transparent turquoise near the shore. A masterful play of light makes the sea in the background dark and threatening, while the foreground is illuminated by bright reflections, like a ray of hope sent to the shipwrecked survivors. The snow-white foaming crests of the waves are painted with meticulous care; they rise from the surface like two hands reaching out to grasp a person and pull him back into the depths. |  | The painting's composition emphasizes the scale of the confrontation between man and nature. Enormous waves, rising in powerful billows, are ready to engulf everything in their path. Against their backdrop, the tiny figures of the shipwrecked survivors seem like grains of sand in an ocean of raging elements. This is a characteristic technique of Aivazovsky and his school, when depicting the majesty of nature. The log from the wrecked ship in the foreground once again recalls the uncontrollable force of the elements. The anxious, restless rhythm of the waves conveys a sense of confusion and fear before the indomitable force of the sea storm. The artist masterfully utilizes chiaroscuro contrasts. The dark masses of water and sky are offset by bright highlights, creating a unique emotional richness in the work.

provenance: The Cecil French collection. | Presented to Mr Jack Redford on the occasion of his marriage 9th October 1948 by his colleagues at The National City Bank of New York, London. | Thence by descent, private collection, UK. | | Exhibited | London, Royal Academy, Winter Exhibition, 1942 (according to label attached to the backboard). | | Frederic Cayley Robinson was a British painter and illustrator renowned for his meticulous draughtsmanship and symbolic imagery. Early in his career, he worked in the Newlyn style, producing seascapes in a naturalistic manner. After moving to Paris in 1891, his work began to reflect the influence of the Symbolist movement, particularly the Nabis group. His style evolved from Impressionist tendencies towards a Pre-Raphaelite approach, and like many artists of his generation, he later travelled to Florence to study the Old Masters, adopting techniques such as tempera painting. Each of these artistic encounters left a lasting imprint on his work. | | Robinson's academic training is evident in the precision of his line and form. He often depicted solitary figures most often women or children set in rural or pastoral landscapes. His use of harmonious, muted colour schemes lent these allegorical themes a sense of calm rather than dramatic intensity. The Little Shepherdess embodies these qualities, with its lone figure in a tranquil pastoral setting, rendered in a subdued palette that enhances its quiet, contemplative mood.

McKibbin, Sargent's Boston, Boston, 1956, pp. 92 and 97. | | This portrait is a study for one of the figures in Sargent's 1920-22 oil Some General Officers of the Great War (National Portrait Gallery, London). | | Sir Charles Macpherson Dobell (1869-1954) was born in Quebec and after his primary education in Canada, attended Charterhouse in England for two years as his father had emigrated to Liverpool due to his employment in the lumber trade. He returned to Canada for his preliminary military training before being commissioned into the 1st Bn. Royal Welsh Fusiliers in August 1890. He served his military apprenticeship in Britain's colonial wars, staying with the 1st Bn. for the next five years, learning how to command men. Postings with the 2nd Bn. The Royal Welsh Fusiliers in Crete, South Africa and China (suppressing the Boxer Rebellion) followed. | | Dobell's rise in the Edwardian decade was meteoric, reflecting his talent as an officer but also his ambition and connections. He left Staff College in 1904 for command in Nigeria, followed by periods in England and South Africa. During this time he married, in March 1908, a widow with two children who duly had their own daughter in South Africa in 1912. On the eve of the outbreak of the First World War he was Inspector-General of the West African Frontier Force. | | The declaration of war found Dobell on leave in England, but given his African experience he was soon given command of the British troops and eventually the Allied Forces in the two German colonies of Togoland and Cameroon. The German defence in Cameroon was stiff and the fighting attritional, but the Allied forces prevailed in February 1916. The victory was celebrated given how stagnant the campaign in France and Flanders had become and Dobell's star rose further. | | Dobell was next posted to the Middle-East in June 1916. His involvement in two failed attempts to take Gaza in 1917 are seen as perhaps the only blot on an otherwise pristine record. Although Gaza was eventually taken by the subsequent command, thanks somewhat to the preparations laid by Dobell and his superiors, he could not escape judgement for the two bloody, failed attempts at the objective from London which was hungry for news of success. On his return home he was immediately posted to India where he would stay until 1920. | | Through his career Dobell was mentioned in despatches nine times, he retired with the honorary rank of lieutenant-general in 1923 and retained links with the Regiment up to the months preceding his death in 1954.

provenance: Acquired from the 'South African Association of Arta-Western Cape Region: An Exhibition of Painting By Stanley Pinker' exhibition, Cape Town, July 1974; | Thence by decent; | A private collection. | | Exhibited | Cape Town, 'South African Association of Arta-Western Cape Region: An Exhibition of Painting By Stanley Pinker', 1974, No. 20. | | Stanley Pinker was born in Windhoek, South West Africa, in 1924. He began his artistic training in Cape Town under the tutelage of Maurice van Essche. Enrolling in a graphic design course before changing programs after attending a life drawing class. Pinker then continued his studies in Europe from 1951. Throughout the 1950s and 60s, the artist worked and studied in London and the South of France, experiencing European modernist movements first hand. | | The formal concerns of the Fauves and Cubists inspired Pinker's experimental and theatrical compositions. In Mr Stephen and Mrs Daphne Woolf at Home, depictions of bodies and objects are reduced to essential shapes and colours. While a composition of two intertwined bodies is implied, there is little differentiation in perspective within the body's contextual and objective space. Pinker commented, "I've always thought of space as something 'tangible' and have been drawn to artists who have used mural-like space rather than artists who create an illusion of space through perspective". (Stanley Pinker in Michael Stevenson, Stanley Pinker, (Cape Town: Michael Stevenson, 2004), p. 19.) In line with this, the present work presents us with a mural-like scene where there is no distinction between the primary subject and background, but in fact an intertwined overall scene. | | The colour palette holds integral significance in not only the aesthetic structures of the work, but also the conceptual narrative in Pinker's use of green, gold, black and white tones. These colours correlated to those used in the African National Congress flag, a nod from Pinker to the contextual framework the painting was created in. While this isn't the first time that Pinker has referenced this colour palette in his work (as it had also more literally been used in works by the artist such as Referendum (1992)), a correlation may also be made to the work's subjects and their relationship to the political party. Known for its opposition to the Apartheid and advocation of the rights of black South African people, the ANC was banned between 1960 to 1990 in South Africa due to concerns of the party's swelling popularity in the face of repression and the violent attacks such as the Sharpeville massacre. A self-described liberation movement, this political party has since remained the largest political party in South Africa since 1994. In intertwining this palette with the composition of the work, the mural-esque content becomes focused rather than generalised as Pinker had himself said on his return to South Africa from London "I started to think that it wasn't enough to paint an idealised specific landscape - the introduction of figures made the situation broader, less specific of place and more specific of content." (p. 17). | | The titles of his artworks are of great significance to Pinker. While little is known of the couple that Mr Stephen and Mrs Daphne Woolf at Home refers to, it easily could be concluded that Pinker had a close relationship with the sitters. The intimacy of the scene gives way not only to the domestic lives of Mr and Mrs Woolfe, but also the closeness they may have had with Pinker. Whilst title-specific, the meaning, like in most paintings created by the artist, appears to the viewer in a mirage fashion. We are left wondering, who are Mr & Mrs Woolf? What is their relevance with the ANC? However, these questions only cement Mr Stephen and Mrs Daphne Woolf at Home as an iconic work within the artist's oeuvre, in keeping with his philosophy: "An essential quality is mystery. For me no good work gives up all its secrets." (p. 20). | | Bibliography | M. Stevenson, Stanley Pinker, (Cape Town: Michael Stevenson, 2004).

provenance: Acquired directly from the artist at an exhibition at the Italian Cultural Institute, Lagos circa. late 1990s– early 2000s; | A private collection. | | El Anatsui began his artistic training at the College of Art, University of Science and Technology in Kumasi, where he was given a grounding education in Western art traditions and practices. Wanting to connect with the arts of his own country, he began to visit the Kumasi National Cultural Centre on weekends. Here he was exposed to weavers, potters, cloth-printers and carvers, all working in indigenous methods. | | El Anatsui began to incorporate elements from these crafts into his own work, forging a distinctly Ghanaian aesthetic. The present work employs the colours and geometric symbols traditionally used for Asante Adinkra cloth. The age-old Adinkra patterns are counter-posed by modern construction techniques. The planks of wood have been cut with a chainsaw and blackened with an acetylene torch. For the artist, the tearing of the saw through wood functioned as "a metaphor for the way in which the western powers had carved up and brutally divided the African continent amongst themselves, ripping through and destroying both local history and culture". | | In Anatsui's hands, as Elizabeth Péri-Willis has described, "wood becomes cloth bearing the traces of codes, scripts and ideograms". This effect is commonly achieved with the use of a rotary saw to create "dense hatched patterns reminiscent of the warps and wefts of woven cloth-based themes", a technique which emphasises the connections between Anatsui's wall pieces and adinkra and kente cloths. | | Anatsui began to collect disused mortars and house posts in 1980s Nsukka, Nigeria. He would then lay all the different pieces of wood on the floor and carve into them, often using a chainsaw. Although when completed, the wooden slats look organised and are each individually numbered on the reverse, they are not necessarily designed to be hung in that exact order. "With the wood, I would put numbers behind the slats serially, but these numbers were just an initial proposal. The arrangements are all just proposals, not the final say." The wooden wall hangings are thus designed to be fluid, with no formal set arrangement. | | El Anatsui's work can be found in the collections of Los Angeles County Museum of Art, Museum of Modern Art, New York, The National Museum of African Art, Smithsonian Institution, Washington D.C., The Newark Museum, New Jersey, Centre Pompidou, Paris, The British Museum, London, Guggenheim, New York and The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. More recently, El Anatsui was commissioned to exhibit his sculptural installations in the Turbine Hall Space at the Tate Modern in London. | | Bibliography | L. Binder, El Anatsui: When I last wrote to you about Africa, (Seattle, 2010). | J. Picton, El Anatsui: A Sculpted History of Africa, (London, 1995), pp.34-36. | E. A. Péri-Willis, 'Chambers of Memory', in J. Picton (ed.), El Anatsui: A sculpted history of Africa, (London, 1998). | El Anatsui: New Worlds, (Mount Holyoke College Art Museum, 2014), p. 41.

provenance: Collection of Bruce Dayton & Ruth Stricker Dayton, Minnesota; | Revere Auctions, November 2021; | A private collection. | | One of the world's most esteemed ceramic artists, Magdalene Odundo's body of work fuses traditional vernacular techniques of pot making with her contemporary aesthetic. Her works are celebrated for their elegant, fluid forms and rich, polished, burnished surfaces, often resembling ancient vessels but with a modern, minimalist sensibility. Moreover, Odundo's explorations extend beyond this cultural crossover with the human body and acts as a fundamental reference in her work. Bold and often surreal, Odundo's work challenges our traditional perception of ceramic making, emphasising their aesthetic rather than utilitarian form that is readily yet delicately encapsulated within the present work. | | "I have become obsessed by form. What was once an embellishment has now become an engagement." (Magdelene Odundo, Angaza Afrika: African Art Now, ed. Christopher Spring, (London: Laurence King, 2008), p. 234.) | | Born in Nairobi, Odundo would move to the UK at the age of twenty-one, receiving a formal education at the Cambridge School of Art and later the Royal College of Art. However, she also spent time at the Pottery Training Centre in Abuja before returning to teach at the Commonwealth Institute in London between 1976-79, before eventually moving back to Kenya and Nigeria to explore traditional practices. These practises included coiling the clay rather than throwing it and burnishing rather than glazing the final product. Through these methods to achieve her fluid forms, Odundo is able to express her own diasporic identity organically and authentically. | | Recognised for the intellectual capacity of her work and cultural importance, Odundo was awarded a Damehood (DBE) for her services to Art in 2008 and an Honorary Doctorate of Arts from the Angela Ruskin University. She has exhibited globally and her work is held in various major institutions. In 2019, over fifty of her works were displayed in The Journey of Things at the Hepworth in Wakefield and the Sainsbury Centre of Visual Arts in East Anglia and featured in the renowned 2022 exhibition Body Vessel Clay at Two Temple Place, London. | | Bibliography | Robert Soppelsa, "Ceramic Gestures: New Vessels by Magdelene Odundo", UCLA James S Coleman African Studies Center, (1996).

provenance: The collection of Dennis Duerden; | A private UK collection; | By direct descent; | A private collection. |  | Jimoh Akolo was a founding member of the Zaria Art Society (1958-62), along with Yusuf Grillo, Bruce Onobrakpeya, and other art students at the Zaria branch of the Nigerian College of Arts, Science and Technology. This group, along with their peers in literature, theatre, music constituted a postcolonial modernist vanguard in Nigeria in the early 1960s. Convinced that a new art appropriate for Nigerian and African political independence must combine indigenous and western modernist aesthetics, forms and processes, this generation of artists set about creating spaces—such as the now-legendary journal Black Orpheus and the Mbari Writers and Artists Club, Ibadan—for the production and discourse of Nigerian and African modernism. |  | Painted in 1963, it is likely that the present work was completed either in England or Nigeria and may well have been included in the collection of works exhibited by Akolo at his 1964 solo Commonwealth exhibition. The foreword for this exhibition catalogue was written by Dennis Duerden. The works were not individually listed in the catalogue. Though it does record that: 'No. 19-34 Painted in 1962-63 in England' and '35-42 Painted in 1963-64 after return to Nigeria'. |  | The geometrical composition of this work could be said to derive from a brief period in the early 1960's when Akolo drew inspiration from the geometrically pattered facades of Hausa architecture common to Northern Nigeria. Through pallet and compositional construction, Akolo presents us with fragmented figures contrasted by the splatter of paint in the final touches of his process.

(illustrated). | | Extracted from Deborah Bell's Desert/Expulsion series that spanned between 1989-1991, World's Body holds stark similarities to World on Fire whilst taking a dominant position in the artists oeuvre. The work depicts a strong stoic female figure making eye contact with the viewer. The male figure is turned away, gazing at the landscape and either rising or setting sun. Pippa Stein says of the compositional choice in World on Fire that the two figures "are in a point-counterpoint relationship: connected, yet apart, opposite yet the same; one dark, one light; looking forward, looking back; animus, anima." The present work holds a very similar dichotomy; the woman is the dominant figure in the eyes of Bell and for the viewers gaze. The figures stand separately, the woman empowered in her stoisicsm: | | I used to stand in the pose of the woman I was painting, and consciously feel what it was like to be that leg, that arm, the particular expression of the face. She was I and not I. She is no longer caught off balance, in impossible high-heeled shoes or twisted into compromised positions. In these paintings, there was a change in embodiment, a new sense of resolve and inner strength, of 'standing solidly on the earth', bare feet rooted to the ground. The woman looks out of these paintings, holding the viewer in gaze, while the man is usually turned away. It was as if in painting her, I was saying, 'Here I am', an yet once I became the observer of the final painting, she stood there quite separate and self-contained and we looked at each other. (p.18) | | Born in Johannesburg in 1957, Deborah Bell is a leading South African painter, sculptor and printmaker who received her Masters degree in Fine Art at the University of the Witwatersrand. Bell has collaborated with Robert Hodgins and William Kentridge on numerous projects such as Hogarth in Johannesburg (1987-8), Memo (1994) and UBU 101 (1997). | | Bibliography | Ricky Burnett, Deborah Bell- Presence, (Johannesburg: Everard Read and Circa on Jellicoe), (2011) | David Krut Publishing Deborah Bell (p.18)

(flip image, and pre signature, illustrated). | John Giblin & Chris Spring, South Africa: the art of a nation, (London: Thames & Hudson, 2016), p. 202. | Stephen Clingman, William Kentridge, (London: Royal Academy, 2022), p. 153. | Carolyn Christov-Bakargiev, William Kentridge, Brussels: Societe des Expositions du Palais des Beaux-Arts de Bruxelles, 1998, p. 163. (exhibition poster illustrated). | | Although dated 1989, Negotiations Minuet was first exhibited between 30 April and 23 May 1990 at William Kentridge's double exhibition at Cassirer Fine Art and Gallery on the Market in Johannesburg: the second, larger venue was added because works such as the multi-sheet arc drawing Develop, Catch-Up, Even Surpass were too big for the intimate Rosebank gallery. The poster for the joint exhibition was based on Negotiations Minuet. | | The drawing features four main figures all of which appear in other works of this time, albeit in different form. The miner, in boots and helmet, with a hyena strapped to his back, appears in the bizarre procession Develop, Catch-Up, Even Surpass, as does the shaded woman under an umbrella in the background; both figures feature in later Kentridge Processions. The figure with a megaphone covering his face on the left is similar to Harry, Lord Mayor of Derby Road in Kentridge's series Industry & Idleness that formed part of the Hogarth in Johannesburg project (1988) as well as Kentridge's first two 'Drawings for Projection' of this time: in Johannesburg, Second Greatest City after Paris (1989), the herring-bone coat is worn by the man at the head of the procession of dispossessed miners humiliated by the rapacious property-developer Soho Eckstein; and in Monument (1990), it is worn by the miner who, bearing the heavy burden of his box of tools on his back, is revealed to be the living monument to Eckstein's civic benefactions. The figure with hugely enlarged blinkers on his head on the far right, leaning dangerously back as he throws himself into the dance, is a version of Soho Eckstein himself. The falling cat beneath Soho probably derives from Hogarth's Industry & Idleness. The slumped figure of a man who appears to have been executed by a firing squad on the left side of the drawing is certainly derived from Goya. | | Notwithstanding Kentridge's title for this work, there were no negotiations taking place in South Africa in1989. On the contrary, the country was in turmoil. In August 1989, P.W. Botha was replaced as State President by F.W. de Klerk who, confronted by a resurgent Mass Democratic Movement, and under huge economic pressure, began to dismantle the instruments of racial segregation. In February 1990 de Klerk unbanned the African National Congress and other political parties; and soon afterwards, he released Nelson Mandela amongst other political prisoners. In 1991, the Group Areas Act, the Land Act and the Population Registration Act, the cornerstones of apartheid legislation, were repealed and, later that year, negotiations with the ANC and other parties were initiated. | | Was Kentridge prescient in naming his drawing Negotiations Minuet? Perhaps the second word of his title gives one a clue. The minuet is usually defined as a slow, stately dance in four-time for two people – which is certainly not the activity of the four principal figures in the drawing. But Kentridge's critical vocabulary at this time was based on irony and the absurd. The title of Develop, Catch-Up, Even Surpass is a quotation from Emperor Haile Selasse exhorting his countrymen to compete with the economies of the developed world. And Industry & Idleness overturns the rewards and punishments for those characters in a bitter critique of the South African economy (and moral order). Moreover, there are no politicians in Negotiations Minuet. Kentridge's figures are all representatives in broad strokes of South African economic relations – the labouring poor, the unemployed, and the arrogant bosses, precariously balanced in a frenetic jig. Verbal descriptions are inadequate because, as Kentridge said at this precise time, | | One of the reasons one is making images in the first place, rather than writing, is because certain objects or parts of the work seem appropriate to it without your being able to give a clear reason why. It's one of the principles I work with to allow disjunctions, to encourage things that shouldn't be together. | | As a matter of fact, Negotiations Minuet was the second title Kentridge gave to this work: it was actually exhibited as Fused into a Particularly South African Riddle. While less poetic, the original title perhaps stresses both the precarity and the extraordinary interdependence of South African labour relations. To make the point of the disastrous irrationality of this situation, Kentridge, as in other works of this time, turned to Goya - for the executed figure certainly but also, less directly, for the four principal figures and their absorption, while reason sleeps, in a monstrous, mindless dance. | | We are grateful to Professor Michael Godby for his completion of the above footnote. | | Bibliography | Carolyn Christov-Bakargiev, William Kentridge, Brussels: Societe des Expositions du Palais des Beaux-Arts de Bruxelles, (1998). | Michael Godby, Hogarth in Johannesburg, (Johannesburg: Witwatersrand University Press, 1990). | Nigel Worden, The Making of Modern South Africa: Conquest, Segregation and Apartheid, (Oxford: Blackwell Publishers, 1994).

provenance: A private collection, US. | | The present work appears at approximately 2 minutes and 55 seconds into the music video titled 'Another Country' by the band Mango Groove. The video opens on a charcoal drawing animation by William Kentridge of a barren landscape dotted with microphones for public addresses. Wind howls in the air, but stops when Claire Johnston, the band's lead, begins to sing. A vessel of water emerges and the scene changes to an animated charcoal drawing of a city with protestors filling the streets. On one building, images emerge of people who have been injured and killed. Later in the video, the protestors surround the towers of loudspeakers and structures, some of which are now covered and bound. It is at this point when the present image appears. Johnston stands as a giant in a sea of protestors, destroying one of the towers. The wrapping of one of the towers reveals a bowl, and the protestors leave the streets. The bowl fills to overflowing with water flooding the streets of the city and washing away the loudspeakers. The scaffolding of another loudspeaker collapses, and the speaker becomes a bucket from which water flows. Johnston gestures again, and a giant bowl of water appears in the sky over a field of protestors, replacing them with a thriving landscape, the bowl again overflowing with water. | | The song was released in 1993 by One World Entertainment, near the end of the negotiations to end apartheid in South Africa and several months before South Africa's landmark 1994 general election, the first democratic election in the country's history. The title song, "Another Country", expressed an optimism about the country's future. There are differing attributions to the songs origins. The notes for the bands 2006 compilation album, 'Moments Away', suggests that it was in response to the Boipatong massacre while the magazine, Femina suggested it was in response to the assassination of Chris Hani, the leader of the anti-apartheid movement. | | The choice of William Kentridge as the animator of the video for "Another Country" was an inspired and informed decision with the artists at the height of his animation powers. This work was made in the same year as his celebrated fifth film Felix in Exile (1994). Kentridge has commented that this film was: | | 'made at the time just before the first general election in South Africa, and questioned the way in which the people who had died on the journey to this new dispensation would be remembered'. | | The work recalls a scene from 'Monument' (1990), a film by William Kentridge which thematically explores notions of exploitation, passivity, responsibility, and power. The year that this work was created in was also a period of transition from the Apartheid. Kentridge calls into question how the Apartheid will be remembered, commemorated, and even appropriated. Comparatively, the present work possesses the relevant tropes such as censorship, social justice, and power yet also displays compositional similarities in the crowds surrounding a shrouded monument. Moreover, both 1990 and 1994 were both significant dates in the evolution out of Apartheid. It could be said that Kentridge was drawing direct visual relevance between each work, both 'Monument' and the present work from 'Another country', to create a full circle moment in this instance. | | Kentridge's process of re-working and altering a singular drawing numerous times to display animated movement in the film has resulted in this conclusive drawing. "The technique I use is to have a sheet of paper stuck up on the studio wall and, half-way across the room, my camera, usually an old Bolex. A drawing is started on the paper, I walk across to the camera, shoot one or two frames, walk back to the paper, change the drawing (marginally), walk back to the camera, walk back to the paper, to the camera, and so on. So that each sequence as opposed to each frame of the film is a single drawing. In all there may be twenty drawings to a film rather than the thousands one expects. It is more like making a drawing than making a film (albeit a gray, battered and rubbed about drawing)." (Lecture, 1993, published in Cycnos: Image et Langage, Problemes, Approches, Méthodes, Nice, vol. 11 no.1, (1994), pp. 163-168. Republished in C. Christov-Bakargiev, William Kentridge, William Kentridge, Societe des Expositions du Palais de Beaux-Arts, (Bruxelles 1998), pp. 61-64). | | We are grateful to the William Kentridge Studio for their assistance with the cataloguing of this lot. | | Bibliography | C. Christov-Bakargiev, William Kentridge, William Kentridge, Societe des Expositions du Palais de Beaux-Arts, (Bruxelles 1998)

provenance: Mr Laurence Graham-Leigh; | By direct descent to the current owner. | | Skunder was born in Addis Ababa in 1937. He remained in Ethiopia until the age of seventeen when he won second prize in the Abstract Art category at the National Art Exhibition. Held to mark the Jubilee Anniversary Celebration of Emperor Haile Selassie, the exhibition resulted in Skunder being awarded a scholarship to study abroad. He embraced the opportunity and undertook training at Saint Martin's School of Art, the Central School of Art and Design, and the Slade School of Fine Art in London, before travelling to Paris. Here, he attended the École Supérieure des Beaux Arts (1955-56) and the Académie de la Grande Chaumière (1957-63). | | Both works are rare, early renditions by the artist yet both display the expressionist brushstrokes and surreal elements that would embody Skunder's later works. Whilst expressional, these works do retain a lens rarely cast by Skunder, that of his domestic life and view. Void of the 'Afrometaphysics' that embody the wider breadth of his oeuvre, the present work allows us a glimpse into the artists worldly reality whilst demonstrating the early dynamism that would develop in his career. | | A similar work was completed by the artists in 1960, compositionally attuned with the Figures in an Ethiopian Street. Both works display women carrying vessels through a street of buildings executed with broad crush strokes. This work is recorded in the Nigerian National Archives by the Harmon Collection as Le March. | | Harar, Ethiopia bears a double sided business card from "L G Leigh, Picture Framers, Hampstead" to on the back of the work. provenance: A private collection. | | Exhibited | Cape Town, Newlands House, (February 1934), (likely exhibited). | | Irma Stern's 'Arum Lilies', that is sometimes described as 'Still Life with Calla Lilies and a Bowl of Fruit', is dated in the lower left corner 1933. Since the flowering season of arum lilies in South Africa is Spring, one can probably date the work between July and September of that year: this would not be inconsistent with either the Spring-like flowers that are arranged with the lilies in the shiny metallic vase or the citrus fruit in the basket and loose on the table in the foreground. The season is significant because it would seem to place the painting after Stern's exhibitions in April and May 1933 in Pretoria and Johannesburg, which are well-documented. In fact, the painting is most likely identical with 'Arum Lilies' that was listed as No. 63 in Stern's exhibition at Newlands House in Cape Town in February 1934. A photograph in The Cape Argus of February 24 1934 shows the artist Edward Roworth in conversation in front of this painting at that exhibition. | | In 1933, Irma Stern's major pictorial concerns were with colour. In an interview that year, Stern reviewed her development since around 1930: | | My main interest up to then had been centred entirely on Africa and its native life. But now a growing interest in colour theory, even to the exclusion of subject-matter, overtook me to such a degree that for two or three years all my work consisted in studying and building up a new palette. | | The year 1931 brought me for a few months to Madeira where I was able to harvest the benefits of my recent studies. | | Most of Stern's work on Madeira was of Expressionist figure subjects such as Two Harlots, The Blind Beggar, etc. But, reverting to less dramatic subject-matter on her return to Cape Town, Stern clearly found Still Life a suitable vehicle for more subtle experiments in colour. Stern's Still Lifes of the early 1930s show the artist experimenting with new ways of modelling the surface of three-dimensional objects, of using colour to create luminosity through illusionist space, and unifying pictorial structures in terms of colour. Her acknowledged mentor in this chapter of her life was Cezanne. | | Modern viewers are somewhat de-sensitised to this aspect of Stern's art. But, for contemporary viewers, this was a feature of Modernism every bit as challenging as her earlier Expressionist subject-matter. A review of 1931, for example, wrote that: | | Miss Stern paints, to judge from her work, in a white heat of imagination. She has the holy rage to create, that Van Gogh had, when fired by an inspiring subject. | | Something of this "white heat" is apparent in 'Arum Lilies' in the primary yellow and blue colours that dominate the composition; in the yellow background that varies between, tellingly, bright white highlights and murky shadows that repeat the tonal range of the lemons in the foreground; and in the brilliant sheen on the metal vase that includes colours that have no other place in the composition. Moreover, the paint application through broken brushstrokes and swipes of the palette-knife – and the bare canvas that suggests the texture of the woven basket - that are apparent on close inspection throughout the painting, tends to confirm the artist's "holy rage" in creating it. | | It may seem strange today to consider the execution of 'Arum Lilies' to be in any way radical. But a review of Stern's Johannesburg exhibition in 1933 under the titles of 'Agonies in Oils' and 'Irma Stern's Chamber of Horrors' had condemned the assertive Modernism of her work and exhibitions of this time did not sell well. Reviews of the Newlands House exhibition noted the hostile critical climate and promised that the "present exhibition of Irma Stern's work will be accompanied by rather fewer alarms and excursions than usual". Moreover, Melvin Simmers, a fellow artist and sensitive critic, wrote of the exhibition in The Cape Argus on February 19 1934: | | There is nothing obtrusive about the pictures in this exhibition. They do not shout at you and compel your attention. Rather, their eloquent silence waits for your appreciation, and then holds it. It is though the subject of the picture would unconsciously confide to you the story which is behind the paint expression... | To Irma Stern, colour is the essential essence in her effect. She uses it, as she says, comparing it to a chord in music, with the necessary harmony both as control and release. | | A note on an exhibition list records that 'Arum Lilies' was bought by a "Mrs Kemp". This was undoubtedly Mrs J.C.G. Kemp who was recorded in the Cape Times of February 17 as having been at the opening with her daughter. The purchase is confirmed, albeit without the painting being named, in Irma Stern's Cashbook on February 13 when Mrs General J.C.G. Kemp began the first of many instalments for the work. The identity of the purchaser is not without interest because General Jan Christoffel Greyling Kemp (1872-1946) had been a Boer hero in the South African War and was, since 1924, the National Party Minister of Agriculture in the Union Government. | | We are grateful to Professor Michael Godby for his completion of the above footnote. | | Bibliography | Irma Stern's Cashbook, National Library of South Africa, Cape Town, MSC 31.3. | Irma Stern's Scrapbook (1914-1946), National Library of South Africa, Cape Town, MSC. 31.18. | Marion Arnold, Irma Stern: A Feast for the Eye, (Vlaeberg: Fernwood Press, 1995). | Michael Godby, Object Lessons: Still Life Paintings by Irma Stern, 1908-1965, (Cape Town: Primavera Publishing, 2025).
