provenance: A private Belgian collection, by whom sold | Sale Lepke, Berlin 25 April 1911, lot 131 (as 'Isembrant') | Possibly Baron Kerssenbrock (according to an hand written note by Friedländer on the reverse of RKD photo 32516 (Annunciation - 'm. einem / zweiten / Flügel') | French Art Market, where purchased by the present owner around 2000 | | Jean Bellegambe, active in his native Douai and across the County of Flanders, stands among the most sophisticated painters of the early sixteenth century in the Franco‑Flemish world. His art reflects the rich interplay of influences from Bruges, Antwerp, and Valenciennes, blending conservative devotional tradition with the refined elegance and jewel‑like palette characteristic of the region's finest workshops. | The present panel originally formed the fourth element of a five‑part polyptych narrating the Life of the Virgin, a work formerly given to 'Isembrandt' (see sale, 1911) but attributed by Max J. Friedländer to Jean Bellegambe, as noted in his own hand on the reverse of a photograph of the complete ensemble preserved in the RKD Institute (inv. 32516). The reconstructed sequence is: | Annunciation (far left); Visitation; Adoration of the Christ Child by the Virgin, Saint Joseph and five angels, with the Annunciation to the Shepherds in the background (centre, immediately to the left of our panel); Presentation of Christ in the Temple (the present panel) and the Assumption of the Virgin with the Apostles gathered around her sarcophagus below as angels bear her heavenward (far right). | | The upper contours of the compositions originally followed the silhouette of a carved Gothic framework, now removed from our panel, though its outline remains clearly visible under raking light—evidence of its original integration within a unified architectural setting. | Although the complete polyptych was still recorded in 1911, no further trace of the missing panels has come to light since then, and their current whereabouts remain unknown. The present painting reappeared independently on the French art market, where it was acquired by the current owner as a work by Jean Maisoncelles (circa 1436-1479) (the attribution presumably made in connection with works at the Chartreuse de Champmol). | Despite a few localized restorations, the painting retains striking freshness of colour, with passages that preserve much of their original brilliance. Notably, in several areas the paint surface reveals the underdrawing, showing the artist's precise preparatory method. | Bellegambe's oeuvre is traditionally divided into two phases. His early style (c. 1508–1525) is rooted in the archaizing tradition of Valenciennes, shaped by artists such as Simon Marmion and Jan Provost, whose workshop he may have known. His later works—to which the present panel most closely relates—show a measured assimilation of Antwerp mannerism, with broadened spatial organisation, heightened chromatic contrasts, and greater narrative vitality, yet retain the compositional clarity favoured by his monastic patrons. Friedländer long ago noted Bellegambe's stylistic proximity to painters active in Antwerp and Bruges, an influence fully evident here in the graceful figures, brillant palette, and delicate modelling. | With its refined execution, luminous colour, visible underdrawing, and survival outside the now‑lost ensemble, this panel constitutes an interesting fragment of a significant lost polyptych and offers valuable insight into the development of devotional painting in the Franco‑Flemish world in the early sixteenth century.

provenance: Sale, Kohn, Paris, 6 December 1999, lot 1, (sold for € 111,288 (FRF 730,000)), where purchased by the present owner | Private collection, France |  |  | Sebastiaen Vrancx, the pioneering Flemish master of cavalry and battle painting, developed a distinctive visual language combining acute observational realism with a carefully constructed, architectural sense of space. Born in Antwerp and trained under Adam van Noort (1562–1641), who also taught Rubens and Jordaens, Vrancx absorbed the rigorous draughtsmanship of the Antwerp Mannerist tradition before refining his approach during several formative years in Italy, where he encountered the perspectival and landscape innovations of Paul Bril (ca. 1554–1626). | Dated 1625, the present painting comes from his fully mature phase, when the artist's battle scenes became increasingly sophisticated in the choreography of horses, tonal subtlety, and clarity of narrative. The artist's ability to organise densely populated cavalry encounters along strong diagonal axes—here cutting through a Flemish village street—reveals the same compositional devices seen in comparable works of the 1620s. A defining feature of Vrancx's oeuvre is his ability to render the movement of horses, a skill that secured his role as one of the founders of the Flemish cavalry‑battle genre, later influencing painters such as Pieter Snayers (1592-1667) and Adam Frans van der Meulen (1632-1690). |  | At the time of the Kohn sale, it was noted that the present lot was due to be included in Joost Vander Auwera's forthcoming catalogue of the artist's works, which is still in preparation.

provenance: Private collection, France | | « [...] Pour marquer à sa mère sa reconnoissance filiale des obligations qu'il lui avoit pour tous les soins qu'elle avoit pris de son éducation, sa piété et sa tendresse pour elle le déterminèrent, à la fin de 1695, de quitter toutes ses occupations pour faire le voyage de Roussillon, et lui rendre chez elle ce qu'il lui devoit » (Hendrik Van Hulst, après 1743, dans Mémoires inedits sur la vie et les ouvrages des membres de l'Academie royale de peinture et de sculpture, éd. Ph. de Chennevières, L. Dussieux, P. Mantz, A. de Montaiglon et E. Soulié, Paris, 1854, t. 2, p. 117). C'est par ces mots que l'ami et premier biographe de Hyacinthe Rigaud (1659-1743), le poète et peintre hollandais Hendrik Van Hulst, explique le retour de l'artiste dans sa province natale qu'il avait quittée pour s'installer définitivement à Paris en 1681. L'attachement de Rigaud à sa mère, Maria Serra, qui l'avait élevé seule et qui soutint sa vocation, n'avait rien perdu de son intensité ; la séparation, précoce, jointe à l'éloignement géographique, rendit plus vif encore ce sentiment envers celle que Rigaud qualifie de « meilleure des mères ». | | Daughter of Antoni Serra, a shopkeeper in Perpignan, and of Hyeronima, Maria Serra (1638–1721) married the tailor Maties Rigau in 1655, with whom she had two sons—Hyacinthe, our painter, and Gaspard—as well as a daughter, Clara. Widowed in 1669, Maria remarried in 1672 to Gaspar Geli (?-1677), a wealthy merchant of the city. Archival documents reveal a woman of energetic temperament, industrious and devout, a member of the Third Order of Saint Dominic and living in bourgeois comfort thanks to her vineyards, in a fine residence in Perpignan. | During his stay in Perpignan in 1695–1696, Rigaud executed two portraits of his mother: one facing forward (oil on oval canvas mounted on panel, H. 0.79 × W. 0.61 m, Thaon (Calvados), Château de Fontaine-Henry, private collection; see Ariane James-Sarazin, Hyacinthe Rigaud. Le catalogue raisonné, Dijon, Faton, 2016, vol. 2, no. P. 471); the other showing, on the same canvas, two orientations of the bust—one in profile facing right, the other in a slight three-quarter turn to the left (Paris, Musée du Louvre, originally an oval oil on canvas. H. 0.83 × W. 1.03 m, inv. 7522; see Ariane James-Sarazin, ibid., 2016, vol. 2, no. P.472). These three poses were intended for his friend, the sculptor Antoine Coysevox, from whom the painter had commissioned a marble portrait of his mother; it was not completed until 1706 (Paris, Musée du Louvre, marble, H. 0.83 m; H. with pedestal 1.59 m; depth 0.28 m, inv. L.P. 502). Four years earlier, in 1702, Rigaud had entrusted another close associate, the engraver Pierre Drevet, with reproducing the frontal portrait of Maria Serra, adorning the print with a dedicatory inscription imbued with filial devotion ("aeternum pietatis monumentum"). | Executed as a counterpart to the Fontaine-Henry canvas and following the same orientation as Drevet's engraving, the drawing presented here focuses on the sitter's features and the principal elements of her clothing, which correspond to the traditional dress of Roussillon's artisan women: a bodice rounded both front and back, fitted with straps beneath which the white fichu passes, forming small wing-like extensions on each side. The velvet veil—something of a Riguadian signature in textile matters—recalls the head coverings of Rembrandt's elderly women (for example, Oxford, Ashmolean Museum, The Royal Collection, inv. RCIN 405000), an artist Rigaud admired fervently. The use of black chalk with white heightening aligns with the technique Rigaud favored in most of his sheets, many of which are preparatory—sometimes squared, sometimes not—for the translation of his most notable portraits by his appointed engravers such as Pierre Drevet. | The economy of means with which the physiognomy is rendered in all its subtlety—note, in this respect, the full brow, the sharpness of the gaze, the small highlight at the tip of the nose, the modelling of the cheeks, lips, chin, and neck—together with the illusionistic softness of the velvet atop the head, is characteristic of the artist. Equally typical is the particularly firm, somewhat drier and quicker manner in which Rigaud customarily guided the engraver's forthcoming work, indicating explicitly where the tool should press more incisively and where the shadows should be emphasized and deepened. These elements support, in our view, the hypothesis that this is a preparatory drawing for the engraving, rather than a copy after the print—especially since our drawing differs from the engraving in several respects, including its tighter framing and plain background, not to mention the absence of the feigned frame present in the print, which must certainly have been the subject of another drawing by Rigaud. | | We are grateful to Ariane James-Sarazin for her assistance in compiling this catalogue note.

provenance: With Jacques Petithory, Paris, where purchased by the present owner in 1969 | Private Collection, France | | This finely executed drawing may be considered a study for Jean-Baptiste Wicar's La Résurrection du fils de la veuve de Naïm, now at the Palais des Beaux-Arts de Lille (P667), a subject drawn from the Gospel of Luke (7:11-17). provenance: Private collection, France | | This striking and monumental canvas, executed by a follower of Giulio Romano, is an accurate and presumably early copy after the celebrated Battle of the Milvian Bridge fresco in the Sala di Costantino, Apostolic Palace, Vatican Museums—a decorative scheme designed by Raphael and executed by Giulio Romano and his workshop circa 1520–1524, it was begun under Pope Leo X and completed during the pontificate of Clement VII. | The composition displays the hallmarks of Roman Mannerism—energetic diagonals, tightly interwoven bodies, and heightened drama—translated with remarkable fluency by an artist very familiar with Romano's visual language. Such familiarity suggests privileged access, for in the early modern period only individuals supported by papal patrons, cardinals, or members of the Roman artistic academies were permitted entry to Vatican spaces where Romano's monumental frescoes could be studied closely. The present work is thus the product of an artist working within or close to these highly restricted circles. | A recent cleaning has greatly enhanced the legibility of the surface, revealing a brilliant chromatic range long veiled by aged varnish. The restoration has brought out the vivid, sharply contrasted Mannerist colours—burnished reds, deep azures, and metallic highlights—that animate the tumult of battle and reconnect the painting to the theatrical intensity of Romano's original inventions.

provenance: Sale, Hampel, Munich 28 September 2017, lot 730 (hammer 50000€) | Private collection, Austria | Sale, Artcurial, Paris, 21 March 2018, lot 112, where purchased by the present owner | Private collection, France | | Painted in 1636, this refined portrait of a jeweller— possibly a son of Nicasius Roussel, goldsmith and jeweller to the court of Charles I— belongs to Adriaen Hanneman's early mature period, when his style had absorbed the elegance and psychological acuity characteristic of his English years. The identification of the sitter aligns with workshop‑related depictions of jewellers from the period. | First trained under Jan Antonisz. van Ravesteyn (1572-1657), early in his career, Adriaen Hanneman travelled to England, where he lived from 1626 to 1638, working at the heart of the Stuart court. There he encountered the leading portraitists of the day—including Anthony van Dyck (1599-1641), whose influence would profoundly shape his refined handling of costume, gesture, and surface texture. His acceptance into elite artistic circles in London, facilitated by patrons such as Constantijn Huygens, places him squarely within the cosmopolitan portrait tradition flourishing around Charles I. | The sitter prominently displays a pearl necklace, a jewel of considerable symbolic resonance in the 17th century. Pearls—highly prized, often costly imports—connoted purity, prestige, and economic power; they frequently appeared in portraits associated with courtly circles, especially in England where their use signaled refinement and access to luxury materials. In the context of a jeweller's portrait, the presence of such a piece not only reflects the sitter's trade but subtly underscores his status, expertise, and proximity to high‑ranking patrons who themselves valued pearls. | When the present work was offered at auction in 2016 (Grisebach, 1 December 2016, lot 309), the note stated that the attribution to Hanneman was confirmed by Eddy Schavemaker.

It was his childhood spent by the sea that decisively shaped the artistic path of Ivan Aivazovsky, who would go on to become an outstanding interpreter of maritime subjects. The sea emerged as his lifelong vocation, as is often the case with those whose lives are inseparably bound to it. | | The artist was renowned for his exceptional speed of execution, frequently completing a canvas within a single working session. This apparent ease and fluidity of brushwork imparts a sense of immediacy and vitality to his paintings, enhancing their expressive power. | | In the painting View of Capri, the tranquil expanse of the Mediterranean extends uninterrupted to the horizon. The subtle movement of the clear, luminous blue waters perfectly conveys the atmosphere of a peaceful southern day on the Italian island of Capri. Aivazovsky's assured command of aerial perspective and his sophisticated treatment of light and shadow create a compelling sense of spatial depth and openness. The small staffage figures along the shoreline function as a compositional device, reinforcing the scale and grandeur of the maritime landscape. | | The painting's colour palette demonstrates the artist's technical virtuosity. Gradual transitions from pure sky-blue tones to delicate, pearlescent hues near the shoreline contribute to the overall harmony of the composition. The expansive sky, occupying a substantial portion of the canvas, shifts subtly from cool blue tones to warmer, golden shades at the horizon. The atmosphere appears saturated with light and marine freshness - a particular state of nature that Aivazovsky was uniquely adept at capturing. | | In this work, Aivazovsky reveals his exceptional sensitivity to the most nuanced effects of light and atmosphere, conveying the calm and stillness characteristic of a languid Italian day.

The figure, seated on the riverbank, looking down at his image reflected in the water, may also be read as a Narcissus‑like youth, situating the work within the mid‑19th‑century French revival of mythological subjects reimagined through a modern, humanised sensibility. | Rare in subject within Carolus‑Duran's production, the canvas offers a revealing glimpse into the painter's artistic evolution in the early 1860s, bridging the academic rigor of his training and the expressive freedom that would later define his mature style—an approach that would, in turn, influence an entire generation, including his most celebrated pupil, John Singer Sargent. | The notable provenance of the painting further underscores its importance: retained initially in the artist's own collection and then inherited by his eldest daughter, it subsequently passed to Mr. Bureau before entering the hands of the distinguished dealer Jacques Seligmann. Seligmann's galleries in Paris and New York were instrumental in shaping leading European and American collections in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, and works handled by him are often marked by their historical significance and exceptional quality. | | The attribution of this painting to Carolus-Duran (1837-1917) has been confirmed by Brame & Lorenceau following a physical examination of the work; it now features in their archives on the artist.

Bischoff: The Life & Art of an American Master, The Irvine Museum, 2010, p. 167, illustrated. | | Franz Bischoff first visited California—off the tail of a Michigan winter—at the turn of the 20th Century. By 1900, he had operated a successful China painting studio in the Greater Detroit area for two decades and recently become an American citizen. In the exuberance of his new status, the new century, and a glorious new climate, Bischoff fell in love with California quickly. He made the leap to greener pastures by 1906, moving his family to Southern California to start the next chapter of his career. | | Bischoff settled in Lincoln Park in South Pasadena where he established himself within the Arroyo Seco and Los Angeles art communities. This cohort included leading landscape painters of his day such as Hanson Puthuff, Benjamin C. Brown, Elmer and Marion Wachtel, and William Wendt. | | Bischoff's move to California marks a clear shift in his career, broadening his scope from still life to landscape painting, naturalism to Impressionism, studio to plein air, object to easel painting, and artistic production to artistic creation. | | At this time, California plein air painting was à la mode and championed by the leading art critic of this period, Antony Anderson of the Los Angeles Times. Anderson and Puthuff founded the Art Students' League of Los Angeles which 'would contribute greatly to the establishment of a progressive art tradition in Southern California.' 1 This specific cultural moment, along with Bischoff's personal trajectory, led Bischoff to find inspiration in his natural surroundings for nearly three decades. | | Picking Poppies, Pasadena dates to around 1910 when Bischoff became involved with the nascent California Art Club. He had also just built a new home and studio in South Pasadena that allowed him to hold public exhibitions very close to the views that inspired him. | | The present work brilliantly captures the floral and landscape subjects that inspired Bischoff along with the artistic and social history of his time. While the work is both a landscape and genre scene, Bischoff exhibits his mastery in Impressionist technique, conveying the movement and immediacy of this fleeting moment. Loose and dappled brushwork capture the ephemeral nature of California golden poppies and wildflowers, and color-laden strokes applied alla prima sculpt form into being. Capturing natural light conditions are solidly an Impressionist concern, and the painting skillfully conveys the diffused light of tree shade on the woman in the foreground and California's characteristic high-contrast, clear light on the women behind her. | | By the same token, the work shows a Modernist self-awareness of art history as a discipline (and the artist's place in it) by referencing the figural compositions of several canonical works as Jean-Francois Millet's, Des glaneuses, 1857, Édouard Manet's, Le déjeuner sur l'herbe, 1862-63, and Peter-Paul Ruben's, The Three Graces, 1630-35. Seen from this position, it is no coincidence that Henri Matisse's, La Danse, 1910—a work that echoes yet breaks from historical precedent—was created around the same time. | | The present work likely depicts the locale of Altadena near North Lake Avenue. Altadena's poppy fields were legendary—one field was so vibrant it was called La Sabanilla de San Pascual (The Altar Cloth of San Pasqual) by Spanish sailors who saw it from the coast. By the turn of the 20th Century, with the advent of modern transportation, these poppy fields became a tourist attraction, accessible by carriage and railway. | | Picking Poppies, Pasadena serves not only as a visual reminder of the fleeting pleasures of everyday life, but also as an important historic record of Altadena, particularly in light of conservation and wildfire recovery efforts today such as The Great Altadena Poppy Project. | | 1 J. Stern, Franz A. Bischoff: The Life & Art of an American Master, The Irvine Museum, 2010, p. 47.

Yearning for the maritime culture that he experienced abroad, in 1913, Hansen traveled to Monterey aboard the lumber schooner Eureka.2 Over the next few years, Hansen explored the aesthetic potential of Monterey's fishing culture. By 1918, he established a year-round residence in Monterey, and by 1922, he fully settled there. 3 | | Hansen's mythic persona preceded him, with much attention paid to his robust stature, Danish Viking heritage, and pedigree as the son of the pioneering Western artist Herman Wendelborg Hansen. He set the aesthetic standards that espoused color and guided the group with the strength of his personality, physical energy, and warm hospitality. With his high-energy and a sturdy build, he had a capacity for long hiking trips and outdoor, plein-air painting that he pursued passionately. He shared his house with several aspiring artists (like August Gay) and held dinners in a raucous atmosphere. Liberally seasoned with garlic and well lubricated with alcohol, the group critiqued and inspired one another. The avant-garde put in sporadic arrivals on the West Coast and when it did, the Six drank it up like one of Gile's home-brews. | | Stylistically, the 1915 Panama-Pacific International Exposition (PPIE) was a transformative influence on the Six. For Gile, there is a palpable shift in style from the early teens through his mature pictures. In The Society of Six: California Colorists, Nancy Boas explains that this shift was in part a reaction to seeing the PPIE works: "After [the exhibition], the Six began applying loose, expressive brushstrokes of varying sizes, using the stroke as an element in its own right...Thus they abandoned the careful finish encouraged in academic work and attempted to reveal their own individuality and spontaneity in the paint surface itself. Combined with heavy impasto in some places and with unpainted areas of the canvas showing through in others, these brushstrokes create a purposeful sketchiness. Now sketchiness became a means of capturing a fleeting moment." 1 Building upon this shifted framework the 1923 exhibition of Contemporary French Art pushed the Society of Six to new heights of color and spontaneity. The fauves "wild beasts" were on view including Henri Matisse, Andre Derain and Maurice Vlaminck. The French critic Louis Vauxcelles applied the label to Matisse and Derain's works in a 1905 exhibition, and it grew to apply the artists themselves. | | The evolution of the Six shifted importantly with the start of their shared exhibitions in 1923. In Clapp's 1923 manifesto for the Society of Six, he concludes in part: In other words, we are not trying to illustrate a thought or write a catalogue, but to produce a joy through the use of the eyes...we have felt, and desire that others may also feel. Clapp—the theorist of the group—would come in for some reproach from his rough-and-tumble friends, as recounted by Siegriest in a 1972 interview: What the hell you writing all this crap down for... Get to painting and quite friggin around. Despite their criticisms, Clapp was speaking truthfully about an underlying goal of the Six. The French influence did not go unnoticed by critics of the time, Josephine Bentham in the Oakland Post Enquirer in March of 1923 referred to the Six as the Latin Quarter Comrades of the East Bay. Terry St. John observed in his 1972 book Society of Six that the turning point for Gile (and Von Eichman) was 1926 when they shifted to a more broadly Fauvist-influenced painting style.2 | | To understand the radical nature of these paintings it is helpful to read H.C. Dungan's review of the show in April of 1926 of the Oakland Tribune where he cautions those who attend that "you should have brought along your amber-tinted glasses, but not having them you will have to get used to the color. There's plenty of it; rich, pure, and let us add, Glorious. Dungan's choice of the word glorious was a preview of the praise he would lavish on the present lot in his review. "'Glorious Hill' by Selden C. Gile one of the outstanding canvases at the Society of Six exhibition at the Oakland Art Gallery. It is a fine example of color harmony and must be seen in the original to be appreciated." 3 | | The contrasts in color and form from the water to the arks to the hills and sky above proved an irresistible subject to Gile. He revisited it in numerous paintings and in 1927 moved north to Tiburon and later to adjacent Belvedere Island. The foreground of Glorious Hills is composed with subdued colors; Gile uses realistic greens and browns albeit with choppy brushwork. The arks and pilings come in for an altogether different treatment. The fauve's love of pure color from the tube is evident in the vibrant reds, pure yellows and saturated blues. All this action in color and form in the arks is framed below by water with long gestural swirls in the white and green and as Dungan calls it "too blue" water. The arks are framed above by the orange and green hills stepping up to the sky with the occasional darker green daubs of trees and maroon shadows. The sky has more of the pure blue, particularly on the edges; however much of it is overlayed with glorious white and butter yellow clouds with some subtle pink hints. The scale of the work serves to emphasize the different skills Gile can bring to bear on one composition. Dungan notes "that's a good sized canvas, but it is much bigger in art than it is in square inches." 4 | | 1 N. Boas, The Society of Six: California Colorists, San Francisco, 1988, pp. 80-81. | 2 T. St. John, Society of Six: William Clapp, August Gay, Selden Gile, Maurice Logan, Louis Siegriest, Bernard Von Eichman, Oakland, 1972. | 3 H.C. Dungan, Oakland Tribune, 'Artists and their Work,' April 4, 1926, pg. S6 | 4 ibid Dugan, p.S6.

provenance: Private collection, Los Angeles, circa 1920's. | By family descent from the above. | Christie's, Los Angeles, May 2, 2001, lot 15. | Private collection, Laguna Beach, California, acquired from the above. | | Exhibited | (Likely) Los Angeles, Cannell and Chaffin, Inc. March 15-27, 1920, and elsewhere. | (Likely) Los Angeles, Los Angeles Museum of History Science and Art, Eleventh Annual Exhibition of the California Arts Club, October-November, 1920. | (Likely) Pasadena, Shakespeare Club, May 1921. | | Literature | Suzanne Muchnic, 'Art and Architecture: Setting the Stage for a California Scene,' The Los Angeles Times, April 1, 2001, p. 252, illustrated. | | When the group of artists now known as the Impressionists held their first exhibition in 1874 it was largely met with poor reviews and general distaste. Over a decade later however, art dealer Paul Durand-Ruel successfully reintroduced this once avant-garde movement to American audiences at an 1886 exhibition with more positive acclaim. From it developed American Impressionism, a light and airy style of painting that captured predominantly leisure pursuits. This movement varied in both style and subject from the dark and rigid manner of the Academic tradition that preceded it and the grittier urban scenes of the Ashcan movement that followed. Throughout the late 19th and early 20th centuries regional manifestations of American Impressionism appeared in Boston, New York, Connecticut and as far West as California, each with their own nuanced interpretations of the French style. Guy Rose's Incoming Fog, La Jolla exemplifies this intersection of French, American, and ultimately California Impressionism in a visual evolution of plein-air painting. | | Born in 1867 on a family ranch in the San Gabriel Valley, Guy Rose is one of few West Coast artists of this period native to California. As the son of a wealthy landowner, Rose experienced a relatively privileged upbringing that afforded him the opportunity to travel. Following his graduation from Los Angeles High School in 1885, Rose first ventured north to San Francisco where he trained at the California School of Design under Virgil Williams and Emil Carlsen. From there he went on to study at the Académie Julian in Paris in 1888. At both institutions, he followed a rigorous curriculum that prioritized time spent in the studio drawing and practicing form. During weekends and summer breaks however, he scheduled visits to the nearby countryside to practice painting directly from nature. It was here that Rose was first exposed to Impressionism and captivated by a style of painting that would gradually inform the rest of his career. | | Rose was not the only American who found the French countryside and Giverny in particular appealing. Together with artists like Frederick Frieseke, Lawton Parker and Richard Miller, they were dubbed 'The Giverny Group' by critics.1 This new generation of expatriate artists continued to embrace the original tenets of Impressionism first championed by Claude Monet - short broken brushstrokes, pure unblended color and emphasis on the effects of light. | | An early example of Monet's fascination with both color and light can be seen in his 1867 work The Regatta at Saint-Adresse (The Metropolitan Museum of Art 51.30.4). Here well-dressed beachgoers spend a leisurely afternoon watching a fleet of sail boats in the harbor town of Le Havre as billowing clouds form above. With a subtle gradation in the tan pigments, Monet perfectly distinguishes the wet versus dry areas of the shoreline. Rose would go on to use a similar effect in Incoming Fog with mossy greens delineating the water level on the rocky outcrop. Another striking similarity between the two works is the use of rapid brushwork to portray depth of field. Just as Monet's scene articulates distinct zones of shallow, moderate, and deep water, Rose's composition is similarly structured, with long fluid strokes beyond the break and shorter rapid ones in the foreground to simulate aerated water tossed about by waves. While Rose never painted the sea during his time abroad, it is clear Monet's influence continued to have an impact on his later works. | | By the time the prodigal son returned to California after more than a decade overseas, he brought with him a vast firsthand knowledge of what was happening in the art world in both Europe as well as on the East Coast. While Giverny continued to host Americans until the outbreak of World War I, artist colonies were simultaneously beginning to develop stateside in areas like Cos Cob, Old Lyme, Shinnecock, Carmel and Laguna Beach. Unlike the East Coast however, California benefited from year-round sunshine making its coastlines the ideal setting for Rose to continue building on the practice of plein-air painting as he reacquainted himself with his home state. | | Early on critics saw merit in Rose's rendering of the sea with Antony Anderson of the Los Angeles Times noting, "Rose had never painted the sea till a year ago, and when he gazed upon the Pacific it must have been with a new and 'wild surmise' for he immediately sat himself down to paint it - and discovered he had come into his own. Luckily for him and thrice luckily for us." 2 From here on, Rose's oeuvre oscillates between images of intense glare and subtle fog as he pushes the boundaries of Impressionism to focus purely on atmospheric effects. In the present lot, fog slowly begins to encroach on the scene from the left side of the composition as the sea and sky blur into one. Meanwhile, the horizon line on the right side of the canvas remains in perfect clarity, at least for the time being as the title would suggest. The duality of the composition captures Rose's mastery of the thick marine layer of Lifting Fog (sold at Bonhams in 2024) and the shimmering brilliant light of Off Point Lobos (sold at Bonhams in 2022). | | Guy Rose remains one of the most distinguished American Impressionists to come out of California, with a forthcoming 2027 retrospective of his work at the Crocker Art Museum in Sacramento attesting to the continued interest in his contribution to plein-air painting. | | 1'Luminism of Giverny,' New York Evening Post, December 20, 1910, p.9. | 2 Antony Anderson, The Los Angeles Times, February 20, 1916.

provenance: Oliver's Mission Art and Curio Store, Monterey, California. | The Redfern Gallery, Laguna Beach, California. | Private collection, Arizona. | Private collection, Northern California. | | Exhibitied | Scottsdale, Arizona, The Fleischer Museum, 1996. | Pasadena, Pasadena Museum of California Art, On Ramps: Transitional Moments in California Art, June 1-September 1, 2002. | | Spirit of the Rodeo belongs to the select number of works that Armin Hansen completed in the Western tradition. Hansen first started producing cowboy compositions in 1913 after a friend took him to a rodeo in Salinas just east of Monterey. 1 Although he had been exposed to Western Art from an earlier age through his father, Herman Wendleborg Hansen, the majority of his own artistic output up to that point largely focused on seafaring culture. Often marked by rain-soaked decks, turbulent seas and weathered fishermen, these maritime scenes still alluded to the frontier with overlapping themes of hard labor and untamed nature. By 1930, Hansen reintroduced the rodeo subject in a Los Angeles exhibition, which stood out among his marines and led a reviewer to declare that Hansen had "gone western."2 | | Hansen's rodeo scenes are not only a departure from his standard subject matter but his use of color as well. His maritime scenes are typically rendered in deep monochrome shades of ultramarine or indigo, primarily cool tones that mirror the cold isolation of life at sea. In contrast to the more somber mood evoked by a cool palette, the present lot shares the same warmer tones as Cowboy Sport and First Feel of Leather (each sold at Bonhams) that capture the liveliness and animation of sport. Here Hansen uses shades of maroon, salmon, orange and vermillion to render various ten-gallon hats, chaps and bandanas. Long shadows are cast in tones of deep forest green. A dab of purple on one rider's spur balances the various shades of mustard that make up the dusty haze, while another in turquoise brings some semblance of focus into the otherwise frenzied scene. Hansen further obscures the spectacle with a cropped composition that enhances the action taking place within the corral. | | Despite verging on abstraction, the finished product is a direct result of Hansen's accomplishments as a draftsman. Each stroke is placed with intention to mimic the line work he perfected in etchings like Cowboy Sport and Over the Top. From the weight of a rider suspended mid-air to the musculature of a bucking bronco, Hansen manages to retain the underlying structures and forms of his subjects in a feat of organized chaos that captures the Spirit of the Rodeo. | | 1 Scott A. Shields, Armin Hansen: The Artful Voyage, Pasadena Museum of California Art, 2015, p. 191. | 2 as quoted in Shields, p. 191.

Harlow & Co., Big Game: An Exhibition of Paintings by Carl Rungius, April 1921. | | Literature | (Probably) New York Times, Art Exhibitions of Paintings, April 10, 1921, Section D, p. 81. | | This painting will be included in the forthcoming Carl Rungius Catalogue Raisonné, directed by Dr. Adam Duncan Harris (an independent project of the National Museum of Wildlife Art). | | Carl Rungius was arguably the most influential American wildlife painter, not only by virtue of his artistic skill but through his education and advocacy. He brought an up-close and personal view of wildlife to the public at-large—particularly with the diorama murals he painted for the American Museum of Natural History in New York—that made a compelling case for the value of land conservation in the 20th Century. | | Rungius was born in a provincial district of present-day Berlin. He developed an interest in art and hunting from a young age, which culminated in attending the Berlin Academy of Arts. Rungius 'was lauded as a painter of moose before he'd ever laid eyes on the living, breathing beast' so when he was invited by his uncle, Dr. Clemens Fulda of New York, to hunt moose with him in Maine, he jumped at the chance. 1 | | Though Rungius was unsuccessful in his first season of moose hunting, this trip in the Fall of 1894—his first to North America—set him on his path. Determined to capture a moose the following Fall, he stayed on for another year with his uncle. | | Rungius made two important connections in 1895—the first was with William Hornaday, a leading figure in America's conservation movement and later Director of the New York Zoological Society; and the second was with Ira Dodge, an outfitter from Wyoming's Wind River Country. | | Hornaday saw a life-sized head-and-shoulders portrait of a bull moose which Rungius had painted after specimens he studied at the American Museum of Natural History and a local taxidermy studio and remarked that 'It looked as if a section with a wild animal in it had been cut out of the Maine woods and framed as an exhibit from the workshop of nature.' 2 The two men became fast friends, and Hornaday introduced him to other prominent sportsmen in New York that became his most influential supporters, including the figurehead of the Bull Moose Party, Theodore Roosevelt. | | Dodge met Rungius at New York's first Sportsman's Show at Madison Square Garden and invited him to hunt for Big Game through the Wind River Range that year. Rungius fell in love with the American West from this trip to Dodge's Box-R Ranch and decided to stay in America permanently. For his remaining years, Rungius split his time between New York City in the Winter; and Wind River, Maine, New Brunswick and Banff in the Summer and Fall. 3 | | Rungius successfully hunted his first moose in 1898, just south of Dodge's dude ranch which Roosevelt had also visited. He continued to develop his fidelity to moose from trekking in New Brunswick, earning a reputation as 'the Rembrandt of the moose.' 4 | | Moose were the most enduring subjects for Rungius, and he captured them across four of the five regions he visited annually. Rungius's painterly approach toward them evolved over time, starting from a highly naturalistic and detailed technique, as seen in Lost Timber, circa 1900 (National Museum of Wildlife Art, JL 2000.116) toward a lively Impressionistic technique, as seen in At the Pond. | | 1 T. Davis, 'Kings of the Hill,' Sporting Classics, July/August 2006, Volume XXV, Issue 4, pp. 110-118. | 2 Ibid. | 3 A. Steven Manford, Behind the Photo: 42 Man Ray Stamps (Paris, 2008), n.p. (ill. stamps) | | Note | Man Ray's Magnolia Blossom is a striking example of the artist's ability to transform a simple natural form into a study of luminous elegance and modernist precision. Taken in 1926, the image features a single, curvaceous bloom, presented in a fluted vase placed on the seat of a café chair. The flower is captured at the moment when its satiny petals unfurl in the sunlight to reveal the tightly coiled carpels at its center. | | Magnolia Blossom was originally published as a full-page reproduction in the April 1927 issue of Vogue France and marks the notable inclusion of photography in the magazine's 'Art and Decoration' section, which duly credits Man Ray for the image. In the Vogue spread, Man Ray's signature appears at the lower right corner of the reproduced print. Over his long career, Man Ray chose to crop the negative of Magnolia in various ways as well as print it in both vertical and horizontal formats. Notably, the cropping in Vogue is very similar to that of the present work. | | The accompanying text dubs Man Ray as "Le Portraitiste des Choses" (the Portraitist of Things) - a subtly surrealist interpretation of a work that veers toward classicism. The caption also emphasizes the controlled harmony and beauty of the image ("presque impudique à force de splendeur" - almost immodest in its splendor). It is this quality which prompted the closing description of Magnolia as "plus pathétiques que la nature même" – more poignant than nature itself. | | Magnolia Blossom was one of Man Ray's favorite images from his robust and hyper-creative body of work made during the 1920s. In 1934, he published the book Man Ray: Photographs 1920-1934 – the first survey of his most important works to date – and selected it for inclusion. Made within the same few years that he created his most daring photographs, such as Le Violin d'Ingres (1924), Noire et blanche (1926), and his many extraordinary Rayographs, Magnolia Blossom exemplifies Man Ray's simultaneous engagement with classical motifs. Shifting subtly between abstraction and representation, this work conveys a vitality, lushness, and optimism that continues to captivate viewers. | | The present print was executed on paper with a silvery cast and was likely printed before 1940. The presence of two posthumous stamps, M28 and M30, indicates that the verso of the mount was stamped after Man Ray's death in 1976. At the time of this writing, the identity of the artist's assistant to whom Man Ray gifted this work remains unknown. Notably in the late 1970s, owners of Man Ray prints often approached the Estate and asked it to authenticate a photograph, which the Estate verified with posthumous stamps. This very special example of Magnolia Blossom has been carefully preserved and enjoyed by Lily Tomlin and Jane Wagner for more than forty years.

This innovative process significantly shaped his creative output in the months that followed. Hockney once remarked, "I love new mediums... I think mediums can turn you on, they can excite you; they always let you do something in a different way. Even if you take the same subject, if you draw it in a different way, or if you are forced to simplify it—to make it bold because it is too finicky—I like that." | | By transforming the photocopier, an everyday office staple of the 1980s, into an accessible and dynamic artistic tool, Hockney redefined perceptions of the machine's potential. While many artists have hesitated to embrace emerging technologies, Hockney has consistently evolved alongside them, always adapting his printmaking to incorporate new technological possibilities, as demonstrated in this work.

provenance: Stephen Wirtz Gallery, San Francisco | Acquired from the above by the present owner in 1980 | | Note | Bonhams is honored to offer a multitude of timeless and captivating images from the Collection of Steve and Martha Smith. | | Steve Smith – a cameraman, filmmaker, author, and avid photographs collector – grew up in a family of amateur photographers. Like many Americans in the 1950's, his family subscribed to Life Magazine, where Steve was introduced to the work of W. Eugene Smith, whose images would inform his lifelong collecting practices. Growing up in the Bay Area among military families, Steve inhaled tales of World War II which inspired a fascination with all things related to the Pacific Ocean. | | In college, Steve majored in Technical Theater and discovered a love for lighting, which heightened his interest in W. Eugene Smith's masterful use of tonality. After graduation, he became a lighting cameraman, traveling the world on various assignments and earning five Emmy awards. Though his professional livelihood depended on moving images, Steve always carried a Domke bag stuffed with Nikons. He enjoyed shooting and printing, both in practice and in profession. | | Steve and Martha travelled the world together and on location, when they weren't working, sought out galleries in every city they visited. Steve particularly admired the Old (photographic) Masters — Paul Strand, Walker Evans, Edward Weston, Henri Cartier-Bresson, and especially Andre Kertesz — all of whom are represented in the collection he and Martha built. In their various homes, they surrounded themselves with this trove of beloved images, each emblematic of the extraordinary life they shared together.

provenance: Artist's studio, Moscow | Ann. auction, Art Contemporain Soviétique, June 25, 1989, Versailles | Private collection, Versailles | | Exhibited | The Aesthetics of the Thaw: New Russian Art between 1956 and 1962, Moscow, Exhibition Hall "Na Kashirke," April 18 – May 2, 1996 | | Literature | Library of New Russian Art, Sergey Kuskov, Nikolai Vechtomov, Paris — Moscow — New York, Third Wave, 1997, p. 87 | | | One of the key figures of unofficial art, Vechtomov was part of the core of the Lianozovo Group and took part in all the major nonconformist exhibitions. After the Second World War he began to experiment with abstract painting, filling small sheets of cardboard with spontaneous brushstrokes. His characteristic surrealist, expressive manner emerged in the 1960s, becoming a kind of reminiscence of his traumatic frontline experience. According to the artist himself, it was precisely the dramatic circumstances of the war that made him an artist. His style is easily recognisable by its striking orange-and-black or red-and-black contrasts, as well as by the lacquered surface of his paintings and the velvety quality of his watercolours. | Often described as an artist of the "cosmic" theme, Vechtomov created tense, fantastical works imbued with an inner glow and filled with isomorphic substances. Assuming the role of a creator, the artist seems to strive to touch upon the mysteries of the universe. His task was to sense and comprehend the laws of existence and to express them through new forms, thereby opening a window onto a new, unknown world of cosmism. Vechtomov's surrealism is far removed from the ideas of Magritte and Dalí, with their psychological automatism and hallucinatory visions. In Vechtomov's work, despite its apparent tragic quality, one senses a desire to anticipate the images of some new life, the forms of a new mode of being. At the same time, the colour palette and biomorphic substances on his canvases serve as reminders of the horrors of war, so familiar to the artist.

provenance: Acquired by the father of the present owner in late 1980s | Thence by descent | | A prominent representative of art brut, Leonid Purygin was one of the most 'atypical' artists of unofficial Soviet art. Lacking any formal artistic education, he began actively painting in the early 1970s. A solitary artist, Purygin chose his own artistic path, creating in a naïve style. The philosophy of his art is based on a unique mythological system filled with a variety of psychedelic characters and enigmatic commentaries. The central figure in his work is almost always the artist himself - Lyonya Purygin. Artist from Nara. A Genius and his interactions with his personal demons. | | The stylistic roots of Purygin's work lie in folk art, icons, and lubok prints. From these sources comes his love of bright colours, wood, folding icons, and folk religious imagery. It was from folk art that Purygin also borrowed the practice of inscribing texts directly into his compositions, often with spelling mistakes and the use of obscene language. The absence of perspective, flat areas of local colour, the monumental scale of the central figure, and the frequent division of paintings into registers characteristic of icons are the key features of the artist's painting.

provenance: Galerie Lelong, New York | Acquired from the above by the present owner | | Exhibited | Huesca, Centro de Arte y Naturaleza, Fundación Beulas, Territorios que Importan, Género, arte y ecología, 18 October 2018 - 20 January 2019 | | | | Ana Mendieta's work endures as a quiet yet unyielding force, tracing the profound bond between human beings and the earth. Untitled presents a simple, intimate gesture in the outline of a female figure inscribed on a delicate leaf. Within this modest form lies the complexity of Mendieta's practice - an oeuvre that has moved through many contexts over time: essentialism, feminism, anti-colonial critique, and the continual transgression of artistic boundaries, perfectly exemplifying the artist's lasting relevance and her remarkable ability to speak across generations. The fragility of the leaf in the present work reflects the vulnerability of the female body, yet its preservation and resilience suggest an enduring strength - a quiet assertion of the body's power to persist. | | Part of a generation of artists whose practices no longer conformed to the conventions of exhibition-making and collecting, Mendieta's work resists containment in any single category. Instead, it exists somewhere between acts and object. In the present piece, she inscribed upon a green leaf, an element that in its very nature was destined to shift, dry, and decay. Time itself becomes a collaborator, transforming the work as matter changes state. Like her performances, Untitled embodies this delicate tension between permanence and impermanence, capturing both a gesture of presence and its inevitable passage into transformation. | | Drawing was an integral part of Mendieta's practice which developed from her years as a student in the Intermedia department at Iowa University. Her sketchbooks from that period are filled with ideas that would later materialise in her earth-body and Silueta works. Throughout her career the artist kept a detailed record of her practice, documenting new, iconic performance pieces and interventions, yet it was only in the early 1980s that drawing emerged as a distinct body of work. Initially, Mendieta experimented with amate, a bark paper made by the Otomí people of Mexico, historically used in ritual contexts since pre-Columbian times. Soon after, she discovered the leaves of the Clusia rosea, also known as the autograph tree, whose thick, leathery surfaces could be inscribed by scratching away the dark outer skin to reveal a lighter layer beneath. Long used by Caribbean schoolchildren for writing and by Spanish colonial soldiers as makeshift playing cards, these leaves carried both everyday and historical resonances. Onto them, Mendieta etched figures that echoed her contemporaneous 'goddess' sculptures, evoking the imagery of Cuba's Taíno culture. In this act, she turned a material once used by colonisers into a site for the preservation and reanimation of indigenous and ancestral forms. Untitled beautifully exemplifies Mendieta's carefully considered process of memorialisation by recording and preserving her memory through an act that honours her native Cuban culture. | | Forging connections with the Earth and the cosmos was central to Mendieta's output, a concern that permeated her whole output but which is perhaps most evident in the Silueta Series. In this emblematic body of work the artist placed her body within the landscape, later also highlighting its absence and the traces she had left within it. Explained by Mendieta herself, "My art is the way I re-establish the bonds that unite me to the universe". Whether inscribed in the earth, or drawn onto it, the body became a conduit for reestablishing ties with the natural world and for articulating a fractured sense of identity. Later in her career, she extended this exploration into freestanding sculptures, in which the personal and performative gave way to archetypal forms, muting ritual presence in favour of lasting, three-dimensional objects. Influenced by artists such as Vito Acconci, Lynda Benglis, Chris Burden, Bruce Nauman, and the Fluxus group, Mendieta continually pushed the boundaries of what art could be. Earth, its elements, and the body itself became at once her medium and her message, expressing the profound, universal bond between humanity and nature, while transcending cultural, social, and historical confines. | | Untitled ultimately invites us to inhabit a space where fragility and strength coexist, where the ephemeral becomes eternal through gesture, trace, and transformation. Mendieta's work does not merely represent the body in nature but fuses both into one inseparable force, an elemental language of soil, flame, and flesh. In her leaves and silhouettes, the personal becomes archetypal, the temporary becomes timeless. Even in its small and delicate form, Untitled resonates as a profound meditation on belonging, memory, and the enduring power of the human spirit inscribed upon the earth.

provenance: Marlborough Fine Art Ltd., Vaduz | Private Collection, Geneva (acquired from the above in 1987) | Thence by descent to the present owner | | Exhibited | Munich, Kunsthalle der Hypo-Kulturstiftung, Fernando Botero: Bilder, Zeichnungen, Skulpturen, 4 July - 7 September 1986, no. 86 (illustrated n.p.) (and later travelled to Bremen, Kunsthalle Bremen, 11 January - 1 March 1987; Frankfurt, Schirn Kunsthalle Frankfurt, 12 March - 17 May 1987) | Madrid, Centro de Arte Reina Sofía, Fernando Botero: Pinturas, Dibujos, Esculturas, 22 June - 15 August 1987 (illustrated p. 96) | | | | A distilled expression of Fernando Botero's renowned figurative style, Muchacha from 1984, presents a young girl rendered with sculptural stability and candid existence. Standing frontally against a muted background, her distinct form is presented with gentle curves and compact proportions, giving the figure a sense of undeniable self-determination, despite the work's modest appearance. Botero deliberately restrains narrative, gesture, and expression, instead giving a self-contained presence to the figure, allowing his signature form and style to stand on its own. Unidealised and uninhibited in her representation, this young girl occupies her frame with unspoken authority, exemplifying Botero's commitment to form and volume as a force of presence, not drama or performance. Executed at the apex of the 'Maestro's' artistic maturity, Muchacha exemplifies the central role of works on paper in Botero's practice, where line and proportion articulate volume with a clarity and authority equal to his paintings and sculpture. | | Born in Medellín, in 1932, Botero undertook formative training in Madrid and Florence, where fascination with the works of the Old Masters profoundly shaped his approach to form, subject, and surface. Instead of functioning as a recreation or retelling, Muchacha acts as a synthesis of Botero's diverse influences. Flawless rosy skin and gently curving volumes take direction from the Renaissance's relationship to the body, yet Botero also echoes Flemish portraiture in the figure's frontal stance and emotional reserve. Subverting the western canon further, Muchacha reflects the grounding, compact nature of pre-Colombian figures, rejecting what he described the "anorexic" standards of European art, replacing idealisation with fullness, containment, and solidity. | | A recurring theme throughout many of Botero's works, the female form has always been a pertinent protagonist in his oeuvre. Muchacha's pink dress, heart shaped hair clip, and bouquet of flowers are all typical symbols of youthful femininity, but her form is diametrically opposed. Even in technique, Botero's use of buildable watercolour, rather than the strict opacity of oil, introduces a visual lightness that contrasts with the perceived weight and solidity of the form. Luminous skin tones and soft shadows temper mass with delicacy, reinforcing the tension between vulnerability and strength that animates the composition. Botero's deep examination of the conventions of art history allowed him to masterfully subvert expectations of the traditionally interlinked ideas of bodily form and self-expression. Affirming Botero's steadfast belief in separating physical embodiment from identity, Muchacha stands strong in her self-expression despite the artist's distortion. | | Executed in 1984, Muchacha emerged during a period of consolidation in Botero's artistic career. Moving to Italy with a new bronze-working studio one year earlier, his renewed commitment to sculpture is expertly reflected in the young girl's, solid, unmoving stance, serving as a translation of physical weight into a two-dimensional landscape. The work was prestigiously exhibited three years later in Madrid's Reina Sofia Museum in the artist's solo exhibition: Pinturas. Dibujos. Esculturas. This was Botero's his first major European retrospective that encompassed bronzes, paintings, and drawings. Presenting Muchacha alongside large portraits and re-interpretations of classical works, the exhibition exemplified the consistency and far-reaching scale of Botero's iconic visual language, as well as his positioning against broader shifts from the figurative towards the abstract in the 1980s avant-garde. Ultimately, Muchacha demonstrates a succinct articulation of Botero's matured visual language, where volume, restraint, and subversion converge to display the artist's mastery and understanding of visual expectation.

provenance: Marlborough Fine Art Ltd., London | Acquired from the above by the present owner in 2006 | | Exhibited | London, Marlborough Fine Art Ltd., Frank Auerbach: Recent Works, January – February 1997, no. 25 (illustrated n.p.) | | Literature | William Feaver, Frank Auerbach, New York, 2009, no. 773 (illustrated pp. 170 and 326) | William Feaver, Frank Auerbach, New York, 2022, no. 773 (illustrated pp. 172 and 368) | | | | Widely regarded as one of the most significant painters of post-war Britain, throughout his illustrious career Frank Auerbach sustained an uncompromising commitment to the creation of a raw and vital image derived from sustained observation of the seated model. The pursuit of this living presence, at once physical and psychological, remained central to his oeuvre. Renowned for the density and authority of his impasto, which powerfully structured and animated the pictorial surface, Auerbach produced some of the most compelling and materially ambitious portraits of the post-war period. His first solo exhibition was held at London's Beaux Arts Gallery in 1956, and in the decades that followed, his work became among the most widely collected and internationally exhibited of any contemporary British artist. Auerbach's approach to portraiture was shaped by a deep engagement with art history, from Rembrandt and Soutine to Giacometti and de Kooning, which informed both the material density of his surfaces and his existential understanding of the figure. | | Painted in 1996, Head of Catherine Lampert belongs to a sustained and intensely focused series of portraits of Catherine Lampert, Auerbach's close friend, biographer, and long-term sitter. The two first met in 1978, when Lampert was organising Auerbach's retrospective at the Hayward Gallery in London and conducted an extensive interview for the accompanying catalogue. Their professional relationship evolved into a profound artistic collaboration: Lampert later became Director of the Whitechapel Gallery in 1988 and curated Auerbach's major retrospective at the Royal Academy in 2001, further shaping the public and critical understanding of his work. Over decades, Lampert sat for Auerbach up to twice weekly, becoming the subject of more than seventy portraits. These works extended and deepened the serial investigations of the human head that had preoccupied the artist since the 1950s, following a lineage of sitters such as Stella West (E.O.W.), Juliet Yardley Mills (J.Y.M.), and his wife, Julia. Through repeated engagement, Auerbach pursued not conventional likeness, but a continually renewed encounter with the physical and psychological reality of the model. | | Head of Catherine Lampert demonstrates Auerbach's dialogue with sitter and tradition through a forceful orchestration of paint. The portrait reveals expressive brushwork and dense impasto, in which a vibrant amalgamation of colour and texture lends the surface an almost sculptural authority. Thickly layered pigment accumulates across the canvas, asserting the materiality of paint even as it forms a recognisable likeness. Lampert described the charged atmosphere of the studio: "Auerbach moves noisily around the room, looks at the painting in the mirror, turns the canvas, stands back, and then rushes up, and like darts or writing on the blackboard fairly brutally tries the next throw or cancels the previous one. He is continuously active, drawing in the air, talking to himself, hardly pausing." (Catherine Lampert, Frank Auerbach Paintings and Drawings 1954–2001, exh. cat. Royal Academy of Arts, London, 2001, p. 62). Her account underscores the physical and psychological intensity of Auerbach's process, an activity defined by constant revision and the gradual accumulation of knowledge about the sitter. | | Dominating the central right-hand passages of the composition in rich impasto, the thickly layered brushstrokes press forward, rising from areas where the paint has been applied with a faster, higher energy, producing a tension between figure and background that is synonymous with Auerbach's celebrated mark-making. Opulent reds, earthy browns, and vibrant yellows converge in a dense topography of pigment. Lampert's head emerges through swirling accumulation of brushstrokes, projecting with almost relief-like force, her facial features articulated through decisive strokes and daubs, each gesture carrying descriptive and expressive weight. Yet despite its material density, the portrait conveys a striking sense of temporal and psychological suspension: "that odd limbo, not an unpleasant state, of drifting from practical self-reminders into daydreams and unquantifiable desires." (Catherine Lampert in William Feaver, Frank Auerbach, New York, 2009, p. 21). | | Although fundamentally a figurative painter, the intensity and singularity of Auerbach's technique render his portraits essentially abstract, reflecting not only the sitter's physical presence but also the artist's emotional and psychological engagement. As Feaver observed, "Auerbach's heads are conceived not as busts or cameos but as presences" (William Feaver, ibid., p. 20), highlighting the existential immediacy of his figures. In Head of Catherine Lampert, his masterful use of colour and decisive painterly gestures conveys a powerful emotional charge, synthesising observation, material density, and psychological depth. Thus, the present work exemplifies Auerbach's inimitable approach to portraiture, in which the act of seeing, the physicality of paint, and the intimacy of human presence converge, producing a work of profound resonance and enduring significance in contemporary British art.

provenance: Private collection, Dordogne; their sale, Martinie Enchères, Brive-la-Gaillarde, 24 November 2018, lot 450. | Private collection, London (acquired at the above sale). | | | Henri Lebasque's Bord de Marne à Lagny belongs to one of the most fruitful and lyrical moments of the artist's career, when Lebasque, newly settled outside Paris for health reasons, immersed himself in the quiet rhythms of life along the banks of the Marne. Executed during his years in Lagny-sur-Marne, this work exemplifies Lebasque's deeply personal synthesis of Impressionist observation and post-Impressionist colour, resulting in a vision of nature suffused with light, serenity, and immediacy. | | | The composition unfolds with graceful assurance. On the left, a stand of trees rises from the riverbank, their trunks rendered not in naturalistic browns but in an animated spectrum of golds, ochres, blues and reds. Their branches arc gently over the water, framing the scene while guiding the eye across the shimmering surface of the river toward the distant village beyond. Lebasque's brushwork is lively and responsive: short, dappled strokes and cross-hatched touches dissolve form into reflection, allowing the water to act as both mirror and atmosphere. Mauves, pinks and soft purples articulate shadow and vibration, a distinctly Impressionist vocabulary used here with remarkable delicacy and control. | | | The chromatic range is dominated by cool blues and greens, enlivened by flashes of rose and pale gold, particularly along the horizon and within the river's reflective plane. These pastel-inflected tones, combined with Lebasque's use of atmospheric perspective, soften the distant banks and village houses, which are suggested with a few deft strokes. The sky, occupying the upper right quadrant, opens the composition outward: light clouds swirl across a pale expanse tinged with pink, reinforcing the sense of fleeting weather and a specific, transitory moment in time. | | | This emphasis on light, reflection, and the water's edge places the painting firmly within the central concerns of Impressionism, yet Lebasque's temperament distinguishes the work from that of his predecessors. While adapting the lessons of Monet, Renoir and Degas — particularly their plein-air practices and attention to optical sensation — Lebasque avoids bravura effects in favour of intimacy and calm. In this zone of contemplation, the river flows quietly, the village rests in the distance, and human presence is implied rather than asserted, reinforcing the harmony between landscape and lived experience. | | | The present work relates closely to Two Fishermen in a Boat on the Marne (1903), now in the collection of the Museo Nacional Thyssen-Bornemisza, a composition of similar scale and format painted during the same period. Both works demonstrate Lebasque's exploration of divisionist brushwork at this moment, a technique he would soon abandon, using finely articulated strokes to achieve extraordinary effects of light, transparency and reflection. Yet while the Thyssen painting introduces figures and a more enclosed framing, Bord de Marne à Lagny adopts a more expansive viewpoint. Here, the artist steps back, allowing greater prominence to the river's reflective surface and the open sky, resulting in a composition of heightened luminosity and spatial breadth. | | | Compared to the Thyssen work, the palette of the present painting is more highly keyed and vibrantly cool, suggesting a different moment of day or season — perhaps early morning or late afternoon in spring or early summer. The foliage appears fuller and more verdant, the blues richer and more varied, ranging from sapphire and turquoise to pale, silvery reflections. The reflection of the trees in the water is rendered with particular care, using tighter, more staccato strokes that lend the surface a crystalline clarity. These subtle distinctions underscore Lebasque's sensitivity to changing light and atmosphere, as well as his commitment to capturing nature as a living, mutable presence. | | | Lebasque's years along the Marne marked a period of consolidation and confidence. Influenced by Pissarro, Luce and Signac — whom he encountered at the Salon des Indépendants in the 1890s — he nonetheless resisted the rigidity of systematic Neo-Impressionism. As Denise Bazetoux observed, Lebasque sought above all to express his own vision of nature, one rooted in joy, balance, and a deeply felt response to the world around him. His landscapes from this time are imbued with what contemporaries recognised as a rare serenity, reflecting both the harmony of his personal life and his profound engagement with the subtleties of light in the Île-de-France. | | | Bord de Marne à Lagny stands as a compelling example of this achievement. At once observational and poetic, it captures the spirit of an artist at ease with his medium, translating the fleeting sensations of colour, weather and reflection into a composition of lasting freshness and grace. In this way, the painting encapsulates the quiet modernity of Lebasque's vision and his distinctive contribution to the evolution of French landscape painting at the turn of the twentieth century.

Holland Collection, New York (acquired at the above sale); their sale, Peachtree & Bennett, Atlanta, 11 October 2014, lot 16. | Private collection, UK (acquired at the above sale). | | Exhibited | Brussels, Galerie des Artistes Français, Le Sidaner, October - November 1931, no. 35 (titled 'Les arbres de la rive'). | | Literature | Y. Farinaux-Le Sidaner, Le Sidaner, L'oeuvre peint et gravé, Paris, 1989, no. 704 (illustrated p. 258). | | | Born on the island of Mauritius, and the son of a long-distance sea captain who disappeared at sea, Henri Le Sidaner grew up in Dunkirk, a northern port city defined by its harbours and tides. Surrounded from an early age by an element that would become a leitmotiv of his artistic practice, water left a lasting imprint on the artist's memory and imagination. Its never-ending capacity for reflective stillness and mesmerising, perpetually shifting reflections became deeply embedded in the artist's memory and imagination, and throughout his career Le Sidaner returned persistently to ports, canals and quiet waterways, making them central subjects of his oeuvre. The present work, Les arbres sur la rive, Quimperlé, stands within this lifelong meditation on water and its poetic resonance. | | Painted in his Versailles studio in 1931, the composition is inspired by the artist's memory of Quimperlé, a modest Breton town situated at the confluence of three rivers, which the artist had visited several years earlier. Working from sketches he had made when he was in Quimperlé, Le Sidaner recreated the scene guided by memory and sensation, likely influenced by important port scenes such as Claude Gellée's (Le Lorrain) Seaport (1644). With its golden light, classical architecture and tranquil water, Claude's celebrated painting similarly transforms a natural landscape into a poetic meditation on atmosphere and stillness — anticipating the quiet, contemplative mood that Le Sidaner would later evoke through his more intimate, Symbolist-inflected handling of light and space. | | Les arbres sur la rive, Quimperlé is set at the end of a sunny day. A hushed luminosity suffuses the scene, wherein vertical trunks rise like quiet sentinels before a canal. The composition is governed by a rhythmic alternation of upright lines and receding space: the trees, evenly spaced along the riverbank, create a measured cadence whose silence is only disrupted by the gentle diagonals of the boats' masts, suggesting the soft, hollow echoes of the boats' hulls as they are lulled by the water. | | The long shadows of the trees, rendered with an almost pointillist sensibility, recall Camille Pissarro's sun-drenched Late Afternoon in Our Meadow (1887), which shares similar tones of muted mauve, powdery blue and pink, and warm yellow on the ground, with small trees casting longer shadows than their height would suggest. These long silhouettes recall the hands of a sundial and suggest at once the passage of time and its slow, unhurried movement, evoking late sunny afternoons that seem to stretch endlessly beneath a generous, lingering light. The elongated trees and the sinuous line they follow along the riverbank, giving the composition a dynamic perspective that draws the eye inward, also recall Claude Monet's Poplars (Autumn) (1891), which shares a similar autumnal light. | | In Les arbres sur la rive, Quimperlé, different colours dissolve into one another in a tapestry of vibrant brushstrokes. The foliage above shimmers with touches of rose, gold and ochre, suggesting autumnal light filtered through leaves rather than sharp contrasts. The canal itself is rendered in softened reflections, its surface a veil of turquoise and pale jade that echoes the shadows on the ground. Creating a mosaic-like surface, Le Sidaner masterfully illustrates light through chromatic vibrancy, with an 'extremely varied and subtle [palette] [...] [where] the oils bind and melt together in delicate harmonies. [...] With him, contours seem to emerge from the interplay of light, and in this respect, he is similar to Claude Monet'. (J. Baschet in L'Illustration, 1924, quoted in Y. Farinaux-Le Sidaner, Le Sidaner, L'oeuvre peint et gravé, Paris, 1989, p. 37). | | Le Sidaner held the Impressionists and Claude Monet in deep admiration, writing that the latter was '[working] to conquer a new light every day.' (H. Le Sidaner, De la lumiere et de la couleur, 1935, quoted in Y. Farinaux-Le Sidaner, op. cit., p. 34). Indeed, for the Impressionists the work was never done, as light constantly changes. One of the most telling examples of this was Claude Monet's quasi-scientific observation of daylight on the same building at different times of day in his Rouen Cathedral series (1892–1894). Le Sidaner pursued this same obsession, which led some critics to say that 'in the past, he seemed to proceed as an Impressionist, painting light on surfaces rather than surfaces themselves' (C. Mauclair, Preface to the catalogue of the Georges Petit exhibition, 1935, quoted in Y. Farinaux-Le Sidaner, op. cit., p. 39). In fact, the light in Les arbres sur la rive, Quimperlé is not so different from that in Monet's Cathédrale de Rouen, Effet de soleil (Fin de journée) (1892), painted at the end of a sunny day. | | In deliberate contrast to the Impressionists, Le Sidaner did not habitually complete his paintings en plein air. Instead, he worked in the studio from sketches made on site and from memory once he had returned home. By distancing himself from direct observation, he freed his compositions from the burden of reality and reshaped the scenes through the filter of memory and sensation. As Camille Mauclair observed, Le Sidaner '[retained] the finest principles of the Impressionist masters in order to employ them in the expression of a psychological ideal altogether different from realism' (C. Mauclair, L'Impressionisme, Son histoire, son esthétique, ses maîtres, Paris, 1904, p. 198). In this way, his painting becomes less an exercise in empirical truth than an act of poetic reconstruction, where memory mediates perception and atmosphere supersedes fact. | | In the paintings of Henri Le Sidaner, human figures are rare, and when they do appear, they are more suggested than truly seen. Here, in a quiet and uncommon moment, a fisherman stands at the centre left, tidying his tools aboard his boat at the end of a day's work. His presence does not dominate the scene; he is barely more than a shadow, almost dissolving into the surrounding light. This absence of clearly defined figures deepens the contemplative mood of the work. The painting feels suspended — poised delicately between reality and reverie — and becomes less a depiction of place than an evocation of atmosphere: a quiet meditation in colour, where light and water captivate the viewer in an instant of reverie. This introspective view, created from memory and old sketches, situates Le Sidaner at a mesmerising intersection between Impressionism and Symbolism. | | Indeed, the painting resists narrative closure. No event unfolds, no figure commands interpretation; instead, meaning arises from the subtle orchestration of stillness. Le Sidaner thus moves away from Impressionism and its objectivity towards Symbolism and its emphasis on mood, suggestion, and inner experience rather than clear narrative. This softly lit landscape feels less like a specific location and more like a poetic evocation of solitude and reverie at the end of a quiet afternoon, reminiscent of Debussy's Prélude à l'Après-midi d'un faune (1892–1894). Both compositions avoid traditional development, dissolve sharp outlines, and create an atmosphere of suspension and introspection in a late sunny afternoon of natural contemplation, thus privileging sensation and the evocative power of suggestion over literal representation. | | In the words of Paul Signac, Le Sidaner was 'a master at creating tender, soft, and silent atmospheres' (P. Signac quoted in Y. Farinaux-Le Sidaner, op. cit., p. 31). Offering a wonderful sentimental evocation of the landscape, Les arbres sur la rive, Quimperlé stands as a compelling example of Le Sidaner's elegiac tone, situating the spectator within the scene, as though standing quietly among the trees, absorbed in solitary contemplation for a moment of respite, at a time when much of European art pursued fragmentation, political engagement, or radical formal experimentation.
