provenance: Gift from the artist to the present owner | | Exhibited | London, Gagosian Gallery, Britannia Street, Damien Hirst: The Complete Spot Paintings 1986-2011, 12 January - 18 February 2012 | | Literature | Jason Beard & Millicent Wilner (eds.), Damien Hirst: The Complete Spot Paintings 1986-2011, London, 2013 (illustrated p. 84) | | | | Executed in 1994,  Argininamine represents an early iteration of the body of work that propelled Damien Hirst to international prominence and critical distinction. Comprised of one hundred and fifty-six meticulously arranged, uniquely coloured dots set in a precise matrix of twelve rows and thirteen columns, Argininamine stands as an early and important example of Damien Hirst's acclaimed Spot series. Each chromatic sphere, while uniform in scale and spatial placement, is distinguished by its individual hue, creating a composition that is both systematically ordered and visually diverse. Despite the potential for infinite permutations within this framework, the overarching themes of life, death, science and art, and conceptual undercurrents resonate consistently throughout the entire series. With a diversely hued palette and distinct composition, Argininamine demonstrates these core principles with a high degree of formal control and precision. | | Emerging as a central figure among the Young British Artists during the late 1980s and 1990s, Hirst and his contemporaries were characterised by an entrepreneurial spirit and an embrace of unconventional, often provocative materials and methods. His first curatorial initiative, Freeze - staged in 1988 while he was still a student at Goldsmiths College of Art - featured two Spot paintings and marked a pivotal moment, catalysing the rise of both Hirst and the YBA collective to immediate recognition within the contemporary art world. Each spot in the series is painstakingly executed by hand using household gloss paint within a rigorously predetermined grid, a practice that interrogates the tension between mechanical precision and the corporeal trace of human intervention. | | Argininamine is part of the most well-known subseries of the Spot series; the Pharmaceutical paintings. These were initially conceived alongside Hirst's renowned Medicine Cabinets and further the artist's lifelong interest in the conversation between faith, art and science. Hirst sees medicine as a potent belief system, in which society is seduced by drugs and persuaded of their capacity to cure all ailments and sustain life, while rarely interrogating their side effects: "Art is like medicine, it can heal. Yet I've always been amazed at how many people believe in medicine but don't believe in art" (D. Hirst, I want to spend the rest of my life everywhere, with everyone, one to one, always, forever, now, London 2006, p. 246). The artist derived the titles of each Pharmaceutical painting from an alphabetical listing of drug names cited in the Sigma-Aldrich chemical company catalogue that he first encountered in the early 1990s. As such, the Pharmaceutical paintings can be seen as an extension of the medical supplies found in Hirst's Medicine Cabinets with each spot signifying an individual pill. | | Through each carefully hand-painted spot, Hirst is able to establish his broader artistic philosophy while creating a distinctive and instantly recognizable visual language. The artist has built upon this discourse over the years, creating a triumphant output of fully unique works that utilize this language. Entirely fresh to the market, Argininamine was included in Gagosian Gallery's ambitious 2012 exhibition series The Complete Spot Paintings 1986–2011, which presented over 300 works from the series across all eleven of the gallery's global locations. Spanning a remarkable range in scale — from minuscule pinhole-sized marks to expansive compositions featuring spots measuring up to 60 inches in diameter — each spot asserts a presence that becomes acutely palpable when viewed in person. This singular exhibition series highlighted the artist's impressive production and investigation of the spot, which is central to Hirst's aesthetic inquiry exploring the dialectic between seriality and individuality. As he reflects: "I've always liked series. [...] You get some sort of security from the repetition of a series. If you say something twice, it's pretty convincing. It's more convincing than if you say it once. I think it's also the implication of the endlessness, which kind of theoretically helps you avoid death. [...] People are afraid of change, so you create a kind of belief for them through repetition. It's like breathing. So I've always been drawn to series and pairs. A unique thing is quite a frightening object" (The artist in conversation with Hans Ulrich Obrist, In the darkest hour there might be light: Works from Damien Hirst's Murderme Collection, London, Serpentine Gallery/Other Criteria, 2008). | | Unfolding across a radiant chromatic spectrum, Argininamine  manifests a structured, contemplative grid that invites reflection on the intricate interrelations among science, religion, art, beauty, life, and death. The seemingly molecular structure of Argininamine suggests a tension between beauty and horror within the sphere of scientific discovery, acknowledging that no matter how deeply we question the mechanics of the world, we remain subject to the unknowable operations of fate. As resonant today as at the time of its creation, this work offers a powerful, lyrical meditation on themes that remain central to the human condition. Through its elegant synthesis of order and emotion, Argininamine epitomises Hirst's enduring engagement with existential inquiry and aesthetic precision.

provenance: Sadie Coles HQ, London | Acquired from the above by the present owner in 2016 | | Exhibited | Venice, The British Pavillion, 56th Venice International Art Biennale, I SCREAM DADDIO, 9 May - 22 November 2015 (another from the edition exhibited and illustrated pp. 91, 93 and 94) | | Illustrated images are of another work from the edition. | | | | Executed in 2015, Sarah Lucas' Gold Cup Maradona is exuberant, monumental and commands attention through its scale, colour, and complex composition. Distinctive within the artist's oeuvre for its imposing size, the present work bears the hallmarks of Lucas' internationally acclaimed work. The result is a striking sculpture that perfectly epitomises the artist's decades-long rebellious yet playful engagement with the art historical tradition of the portrayal of the human form, challenging traditional notions of gender, sexuality and identity. Through its twists and bulges, the present work depicts an anthropomorphic cast whose natural bodily contours mirror and reshape reality. With Gold Cup Maradona, Lucas elevates bravado and bodily excess to an epic status, gleaming with irreverence and audacity. | | First presented on the portico of the British Pavilion at the 56th Venice Biennale in 2015, Gold Cup Maradona asserts both physical and conceptual dominance. Originally conceived specifically for this site, the sculpture exemplifies Lucas' long-standing commitment to creating work in direct and thoughtful dialogue with its surroundings. During its Venice presentation, the boldly masculine, fluid contours of Gold Cup Maradona sprawled across the British Pavilion's entrance, dynamically disrupting the restraint of its neoclassical façade while simultaneously enticing viewers into the pavilion by provoking curiosity through its irreverent presence. The figure's towering phallus audaciously sliced through the Gran Bretagna sign, yet this irreverent act was accompanied by a thoughtful engagement with art history: the sculpture occupied the same site as Henry Moore's Double Standing Figure in 1948. Here, Lucas established a purposeful challenge between the comical representation of the sexualised male form and Moore's abstract figures, which intended to represent the optimistic and humanist values embodied in modernism. Notably, at the time of the 56th Venice Biennale, only four women prior to Lucas had been selected to exhibit in the British Pavilion: Barbara Hepworth in 1950, Bridget Riley in 1968, Rachel Whiteread in 1997, and Tracey Emin in 2007. As such, the commanding sculpture that greeted visitors served as a powerful articulation of Lucas' mature confidence in her position as a leading British female artist at the time of the work's creation, a distinction that the artist still carries today. | | Lucas is widely associated with sculptural depictions of the female body fashioned from soft fabrics and pliable materials – most notably tights, which openly allude to conventionally feminine objects and rituals. Gold Cup Maradona, by contrast, turns to the male form and to bronze, a resolute and weighty material often coded as robust or even masculine. Yet through this medium Lucas deftly conjures a sense of bodily suppleness, lending the sculpture an inviting tactility and warmth that temper its imposing presence despite the material's inherent hardness. In doing so, the work conveys a delicacy and vulnerability comparable to that found in her fabric-based pieces. This portrayal of the male body, poised between figurative abstraction and sexualised formalisation, carries a palpable vitality and fragility akin to that sensed in the artist's flexible textile sculptures. | | The choice of yellow is reminiscent of Lucas' recurring engagement with eggs, evident throughout her practice, where these function both as humorous references to the female body and as symbols of fertility and reproduction. One of the most recognisable works by the artist is Self Portrait with Fried Eggs, from 1996, where two fried eggs were placed on the artist's breasts as a playful representation of femininity and fertility while defying common representations of women through the male gaze. The incorporation of eggs throughout the artist's practice "put[s] the fate of the egg – typically understood as the female reproductive cell – into the hands of women, perhaps alluding to political debates concerning women's rights over their own bodies" (Margot Norton, Sarah Lucas Au Naturel, New York 2019 p. 99). As Lucas herself explains, "So why yellow? Is it because I've been wondering, in terms of the two large sculptures, what colour they should be? Or is [it] because I've been wondering how to get eggs into the thing?" (S. Lucas, I SCREAM DADDIO, London, 2015, p. 52). Lucas experimented extensively with different shades of yellow, testing them on various surfaces and observing how they shifted under changing light conditions and at different times of day. Ultimately, the artist chose a colour called Gold Cup, a vivid yellow, for the present work, exhibited on the outside of the pavilion, and Deep Cream, a slightly paler variation, for its sister-piece exhibited inside, with each colour contributing its name to the work's title. | | Renowned for her bold, mischievous, and unapologetically provocative approach, Lucas' practice is defined by irreverent humour and the inventive use of visual puns and crude euphemisms. Working across sculpture, photography, and installation, her work consistently engages the body in its physical, cultural, and psychological dimensions. With both wit and sincerity, Lucas addresses themes of sex, mortality, and British identity, embracing sensationalism as a strategic and critical tool rather than mere shock. Her suggestive forms deftly undermine clichés propagated by popular media, while her sustained interrogation of gender foregrounds the performative nature of femininity and masculinity. Gold Cup Maradona stands as a confident and celebratory culmination of Sarah Lucas' sculptural prowess, uniting humour, provocation, and historical awareness within its fluid, imposing and striking forms. Through its monumental scale, radiant colour, and deliberate engagement with site and gender representations, the present work asserts Lucas' authoritative voice within British and international contemporary art, leaving an enduring and unforgettable impression on both the pavilion and its viewers alike. | |

provenance: Gift from the artist to the present owner | | | | Executed circa 1995, Beautiful, Dental, Brushing, Full Mouth Rehabilitation, Thank You Painting is an early and luminous example of Damien Hirst's iconic series of Spin paintings. Hirst initiated this body of work in 1992, experimenting with the centrifugal force of a rapidly rotating circular canvas onto which he poured vivid streams of household paint. These celebrated Spin paintings captivate through their vibrant kineticism, generated by the spontaneous operations of chance, as the artist's own hand is nearly removed from the final composition. The methodology of the present work recalls Jackson Pollock's revolutionary drip paintings, through which Pollock pioneered a technique of dynamically dripping and pouring skeins of paint onto canvas or paper spread upon the floor beneath him. Similarly animated and bursting with chromatic intensity that seems to extend beyond the canvas's perimeter, Hirst's Spin paintings engage the uncertainty inherent in human experience, emblematic of the artist's enduring pursuit to transcend predetermined limits within his own artistic practice. | | Shaped by postmodernism's privileging of chance and the aleatory, Hirst's Spin paintings stand in marked contrast to his methodical Spot series, though both interrogate the notion of an imagined mechanical artist, which is a conceit Hirst has provocatively sustained throughout his diverse oeuvre. Beautiful, Dental, Brushing, Full Mouth Rehabilitation, Thank You Painting unites the automatic with the tactile, creating organic, unique painterly gestures through a regulated process. The tension between automation and chance lies at the heart of Hirst's practice, through which he seeks to unsettle convention and extend the formal and conceptual boundaries of painting, while reaffirming his enduring engagement with mortality, where chance and control remain inextricably entwined. | | As with much of Hirst's oeuvre, the apparent simplicity of the spin painting technique is inseparable from his fundamental interrogation of art's function and value. The artist has recounted that the series was inspired by childhood memories of watching Blue Peter presenter John Noakes demonstrate a variant of the process using a motorised cardboard spinning device. Some time after viewing the broadcast, Hirst attended a school event where he first attempted spin painting himself, recalling a sustained fascination and near-obsessive compulsion to repeat the act again and again. Ironically, Hirst later inaugurated his own spin painting enterprise within a comparable milieu: after producing several early works in his Brixton studio in 1992, he established, the following year, a spin art stall with fellow artist Angus Fairhurst at Joshua Compston's street fair A Fête Worse than Death. For the occasion, the performance artist Leigh Bowery famously transformed Hirst and Fairhurst into clowns, and visitors were invited to produce their own spin paintings, which the artists signed upon completion. | | In 1994, whilst living in Berlin, Hirst commissioned the fabrication of his own spin machine, a development that marked the moment at which the series began to take shape. Created circa 1995, the present work encapsulates the euphoric ecstasy of these early investigations. As the Spin paintings became increasingly popular, Hirst never lost his childlike sense of wonder in the process that had inspired him as a young boy. It remained, for him, 'a miracle of technology'; 'I really like making them', he professed. 'And I really like the machine, and I really like the movement. Every time they're finished, I'm desperate to do another one' (D. Hirst, quoted in D. Hirst and G. Burn, On the Way to Work, London 2001, p. 221). Ultimately, these works function as unrestrained affirmations of the power of painting: by removing his own hand directly from the process, Hirst reawakens a primal sense of awe in its unpredictable possibilities. | | Hypnotic in composition and resplendent in chromatic brilliance, Beautiful, Dental, Brushing, Full Mouth Rehabilitation, Thank You Painting is an exquisitely executed work that provides a kaleidoscopic and meditative experience for the viewer. |

provenance: Galerie Durant-Dessert, Paris | Private Collection, France (acquired from the above in 1989) | Anon. sale, Sotheby's, New York, 12 May 2016, lot 139 | Acquired from the above by the present owner | | Literature | Exh. cat., Alighiero Boetti, Ravenna, 1984, no. 7 (illustrated pp. 44-45) | Bernard Blistène, 'Fontana Burri Manzoni e l'Arte Povera: La Mauvaise Question', in Artstudio, No. 13, Summer 1989 (illustrated p. 27) | Martin De Luca & Massimo Minimmi (eds.), Alighiero e Boetti, Ravenna, 1990, no. 46, p. 55 | Mark Kremmer, 'Lightness as a Weapon. On the Work of Alighiero e Boetti', in Archis, No. 2, February 1995 (illustrated p. 71) | Lara Vinca Masini, Arte Contemporanea, La Linea del Modello, Arte Come Progetto del Mondo, Florence, 1996, no. 3136 (illustrated p. 617) | Jean-Christophe Ammann, Alighiero Boetti, Catalogo generale, Tomo secondo, Opere 1972-1979, Milan, 2012, no. 951 (illustrated p. 287) | | | | Mettere i verbi all'infinito, from 1978, is a defining work from Alighiero Boetti's celebrated lavori biro series (or ballpoint drawings), which examine the intersections of linguistic, numerical and visual systems. Initiated in 1972, the series employs the modest medium of the ballpoint pen to generate densely textured fields of colour, composed of accumulative strokes and punctuated by small, luminous white commas. Through this controlled yet open-ended process, Mettere i verbi all'infinito beautifully articulates Boetti's sustained engagement with structure, language, systematisation and the production of meaning. | | Though seemingly dispersed randomly across the page, each comma is meticulously positioned to correspond with a specific letter of the alphabet, identifiable by tracing their sequence against the key along the left-hand side of the composition. As Boetti explained, "A word turns into a sign, into a compilation of commas with a meaning... you must render the comma as something that is not stable" (the artist quoted in Alighiero Boetti: Mettere al mondo il mondo, Frankfurt, 1998, p. 63). Moving from left to right, the viewer gradually deciphers the coded message, which in this instance reveals the title: Mettere i verbi all'infinito. In engaging the viewer in this process of revelation, Boetti constructs a subtle yet playful game that simultaneously deconstructs and celebrates the capacity of letters to convey information, while poetically acknowledging his enduring fascination with language and wordplay. The work destabilises the perceived authority of the Latin alphabet, exposing it as an artificial system governed by arbitrary rules rather than a fixed conduit of meaning. In doing so, it evokes a sustained tension between control and uncertainty, logic and intuition, as comprehension emerges incrementally through careful attention. This delicate oscillation between order and unpredictability exemplifies one of Boetti's central preoccupations: ordine e disordine, opposing forces that coexist in a state of continual flux, shaping the conceptual framework of his practice. | | Made up of three individual panels, each painstakingly filled with rich, subtly gradated fields of royal blue ink, Mettere i verbi all'infinito presents a shimmering vision of space, the white commas appearing like a mysterious astronomical constellation or a series of falling raindrops against its expanse. While the laborious process demanded a heightened level of attention to ensure the surface was filled as densely as possible, a number of subtle textural shifts can be detected throughout. Each panel is imbued with the distinctive rhythm of its maker, resulting in fluctuating fields of colour that appear to undulate across the composition. These variations depend on numerous factors: from the quality of the pen and the pressure applied, to the speed of each stroke, the temperament of the maker, and even the gradual loss of pigment as the pen began to run out of ink. | | In each of the lavori biro works, Boetti employed a group of collaborators to realise his vision. While the artist developed the concept and defined the basic grid pattern, the execution of the composition was entrusted to others. A similar method was used in the artist's Arazzi and Mappe series, both of which relied on the technical skills of Afghan embroiderers. By adopting this process, Boetti established a form of relational aesthetics through which he explored the role of the artist as a conceiver rather than the sole creator of a work of art. In the case of the biro drawings, he drew assistants from his local neighbourhood of Trastevere in Rome and requested that each alternating panel be coloured by a member of the opposite sex. Armed with a clearly defined set of rules, his collaborators spent countless hours filling the panels with intricate layers of cross-hatching, a time-intensive process Boetti felt was intrinsic to the nature of the works: "The drawings in Biro are concentrates of time" (the artist quoted ibid, p. 59). | | This embrace of systems tempered by chance situates Mettere i verbi all'infinito in dialogue with the conceptual framework of Arte Povera, with which Boetti was closely associated in the late 1960s. Despite its materially modest components, everyday ballpoint pens and the labour of non-professional collaborators, the work extends beyond the movement's emphasis on physicality and process. Boetti redirects Arte Povera's anti-hierarchical ethos toward immaterial systems of language, time, and collective authorship. While resonating with the movement's resistance to industrialisation, commodification, and rigid formalism; the lavori biro depart from its material focus, privileging conceptual structures and delegated production as instruments for interrogating authorship and meaning. The visible traces of labour, the openness to error, and the gradual accumulation of ink, function not merely as evidence of process, but as markers of a philosophical inquiry that surpasses the movement's original scope. | | Executed in the 1970s, a decade that consolidated Boetti's conceptual interests, Mettere i verbi all'infinito emerges from a broader exploration of systems as both formal frameworks and metaphors for ordering the world. During this period, Boetti developed parallel bodies of work, most notably the Mappe, which charted geopolitical change, while also formalising his fascination with duality through the adoption of his doubled name, Alighiero e Boetti. Across these projects, he mobilised language, cartography, and delegated labour as interrelated strategies for examining authorship and temporality, holding structure and unpredictability in deliberate tension. In bringing these concerns together, Boetti's practice reflects an enduring interest in how meaning is shaped through processes that exceed individual intention. | | Mettere i verbi all'infinito transforms a deceptively simple system into a work of profound complexity and elegance. It exemplifies Boetti's capacity to balance conceptual rigor with chance and human variation, producing a composition that is simultaneously intellectually exacting and visually compelling. In its quiet complexity, Mettere i verbi all'infinito stands as a powerful testament to Boetti's ingenuity.

provenance: Opera Gallery, Monaco | Acquired from the above by the present owner | | | | Manolo Valdés occupies a unique position in postwar European art; an archeologist of mythologies who reveals the tension between historical and contemporary spectacle, examining and producing art that engages deeply with the sociocultural potentialities of image-making and iconography. In the present work, Reina Mariana, Valdés' vision crystalises in a reanimated silhouette of the Spanish Golden Age. Lucent and amethyst-like, it presents as an object of nature – a piece derived from natural creation and order. Sublimated in this idea is the crux of Valdés' project: to upend the ideologies embedded in images of power. | | Emerging during the final decades of the Franco regime in Spain, for Valdés and his artistic comrades art was a vehicle for critique and cultural reclamation. A founding member of the Equipo Crónica in 1965, alongside Rafael Solbes and Juan Antonio Toledo, the group approached art history as an active archive, reconstituting images belonging to the Spanish tradition as a form of Pop art inflected through a politicized lens. "We used 'pop' but questioned it. We took the images (language) but knew it had to be different from the United States. We felt that American pop lacked the political content [...] We relied heavily on historical painting, which we converted into pop. For us the Museo del Prado represented the utmost expression of popular culture. Its contents became our main source of inspiration" (the artist quoted in: "Artist interview: Manolo Valdés (Equipo Crónica)", Tate, September 2015, Online). | | By reworking canonical paintings alongside comic-strip graphics and contemporary political imagery, Equipo Crónica exposed how cultural authority is imposed and disseminated. Their project was neither parody nor homage, but a critical investigation into how images accumulate meaning through repetition and institutional framing. After the dissolution of the collective in 1981 following the death of Solbes, this sustained dialogue with art history has been the driving force of Valdés' own practice, reenvisioning the works of Velázquez, repurposing the tools of Picasso and Matisse, Cubism and the Fauves. | | The present work employs Valdés' most prominent leitmotif, taking one of the most recognisable images of Spanish court painting, Velázquez's own 1652–1653 Portrait of Mariana of Austria – in the collection of the Museo del Prado – as it's departure point. The domed features of the subject's extravagant coiffure and architectural dress are inseparable from the work of Valdés. In his stripping of identity from the original image, Valdés emphasises collective memory over biography; the figure becomes less a historical person than a cultural symbol. | | Reina Mariana embodies a worldview that remains in living memory for Spain: history is neither neutral nor passive but is continuously reconstructed; that absolute power corrupts absolutely. The translation of a Baroque royal portrait into a contemporary sculpture demonstrates a fluidity at the heart of image-making. In its immaculate surface Reina Mariana conceals the hand of the artist, reaffirming the mediated perfection of reproduced images but also the natural order implied by autonomous, inhuman objects. Part-sculpture, part-monument, the present work is an elegant window through which the spectator glimpses the essential transparency of images that seek to project power or fortify ideology. | | Valdés has long since achieved global stardom and institutional acclaim, his sculptures appearing in public spaces of major cities around the world for decades, most notably representing Spain at the 48th Venice Biennale in 1999, and in 2006 being honored by the Museo Reina Sofía with a comprehensive career survey. There is little doubt in his international standing as an artist who has produced one of the most consistent and compelling bodies of work to emerge from Spain in the latter half of the 20th century.

Le Normand-Romain, The Bronzes of Rodin, Catalogue of Works in the Musée Rodin, Vol. I, Paris, 2007, pp. 335-337 (another cast illustrated p. 334; terracotta version illustrated p. 335; plaster version illustrated p. 336; marble versions illustrated pp. 336 & 337). | | One of Auguste Rodin's most celebrated sculptures and among the greatest commercial successes of his career, Eternal printemps was conceived in 1884 at a moment of profound emotional and artistic intensity. The work emerged during Rodin's passionate relationship with Camille Claudel, who had recently joined his studio as an assistant and whose presence would prove transformative to his art. Originally developed as part of La porte de l'Enfer — the monumental bronze doors inspired by Dante Alighieri's Inferno, commissioned in 1880 — the rapturous embrace of the lovers was ultimately deemed too hopeful in tone for Rodin's vision of damnation and despair. Freed from that context, Eternal printemps evolved into an autonomous celebration of desire, vitality and enduring passion. | | The entwined figures evoke the tragic lovers Paolo and Francesca, condemned in Dante's narrative to an eternity of wind-tossed embrace. Yet Rodin transforms literary fate into sculptural exaltation. The female nude, derived from the sensuous Torse d'Adèle — named after Adèle Abruzzesi, one of Rodin's most favoured Italian models — arches upward with luminous abandon, while the male figure responds in a sweeping counter-curve, his body seemingly suspended in air. Their union is both precarious and ecstatic, poised at the threshold between physical gravity and emotional transcendence. | | Rodin often described his working method as one of perpetual revision, likening sculpture to a language whose grammar and syntax could be endlessly reconfigured. Figures were reused, adapted and recombined in an ongoing search for expressive truth. In Eternal printemps, this process reaches an extraordinary synthesis: concave and convex forms interlock in a tightly coiled rhythm, while the lovers balance upon a rough, insufficient base that heightens the sensation of motion and risk. The male figure's feet barely touch the ground — one hovering in space, the other hanging over the edge — so that the woman's kneeling body becomes his sole anchor. | | The emotional charge of the work is inseparable from Rodin's relationship with Claudel. Their affair, which began soon after her arrival in his studio in 1882, marked one of the most fertile periods of mutual influence in modern sculpture. Claudel's own works — most notably Sakuntala (1886) and La Valse (1889) — echo the same entwined dynamism and crossed structural axes that animate Eternal printemps, suggesting a shared sculptural vocabulary developed in near tandem. In a letter written to Claudel in 1886, Rodin spoke of his "furious love" and "violent passion" — words that find palpable form in the sculpture's outstretched arms and charged interdependence. | | Rodin later claimed that the idea for Eternal printemps came to him while listening to Ludwig van Beethoven's Symphony No. 2. Reflecting on the music, he remarked on the suffering embedded within its exuberance, and on how this paradox inspired the sculptural vision he would realise. The work was also known under alternative mythological titles — Zéphyr et la Terre and Cupidon et Psyché — a strategy that allowed Rodin to cloak its overt eroticism within the legitimising framework of classical allegory. | | The sculpture's early reception cemented its significance. In 1886, Rodin presented a plaster cast of Eternal printemps to Robert Louis Stevenson, in gratitude for a public defence of his work in the London press. The group was exhibited at the Salon of 1897, and its immediate popularity prompted Rodin to authorise multiple versions. A second iteration, featuring an enlarged base and rocky support, became the model for the editions produced by the Barbedienne foundry between 1898 and 1918, following Rodin's exclusive contract with Gustave Leblanc-Barbedienne. These casts, produced in four sizes, ensured the sculpture's widespread dissemination while retaining the expressive daring of the original conception. | | At the heart of Eternal printemps lies a rare union of lyricism and tension. The lovers' embrace is not static but charged with anticipation, as though caught in the suspended instant before complete surrender. The gesture of the male figure's raised arm — curved, open, unresolved — infuses the composition with a sense of emotional propulsion that seems to lift the figures beyond the limits of the physical world. As critics have observed, Rodin here gives sculptural form to extreme states of feeling, allowing passion itself to shape space and mass. | | Eternal printemps stands as one of Rodin's most enduring images of love: ardent yet fragile, sensual yet monumental. Born from personal passion and refined through relentless formal experimentation, it distils the sculptor's belief that human emotion — when rendered with honesty and intensity — could achieve the timelessness of myth. In this work, a fleeting moment of embrace becomes eternity itself.

Le Normand-Romain, The Bronzes of Rodin, Catalogue of Works in the Musée Rodin, Vol. II, Paris, 2007, pp. 413-414 & 417-419 (another cast illustrated p. 417, fig. 4). | | | That mask determined all my future work. It is the first good piece of modelling I ever did. From that time I sought to look all around my work, to draw it well in every respect. I have kept that mask before my mind in everything I have done... In fact, I have never succeeded in making a figure as good as 'The Broken Nose'. | - Auguste Rodin | | | Conceived at the very outset of his career, Masque de l'Homme au nez cassé is widely regarded as Rodin's first true masterpiece and a work against which he measured his sculpture for decades thereafter. As an early experiment, it announces with startling clarity the artistic principles that would define Rodin's revolution of modern sculpture: truth to life, psychological depth, and a fearless rejection of academic idealisation. | | The model for the work was an ageing Parisian labourer known as Bibi, whose battered features — most notably his broken nose — bore the visible marks of a life lived hard. Rodin was drawn precisely to this physical history. Yet rather than presenting the sitter as a figure of social realism alone, he deliberately fused contemporary observation with classical allusion. The hair is arranged in a stylised manner, bound with a fillet evocative of ancient Greek portrait busts, subtly aligning this anonymous working man with the lineage of philosophers and sages from antiquity. In this physiognomic frankness — where so-called ugliness becomes a bearer of wisdom — Rodin evokes the tradition of ancient portraits of figures such as Socrates and Roman marble heads, elevating character and experience above ideal beauty. In doing so, he bridged the perceived divide between the modern streets of Paris and the timeless human condition. | | This tension lay at the heart of the work's initial rejection. When submitted to the Salon in 1864, the sculpture was refused, reportedly criticised for its unvarnished realism and fragmentary character. At a moment when French academic sculpture remained wedded to smooth ideal forms, Rodin's insistence on fractured surfaces, asymmetry and expressive modelling proved unsettling — a reaction intensified by contemporary anxieties surrounding Social Realism. The refusal was emblematic of the institutional resistance he would face repeatedly in his early career, and it would be more than a decade before he submitted another sculpture to the Salon, returning in 1875 with a marble version of L'Homme au nez cassé, which was finally accepted. | | The fragmentary nature of the mask is itself integral to its power. According to contemporary accounts, the original plaster bust partially collapsed during an exceptionally harsh winter, when Rodin was working in a poorly heated makeshift studio. Rather than discarding the damaged work, he chose to preserve and develop the mask alone. This decision — radical for the 1860s — reveals Rodin's early understanding that a fragment could convey greater intensity than a finished whole. The truncated form concentrates attention on the face, amplifying its psychological immediacy and sculptural force. In this respect, Rodin's approach resonates with his profound admiration for Michelangelo, whose unfinished Slaves, encountered in the Louvre, demonstrated how incompletion could heighten expressive power and emotional truth. | | Technically, the work demonstrates Rodin's deep engagement with historical sculptural practices. He revived the ancient method of modelling by profiles, constructing the form through successive viewpoints rather than submitting to a single frontal ideal — a practice so convincingly rediscovered that, in 1878, the sculptor Jules Desbois famously passed the work off as an antique to his fellow students at the École des Beaux-Arts. The surface remains animated and irregular, bearing the imprint of the artist's hand and resisting the polished finish prized by academic convention. Far from diminishing the sitter, this treatment imbues the mask with remarkable dignity and humanity, suggesting an implicit tenderness beneath its rugged exterior. Classical structure is thus infused with a distinctly modern vision of Paris and its eclectic cast of characters, recalling the incisive social observation found in the work of Honoré Daumier. | | Rodin himself considered L'Homme au nez cassé a foundational work, cherishing it throughout his life, carefully restoring the damaged model and returning to the subject in multiple variations. Its reputation grew steadily: the sculpture won a gold medal in Nice in 1880, was exhibited at the Grosvenor Gallery in London in 1882 — where it was admired by leading figures including Sir Frederick Leighton, who acquired a cast for himself — and appeared in progressive exhibitions such as the Salon des XX in Brussels in 1887. The work exists in numerous versions, distinguished by subtle variations in format and modelling; however, casts of the type I, premier modèle remain closest to Rodin's original conception and are especially prized for their immediacy. Closely related examples are held today in major institutional collections, including the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Ashmolean Museum, and the Harvard Art Museums. | | The importance of the present cast is further underscored by its distinguished provenance. The first documented owner was Otto Charles Henry Gutekunst, the influential British art dealer, collector and co-owner of P. & D. Colnaghi & Co., whose collection included significant Old Master and modern works. While the absence of earlier provenance prevents the identification of the sculpture's initial buyer, the present work appears to be identical to the cast made by Gruet Jeune and given by Rodin in 1884 to the artists Jean-Charles Cazin and Marie Cazin. | | Masque de l'Homme au nez cassé is widely recognised as a critical turning point in nineteenth-century sculpture. It announces Rodin's break from academic orthodoxy and his emergence as an artist capable of uniting realism, classicism and psychological insight within a single form. More restrained and introspective than the expressive dynamism of later works such as L'Éternel Printemps, the mask nevertheless possesses a quiet radicalism. In its uncompromising humanity, it stands as a powerful assertion of Rodin's belief that modern sculpture must begin not with ideal beauty, but with lived experience.

Schwarz, Man Ray, The Rigour of Imagination, London, 1977, no. 90 (illustrated p. 91, without the dedication). | Exh. cat., Man Ray, 1890-1976, Ronny van de Velde, Antwerp, 1994, no. 493 (illustrated without the dedication). | | | The following works come from the estate of Hugo and Selma van de Perre, a couple whose lives and friendships were deeply entwined with twentieth-century European culture. United by intellectual curiosity and a shared commitment to art, literature and political thought, they assembled a collection shaped less by connoisseurship alone than by personal connection. Much of it derives from the estate of E. L. T. Mesens, the poet, artist and gallerist who played a decisive role in shaping Surrealism in Britain following the 1936 International Surrealist Exhibition in London. | | Hugo van de Perre, the son of Alfons van de Perre, founder of the Belgian newspaper De Standaard, was a journalist, cultural commentator and close confidant of Mesens. Their friendship was both intellectual and deeply personal. When Mesens died in 1971, Hugo wrote his obituary — Elegie om E.L.T. Mesens — published in De Spectator (Brussels) in June of that year. In it, he described Mesens not merely as a Surrealist organiser or polemicist, but as a fiercely independent spirit, defined by loyalty, moral conviction and a belief in art as a lived position rather than a profession. The text reveals a friendship founded on shared values: resistance to conformity, devotion to artistic freedom, and an unwavering commitment to the ethical force of culture. It was Hugo, as executor of Mesens' estate, who ensured that many of these works were preserved within a private collection shaped by memory and trust. | | Selma van de Perre was a Dutch–British freedom fighter and member of the wartime resistance, later settling in London where she studied anthropology and sociology and worked at the BBC. She and Hugo married in 1955 and remained deeply engaged with cultural life in Britain and on the Continent. After Hugo's death in 1979, Selma continued his work as a foreign correspondent for Belgian broadcasters and newspapers, reporting particularly on British art and music. The collection they formed together reflects this outward-looking sensibility: international in scope, human in scale, and attentive to the emotional charge of works made and exchanged among friends. | | A jewel of the present group is Man Ray's Rêve du 25 nov 1936, a drawing of exceptional intimacy and historical resonance. Executed in 1936 as an illustration for Les Mains libres, Man Ray's celebrated collaboration with Paul Éluard, the present sheet is uniquely inscribed and dedicated by the artist to Mesens — 'pour Édouard son ami'. The work's early exhibition history underscores its importance within the international dissemination of Surrealism: shown at major early Man Ray exhibitions at the Valentine Gallery in New York in 1936, at Galerie Jeanne Bucher in Paris in 1937 — one of the leading avant-garde galleries of the period — and later at the The London Gallery in 1939, the epicentre of British Surrealism under Mesens' direction. | | Man Ray often explained that many drawings for Les Mains libres were made immediately upon waking, translated directly from dreams before rational interpretation could intervene. The present work belongs to a moment of intense retrospection. In November 1936, Man Ray was in New York for the landmark exhibition Fantastic Art, Dada, Surrealism at the Museum of Modern Art — a symbolic homecoming after fifteen years in Paris. From his hotel terrace overlooking Central Park, he photographed the city, later cropping out a synagogue that had anchored the original image — a quiet but telling gesture reflecting his complex relationship to Jewish identity, which he had long masked through name changes and self-reinvention. The composition of that photograph is directly evoked in the present work, which evokes the impressive verticality of Fifth Avenue's high rise buildings, intersected by the environs of Central Park. The drawing's airborne locomotive evokes not only Man Ray's childhood memories and early fascinations with machines, but also the notorious 1895 train crash at the Gare Montparnasse in Paris, an image widely circulated in illustrated newspapers and lodged in the modern imagination. Within Surrealism, trains recur as potent symbols — such as in the works of Belgian Surrealist Paul Delvaux — embodying passage between realms, between dreams and waking life, reality and fantasy. Here, the train becomes an agent of psychic transit, a vehicle of unconscious return. | | That this drawing passed directly from Man Ray to Mesens, and from Mesens' estate into the collection of Hugo and Selma van de Perre, is profoundly significant. It encapsulates Surrealism not merely as an aesthetic movement, but as a network of lived relationships, sustained by generosity, loyalty and shared belief in art's capacity to bridge inner and outer worlds. Seen alongside works by Méret Oppenheim, António Pedro and Mesens himself, the present work anchors the collection as a testament to Surrealism's human core — an art of friendship, exchange and imaginative freedom, preserved here with remarkable integrity.

Lemoisne, Degas et son oeuvre, Vol. III, Paris, 1947, no. 1180 bis (illustrated p. 685). | | | The original pastel from which this counterproof was executed, Après le bain, currently resides in the State Hermitage Museum, Saint Petersburg (recorded in: P.A. Lemoisne, Degas et son oeuvre, Vol. III, Paris, 1947, no. 1179 (illustrated p. 685); and sold: the artist's estate; their sale, Galerie Georges Petit, Sale III, Paris, 9 April 1919, lot 74). Degas held the work in particular esteem, using his experimental counterproof process to transfer and reverse the onto a second sheet. To produce such works, Degas placed a new sheet over the original pastel and introduced controlled moisture before applying pressure, allowing the image to transfer in reverse. This process not only sharpened compositional relationships but also introduced subtle tonal variations and surface effects inherent to the technique. Degas frequently treated these counterproofs as autonomous works, reworking them further in pastel or charcoal, and valuing them as opportunities for refinement of his compositions. Although the technique had largely fallen out of use by the nineteenth century, it appealed to Degas for the productive tension it created between chance and control. Such works occupy a distinctive place within his practice, reflecting both technical experimentation and aesthetic refinement. | | The present work was formerly in the collection of Julie Manet, daughter of Berthe Morisot and Édouard Manet. Together with her husband, Ernest Rouart – whom Degas mentored in painting and drawing – she assembled one of the most distinguished private collections of Impressionist art in France, including important works by Manet, Morisot, Degas, Monet, Renoir and Pissarro. The Rouart family occupied a central position within the Impressionist circle: Henri Rouart, Ernest's father, was both a painter and one of the earliest and most important patrons of Degas and his contemporaries, forming a collection that later entered museums worldwide. Degas played an active role in encouraging the relationship between Ernest Rouart and Julie Manet, both of whom he knew intimately, and whose union further strengthened the close personal and artistic bonds between the Manet, Morisot, and Rouart families. The present work thus embodies both Degas's relentless technical experimentation and its intimate passage through one of the most significant lineages of Impressionist art.

Strobl, Gustav Klimt, Vol. III, Die Zeichnungen, 1912-1918, Salzburg, 1984, no. 2781 (illustrated p. 167). | | | Before his death in 1918, Gustave Klimt focused extensively on figure studies in pencil, exploring the autonomous expressive potential of line. Stehender Akt nach rechts is a compelling example from this mature period. Devoting particular attention to the standing female nude, Klimt rendered these subjects with remarkable economy of means, moving away from the decorative density of his celebrated paintings. | | In the present work, the model stands oriented to the right, her body articulated through a refined, continuous contour. The figure's weight settles subtly into one hip, forming a gentle contrapposto that recalls the classical canon. Yet the treatment diverges fundamentally from nineteenth-century academic life study: rather than constructing the body through chiaroscuro and anatomical modelling, Klimt privileges line as the primary vehicle of form. Limbs and torso are defined by contour alone, and the volumes of the body emerge with deceptive simplicity. | | Detached from mythological or allegorical narrative and presented without contextual framing, the model exists in a space that is neither constructed nor described. The blank expanse of paper surrounding the figure thereby reinforces the autonomy of line. In contrast to academic tradition, which sought to stabilise the body within a codified system of proportion and moral decorum, Klimt approaches the female figure as a living, mutable presence. | | The model's head, delicately articulated, introduces a psychological dimension that distinguishes the work. Although minimally described, the facial features anchor the figure's corporeality and suggest an individual presence rather than an abstract type. In this respect, Klimt revisits the long tradition of the academic standing nude only to reconfigure it: the body is neither heroic nor didactic, but intimate, contemporary and profoundly human. | | Executed in the final years of his life, Stehender Akt nach rechts reflects an artist who, having traversed the realms of Symbolism, Secessionist decoration, and painterly opulence, returned to drawing as a site for concentrated inquiry. In its restraint and clarity, the sheet stands as a testament to Klimt's profound redefinition of the nude — no longer a vehicle of academic virtuosity, but a locus of modern subjectivity and the enduring primacy of line.

Strobl, Gustav Klimt, Vol. II, Die Zeichnungen 1904-1912, Salzburg, 1982, no. 1334 (illustrated p. 63). | | | Executed circa 1903–1904, Sitzender Frauenakt von vorne belongs to a pivotal moment in the development of Gustav Klimt, when drawing assumed a central role in his reimagining of the female figure, at a time of quiet but decisive departure from academic convention. These years coincide with the artist's early maturity within the Vienna Secession, a period during which his studies of the nude became increasingly autonomous, exploratory, and psychologically resonant. | | The model is shown seated and viewed from the front, her body folded inward upon itself. Her bowed head and curved spine establish a rhythmic, sinuous movement, articulated through a sequence of soft, looping contours that travel across the figure like a slow breath. Rather than constructing the body through tonal modelling or anatomical exactitude, Klimt allows form to emerge almost entirely from the delicacy of the pencil line. The figure seems less built than revealed. | | Such an approach marks a profound departure from the nineteenth-century academic life study, in which the seated nude functioned primarily as an exercise in proportion, structure, and ideal form. Here, Klimt abandons the stabilising conventions of spatial setting, directional light, and volumetric shading. The body floats outside measurable space, freed from the weight of environment and narrative. | | At this moment, Klimt was deeply engaged with the expressive and symbolic potential of the female body. The lowered head, obscuring the face, shifts attention away from individual likeness toward a state of inwardness. Identity dissolves into posture, as psychology is conveyed through curvature and restraint. In Sitzender Frauenakt von vorne, line becomes a sensitive instrument of perception, tracing not only the contour of the body but the atmosphere of introspection that surrounds it. The drawing thus participates in a broader transformation: the female nude is no longer presented as an academic exemplar or allegorical type, but as a locus of modern subjectivity. | | Sitzender Frauenakt von vorne therefore exemplifies Klimt's early mastery of linear expression, laying the groundwork for the increasingly fluid and experimental figure studies of the following decade. It stands as a testament to his investigation into the expressive capacity of contour, at a moment when modern art was rethinking the human form.

provenance: Private collection, UK (acquired directly from the artist in the 1960s). | Private collection, UK (by descent from the above). | | | Born into a Romanian Jewish Hasidic family, Reuven Rubin was a pioneer of Israeli art, instrumental in shaping a distinctive modern painterly language associated with Eretz Yisrael. Having spent his formative years in Romania, France, the United States and Palestine, Rubin developed a deliberately naïve style informed by his travels and by European modernism. This synthesis found expression in bold colour, simplified form and a childlike sense of wonder that permeates his oeuvre. In The flute player, this so-called 'primitive' manner is especially evident in the vibrant greens, reds and purples that animate the composition with rhythmic intensity. | | The painting draws on a key Hasidic tale centred on a simple shepherd boy who cannot read or pray, yet longs to participate in the Yom Kippur service of the Baal Shem Tov, the Jewish mystic regarded as the founder of Hasidic Judaism. Unable to express himself through words, the boy plays a single, heartfelt note on his flute. This pure and unmediated act of devotion was said to affirm that sincere longing and spiritual intensity surpass formal knowledge and learned ritual. In Hasidic teachings, the flute player thus became a potent symbol of raw faith, serving as a bridge between the earthly and the divine. | | The present work may therefore be understood as emblematic of a broader moment in which Jewish artists sought new visual languages through which to articulate cultural, spiritual and national identity. For Rubin in particular, the flute-playing shepherd came to embody a renewed Hebrew spirit — at once ancient and modern — in which faith, landscape and the ideals of national revival converge in a single, resonant image. | | The owners of the present work look fondly upon their memories of meeting Rubin and his wife Esther in Tel Aviv, visiting the artist in his studio and engaging directly with his painted world. It was in this intimate setting that they encountered and acquired The flute player. Having remained in the same private collection since its acquisition, the work retains a direct and personal link to the artist himself, standing not only as a poetic expression of Rubin's vision, but also as a testament to the lived relationships that shaped and sustained his artistic life.

provenance: Kurimanzutto, Mexico City | Acquired from the above by the present owner | | Exhibited | Mexico City, Anahuacalli Diego Rivera Museum, Nuds, 21 April - 8 July 2012 (in collaboration with Kurimanzutto, Mexico City) | | | | Executed in 2012, Maradona belongs to a significant body of sculptural work in which Sarah Lucas reconfigures the human figure through a vocabulary of provisional materials and abject humour. Emerging from the context of the Young British Artists in the early 1990s, Lucas has consistently challenged art historical conventions surrounding the nude, gender representation and sculptural monumentality. In Maradona, these concerns are distilled into a work that is at once formally spare and conceptually layered. | | The sculpture is constructed from aluminium wire framework wrapped with tape and padded with cotton, over which taut Lycra stockings are stretched to create a sagging, flesh-like surface. The figure is anchored and partially elevated by stone bricks, whose weight and rectilinear geometry contrast sharply with the soft, knotted materiality above. Lucas's materials are deliberately unheroic: industrial wire, hosiery and building blocks replace marble or bronze, subverting the grand tradition of figurative sculpture. The resulting form appears at once skeletal and bodily; its limbs contorted into a configuration that resists stable anatomical reading. As in many of Lucas's works, the body is suggested rather than described; it is fragmented, doubled back upon itself, and ambiguously gendered. | | The title Maradona invokes the legendary Argentine footballer Diego Maradona, a figure synonymous with virtuosity, charisma and scandal. This reference introduces a charged interplay between cultural mythology and physicality. Maradona's athletic prowess, particularly his balance, agility and controversial "Hand of God" goal, resonates ironically with the sculpture's precarious equilibrium and improvised construction. Lucas does not offer portraiture; instead, she mobilises the name as a cultural signifier, collapsing distinctions between high art and popular culture. The monumental expectations associated with a sporting icon are undercut by the work's awkward, anti-classical stance. | | Formally, the sculpture engages with the legacy of the reclining nude, a genre historically bound to ideals of beauty, passivity and erotic display. Lucas destabilises this lineage. The figure in Maradona neither reclines gracefully nor asserts heroic dominance; it slumps, twists and resists visual mastery. The stretched stockings evoke skin, yet their translucency exposes the armature beneath, denying illusionism and foregrounding construction. This oscillation between surface and structure mirrors Lucas's broader interrogation of how bodies are culturally constructed and consumed. | | The bricks function both structurally and symbolically. Their earth-bound solidity contrasts with the elastic tension of the hosiery, introducing a dialogue between weight and lightness, permanence and improvisation. They also suggest the language of minimalism, recalling the industrial units of 1960s sculpture, yet here they serve not as autonomous forms but as supports for an unruly, quasi-figurative mass. Lucas thus stages a confrontation between modernist formalism and corporeal excess. | | The present work was exhibited in the artist's solo exhibition at the Anahuacalli Diego Rivera Museum in 2012, where it was situated among sculptures and installations that further examined themes of embodiment, materiality and cultural symbolism. Within this context, Maradona formed part of a broader exploration of how the body - athletic, sexualised, celebrated or abject - is constructed and reconfigured through both physical matter and linguistic designation. | | At once irreverent and exacting, Maradona distils the central tensions that define Sarah Lucas's sculptural practice. Monumental in implication yet provisional in execution, the work refuses the stability and authority historically granted to the figure, proposing instead a body that is elastic, contingent and perpetually renegotiated, shaped as much by cultural projection as by physical structure. In its precarious calibration of weight and levity, humour and critique, the sculpture encapsulates the clarity of vision and material intelligence that have secured Lucas's position among the most influential artists of her generation. Over more than three decades, the artist has remained unwavering in her commitment to challenging the hierarchies of both form and subject matter, expanding the possibilities of sculpture through unorthodox materials and a distinctly incisive wit. Maradona not only stands as a pointed meditation on how icons are constructed and undone, but also as a compelling testament to the artist's sustained and consequential contribution to the development of contemporary sculpture in the twenty-first century.

provenance: Private Collection, Barcelona | Acquired from the above by the present owner | | Exhibited | Bruges, Garden of the Groeninge Museum, A Journey Between Matter and Light, Pablo Atchugarry, 24 June - 31 October 2006 (illustrated p. 236) | | Literature | Exh. cat., Pablo Atchugarry, Le infinite evoluzioni del marmo, Lecco, 2001 (illustrated p. 117) | Carlo Pirovano, Atchugarry, Catalogo generale della scultura, Vol. I, Milan, 2013, no. 43 (illustrated p. 331) | | | | Rising with serene authority, Pareja Estelar by Pablo Atchugarry unfolds as a poised and meditative exploration of vertical form, its elegant silhouette commanding attention and inviting contemplation. Carved from pink Portugal marble, animated by darker veins of red and orange, the work bears visible traces of geological time. These natural markings traverse the polished surface like organic currents, underscoring the dynamic interplay between material permanence and sculptural refinement. Under Atchugarry's hand, the marble is neither passive nor resistant; it is transformed into a resonant medium for light, movement, and spiritual suggestion. Extending to over two meters high, the sculpture asserts a commanding presence while retaining a sense of ethereal lightness. | | A committed practitioner of direct carving, Atchugarry approaches marble with sustained attention to it's essential plastic qualities, surface modulation, texture, spatial articulation, and the orchestration of light. Despite its considerable mass, the sculpture conveys an impression of levity. Its attenuated, ascending contours seems to counteract gravity, creating a visual tension between weight and lift. The pronounced verticality establishes a compositional logic of ascent: elongated pleats rise in rhythmic succession, gathering and releasing in a sequence of shadowed recesses and illuminated ridges. As the viewer moves around the work, the nearly symmetrical folds generate subtle variations in light and depth, producing a form that appears animated and responsive. At its centre, a restrained opening introduces a measured void, a spatial pause that invites contemplation and suggests both interiority and latent potential. | | Atchugarry's aesthetic language situates his practice within a distinguished sculptural lineage. His reverence for marble recalls the disciplined material engagement of Michelangelo and the refined neoclassicism of Antonia Canova, while his sensitivity to abstraction and void resonates with the formal investigations of Henry Moore and Isamu Noguchi. Parallels may also be drawn with Constantin Brancusi, particularly in the pursuit of essential form and transcendence through reduction. Yet Atchugarry's sculptural voice remains distinctly his own. His sustained commitment to hand-carving, coupled with a humanistic sensitivity to rhythm and proportion, imbues each work with a sense of intimacy and deliberation. The recurring upward thrust that characterises much of his oeuvre operates not merely as a formal device but as an expressive gesture – an articulation of aspiration and continuity. | | The warm tonality of the pink marble tempers the austerity often associated with stone, introducing subtle chromatic softness that enhances the sculpture's emotive presence. Light glides across its polished planes and gathers in its recesses, activating the surrounding space and reinforcing the work's dialogic relationship with its environment. | | Ultimately the present work may be understood as both material and metaphysical: firmly grounded in the substance of marble yet orientated towards transcendence. It stands as a compelling demonstration of Atchugarry's technical mastery and conceptual clarity, offering collectors a work that unites historical awareness, formal sophistication, and contemplative resonance.

provenance: Vrej Baghoomian Gallery, New York | Anon. sale, Sotheby's, New York, 29 September 1994, lot 486 | Private Collection, Spain | Acquired from the above by the present owner | | | | Painted in 1983, the present work belongs to a decisive formative moment in George Condo's oeuvre, a period in which the artist first consolidated the pictorial language that would define his career. Executed only a few years after his arrival in New York and at the dawn of his mature practice, this canvas demonstrates Condo's early synthesis of painterly tradition, cartoon distortion, and psychological fragmentation, an approach he would later describe as "Artificial Realism." | | Set against a dark, atmospheric ground animated by calligraphic red and white arabesques, the composition is dominated by a suspended, mask-like head that appears to hover in indeterminate space. The figure is neither fully human nor entirely abstract; rather, it is an amalgamation of anatomical fragments, vegetal forms, and painterly invention. A central white, bone-like structure bisects the face vertically, suggesting both skeletal armature and heraldic device. Around it cluster bulbous, jewel-toned forms, grapes, fleshy protrusions, and ocular motifs, that destabilise any singular reading of the image. The work oscillates between still life, portrait, and grotesque spirit. | | This hybridity is characteristic of Condo's early 1980s production; while contemporaneous with the resurgence of figurative painting in New York, his work diverged from the raw immediacy of Neo-Expressionism by engaging more self-consciously with art history. Even at this early stage, Condo's figures evoke the compositional gravity and chiaroscuro of Old Master painting, filtered through a lens of distortion indebted to modernism. The present work reveals an artist testing the elasticity of representation: features are exaggerated, displaced, or multiplied, yet remain coherently structured within a classical vertical format. | | The black ground, energised by looping linear gestures, further situates the painting within the experimental climate of the early 1980s. These marks function simultaneously as spatial framework and expressive residue, enclosing the central head while allowing it to vibrate against the void. The tension between containment and dissolution, between classical order and grotesque excess, would become a defining dialectic throughout Condo's career. | | Most importantly, 1983 marks a period in which Condo began to move beyond straightforward caricature toward a more complex psychological construction of the figure. The fragmentation seen here anticipates the multi-perspectival faces that would later culminate in his concept of "Psychological Cubism." In this early work, however, the fractures are more visceral than analytical; the image feels grown rather than constructed, organic rather than architectural. The thick, confident brushwork and saturated palette convey a young artist asserting both technical command and conceptual ambition. | | Untitled stands at a critical juncture in the artist's trajectory; it is neither tentative nor derivative, but rather it evidences the moment in which Condo's distinctive visual language crystallised. The present work captures Condo's emergence as a leading figure in postwar figurative painting. The suspended, fractured head balances classical compositional rigor with expressive invention, revealing a painter already redefining representation through psychological and formal complexity. This work crystallises the ambitions of Condo's early years, positioning the artist at the forefront of a generation reshaping portraiture and stands as a compelling testament to the originality and enduring impact of his formative breakthrough.

provenance: Ben Thanh Art & Frame and Galerie Nguyen, HCMC, Vietnam. | Acquired from the above by the present owner in 2013. | Private collection, Asia. | | Bui Huu Hung | 家庭 | 漆 木板 | | 簽名：bui huu hung（左下） | | 來源 | 越南胡志明市Ben Thanh Art & Frame 及 Nguyen藝廊 | 現藏家於2013年得自上述來源 | 亞洲私人收藏 | | | In the field of contemporary Vietnamese art, Bui Huu Hung stands as a beacon of both tradition and modernity. Born in 1957 in the cultural heart of Vietnam, Hanoi, Hung began his artistic journey at the age of 18, drawn to the ancient allure of lacquer painting. His search for authenticity led him to experience and engage with diverse aspects of Vietnam's rural life, where he immersed himself in the heritage of this intricate art form. | | Following his military service in 1978, Hung's quest for artistic excellence led him to the Hanoi College of Fine Arts. There he refined and mastered the techniques of lacquer painting. | | The artist's use of gold foil in his paintings is not merely decorative. It imbues his work with a dynamic play of light, bringing textures and colours to life with a radiant glow. This technique, coupled with his innovative use of space, gives his subjects an ethereal quality, as if they existed beyond the temporal world. | | Bui Huu Hung's art is a bridge between the past and the present, a fusion of time-honoured methods and contemporary sensibilities. Through his paintings, he not only preserves the legacy of Vietnamese lacquer painting but also redefines it, ensuring its relevance in the world of modern art.

provenance: Ben Thanh Art & Frame and Galerie Nguyen, HCMC, Vietnam. | Acquired from the above by the present owner in 2013. | Private collection, Asia. | | Do Xuan Doan | 祭月 | 漆 木板 | 2006年作 | | 簽名：D X Doan 06（右下） | | 來源 | 越南胡志明市Ben Thanh Art & Frame 及 Nguyen藝廊 | 現藏家於2013年得自上述來源 | 亞洲私人收藏 | | | Do Xuan Doan, born in 1937, is a distinguished Vietnamese artist renowned for his contributions to modern and contemporary art. provenance: Acquired directly from the artist by the present owner in Vietnam in 2007. | Private collection, US. | | 鄧春和 | 生命循環 | 油彩 畫布 | 2007年作 | | 簽名：HOA 8/2007（左下） | | 此作經藝術家本人再認證 | | 來源 | 現藏家於2007年於越南直接得自藝術家本人 | 美國私人收藏 | | | Born in 1959, Dang Xuan Hoa occupies a central place in post-Doi Moi Vietnamese art. His work is distinguished by a visual language that combines the distilled clarity of folk art with the chromatic intensity of Post-Impressionist modernism. Rather than descriptive realism, his canvases are shaped by a search for emotional and symbolic resonance, with figures simplified to their essential forms and their presence conveyed through quiet gestures and finely drawn contours that recall the graphic precision of woodcuts or collage. Through self-portraits, family scenes and still lifes, Hoa weaves intimate narratives rooted in the rhythms of daily life. Yet his imagery consistently transcends the anecdotal. Ceramic vases, flowers, oil lamps, fruit bowls and cats recur as emblematic objects, functioning not as decoration, but as vessels of memory, identity and cultural inheritance. Through this interplay of human presence and a symbolic world of objects, Hoa constructs a pictorial universe that is both familiar and metaphysical, inviting viewers to look beneath the surface of the everyday. | | This large‑scale work belongs to Hoa's Life series, a period in which he shaped a more open and resonant visual language to explore the emotional, familial and spiritual threads that run through human experience. At the heart of this series is the fused grey couple, a recurring emblem that carries a quiet spiritual charge. Appearing across several works from the period, this elongated, merged figure gathers the idea of unity into a single, distilled form. Its muted colour and pared‑back outline strip away narrative detail, allowing it to stand as a constant presence within the series. It becomes an abstract expression of shared consciousness, mutual dependence and the cyclical nature of human bonds. | | In this painting, the grey union figure lies along the horizontal axis, giving the composition its quiet foundation. Rather than showing two bodies in contact, it appears as a single, continuous form, suggesting unity as an inner condition rather than an outward gesture. Its presence is calm and introspective, a still centre that lends the work its reflective, almost meditative atmosphere. | | Beside this emblematic couple stands a second composite figure, upright and two‑faced, one side male and the other female. If the grey couple functions as the spiritual emblem, this dual-gender figure operates as its physical incarnation, representing a more physical, earthly form. Its stance, its doubled face and its solid outline introduce a gentle contrast to the reclining stillness of the union figure. Together, the two forms evoke a dialogue between essence and appearance, inner life and outward presence, spiritual unity and the dualities of lived experience. | | A constellation of objects and small attendant figures unfolds around them, each rendered with the clarity of an emblem. Drawn from Hoa's long engagement with still life, these motifs act less as descriptive details than as traces of memory, domestic habit and cultural continuity. Their placement within the flattened space recalls the visual logic of folk painting and ancestral shrines, where objects and presences share the same plane without hierarchy. The painting's saturated fields of colour heighten this sense of symbolic stillness, setting the central forms against backgrounds that feel almost iconic. Here, colour is not used to describe the visible world but to set the emotional tone, giving the work its contemplative atmosphere. | | In bringing together these emblematic bodies, incarnated identities and symbolic objects, Hoa gives shape to the central concerns of his Life series: relational harmony, domestic interiority and the quiet metaphysics of everyday existence. The grey union figure, repeated across the series, serves as the spiritual emblem through which these themes are gathered, while the two‑faced vertical figure lends them physical presence. Together, they give the series its distinctive coherence and emotional depth.

provenance: Acquired directly from the artist by the present owner in Vietnam in 2006. | Private collection, US. | | Nguyen Tu Nghiem | 扶董天王聖揀 | 設色紙本 | 1975年作 | | 簽名：nge 75（下） | | 來源 | 現藏家於2006年於越南直接得自藝術家本人 | 美國私人收藏 | | | Nguyen Tu Nghiem, born in Nghe An in north‑central Vietnam, trained at the École des Beaux‑Arts de l'Indochine from 1941 to 1945 and later continued his studies at the Vietnam Fine Arts College under To Ngoc Van during the Viet Bac years of 1946 and 1947. This early formation, shaped by both academic discipline and the cultural life of the resistance, laid the groundwork for one of the most distinctive artistic voices in modern Vietnamese painting. | | Working primarily in lacquer and gouache, he developed a highly individual style that moved beyond academic naturalism and drew deeply on the visual language of traditional Vietnamese art. Together with Bui Xuan Phai, Nguyen Sang and Duong Bích Lien, he is recognised as one of the four great masters of Vietnamese modern art, a group whose work helped define new artistic directions in the decades surrounding the period of Doi Moi. | | Nguyen Tu Nghiem's paintings reveal a sustained interest in the expressive potential of traditional motifs. His celebrated depictions of Thanh Giong and his recurring interpretations of the Vietnamese zodiac show how myth and symbolism could be reimagined through a modernist lens. Equally characteristic are his paintings of dancers, in which movement is distilled into rhythmic, stylised forms. These works evoke the energy of village festivals and ceremonial performance, yet they remain anchored in the structural clarity and abstraction of modern art. | | In 1996 he received the Ho Chí Minh Prize for Literature and the Arts, a recognition of his lasting contribution to Vietnam's cultural heritage.

provenance: Acquired directly from the artist by the present owner in Vietnam in 2007. | Private collection, US. | | Dinh Y Nhi | 安檢 | 油彩 畫布 | 2007年作 | | 簽名：Nhi 2007（左下） | | 來源 | 現藏家於2007年於越南直接得自藝術家本人 | 美國私人收藏 | | | Dinh Y Nhi (born Hanoi, 1967) is one of the few women artists to have made a significant impact on Vietnam's art scene in the early 1990s, a period still shaped by male dominance and by the expectation that women artists should remain within decorative or traditionally 'feminine' modes of expression. Her refusal to be defined by these expectations has shaped her entire career. From the outset, she positioned herself against aesthetic softness and narrative comfort, instead developing a language of psychological tension, minimal figuration and emotional directness. This stance established her as an important and occasionally disruptive presence within a rapidly shifting cultural landscape. | | From the early 2000s, Dinh Y Nhi extends her commitment to minimal figuration of her early years into a more expressive, psychologically charged idiom, using colour, distortion, and textual fragments to articulate the pressures of contemporary Vietnamese life. Her figures rarely settle into stable identities. They twist, stretch, or lean forward as if caught between self‑assertion and exposure, their expressions hovering in a state of unresolved tension. Colour is introduced more fully in her later practice. It functions not as embellishment but as atmosphere. Reds, ochres, and dense blacks create emotional climates. In these climates the figures appear to struggle for equilibrium. | | Security Checked (2007) is a prime example of this mature phase. Three distorted figures occupy the foreground, their limbs extended and their hollow eyes fixed in an uneasy state of awareness. The vivid, layered and agitated red background heightens the sense of psychological heat. The phrase 'SECURITY CHECKED' appears in uneven strokes across the lower register. Instead of talking about a real checkpoint, it brings to mind the feeling of being judged in all sorts of ways, socially, institutionally or emotionally, in a society that's figuring out new ways of moving and being regulated. The text acts as atmospheric pressure rather than narrative cue, reinforcing the idea that the figures are caught in a moment of inspection. | | The painting's power lies in its refusal of specificity. These are not individuals undergoing a particular event; they are embodiments of a broader condition, suspended between autonomy and external judgement. This approach allows Security Checked to distil the concerns that run through Nhi's practice. These concerns include the instability of identity, the tension between visibility and vulnerability, and the quiet violence of being measured. The work also highlights her importance as one of the few women artists of her generation to express such themes with such clarity.
