Lot Note:
Shad Fisherman No. 2 exemplifies a key moment in John Fulton Folinsbee’s transition from Impressionism toward a bolder, more uninhibited strain of Modernism. While firmly rooted in the observed reality of riverside labor in his beloved Pennsylvania, the painting transcends pure representation to achieve what Folinsbee increasingly sought in his mature work: a synthesis of modernist execution with Impressionist sensitivity conveyed through atmosphere, color, and the interplay of light. Indeed, and as Kirsten Jensen aptly observes, “the real subjects of Shad Fisherman No. 2 are light—the stark contrasts between the looming clouds and the summer sky—and the moody anticipation of the storm to come."

The fishermen, quickly sketched in a strokes, were among Folinsbee's favorite subjects. Although they add a bit of human activity, here they merely serve as a means to cast the various effects of the light, some blinding white while others blend with the blue-shadowed casting net, thus heightening the drama of the coming storm. Here, Folinsbee departs from the more linear construction of his earlier industrial landscapes, which marked his first attempts at Modernism, and instead orchestrates a swirling vortex of movement, using sweeping brushwork and intensified tonal contrasts to accentuate the dramatic effect of the moment, thus underscoring the emotional power of what appears to be, at first glance, a very mundane activity.

Shad Fisherman No. 2 is emblematic of Folinsbee’s finest works from the late 1930s in that it embodies the artist’s deepening engagement with Modernist ideas, particularly the atmospheric mysticism championed by Arthur Bowen Davies, whom Folinsbee deeply admired (alongside Robert Henri), and whose landscapes Duncan Phillips praised for their affinities with Cézanne and El Greco. The darkened palette, heightened shadow-play, and compressed composition in the present work all reflect this influence, transforming the scene of shad fishing into an eternal, almost mythical American life tableau, which would led contemporary art critic Edward Alden Jewell to hail Folinsbee as “one of the lords of impasto, who can swing his brush with an authority that is boisterous but that seldom falls short of capturing the effect desired.”

Lot Note:
Born in Summit, New Jersey in 1876 and trained at Columbia University’s School of Architecture, Colt initially joined a New York architectural firm before abandoning the discipline altogether, eager to escape what he once described as the restrictive demands of “clients’ tastes or whimsies.” Drawn instead to the freedom of artistic expression, Colt settled at Phillips’ Mill, where he formed a close friendship with William Langson Lathrop, Edward Willis Redfield, Daniel Garber, Charles Rosen, Rae Sloan Bredin, and Robert Spencer–the first generation of New Hope School painters. Though he pursued painting, design, and crafts with equal devotion, Colt is remembered today primarily for his luminous Impressionist landscapes, which he composed in the studio because of a chronic heart condition that prevented prolonged outdoor study.

The present painting stands apart within the limited corpus of Colt’s work. The largest known oil by the artist, it represents one of his most ambitious surviving compositions ever to appear on the market. On the monumental canvas, Colt inscribes a now-vanished chapter of life along the Delaware River with an almost cinematic immediacy. Rather than offering a distant vista, Colt brings the viewer directly onto the river, where the diagonal movement of a barge contrasts gently with the horizontal (and echoing) banks as well as the rustling canopy of trees overhead. A figure stands at the stern, pole in hand, while a team of mules waits at the riverbank; small yet evocative details that anchor the composition in lived history. In this sentimental view, Colt memorializes the everyday labor and quiet poetry of river life before mechanization transformed the region’s rhythms forever.

Colt’s brisk, shimmering brushstrokes animate the reflections on the river’s surface, while the bright, sun-filled palette envelops the entire composition in a sense of warmth and pastoral calm. The canvas resonates with nostalgia, not only because it preserves a nearly forgotten mode of transportation, but because Colt renders it through a screen of dappled light, mirrored water and soft atmospheric haze, which transforms the industrial subject into an homage to the enduring beauty of Bucks County.

Colt died suddenly of a heart attack in 1926, leaving many canvases unfinished and an even greater number tragically destroyed by subsequent occupants of his home. This historic loss makes the reappearance of the present canvas on the market even more exciting and momentous.

Lot Note:
In Frog Hollow, Garber's characteristic delicate touch and carefully rendered dab-like brushwork is on full display, though largely in the upper portion of the painting. In the lower portion of the painting, he has instead opted to employ a looser, less tightly controlled approach, using long, single blue and pale-yellow brushstrokes in the foreground to depict the local autumnal ground cover. This square-sized composition employs the Pennsylvania Impressionist's characteristic brown, green, and blue tonalities–the latter most evident in parts of the stream and the gentleman's pants at left as he attends to a wood pile. Though Garber once described his landscapes as having "a mass of detail in the mass," the overall effect of the present work is one of a poetic quietude. Interestingly only one other painting of Frog Hollow has appeared at auction (Freeman's, Philadelphia, December 2002).

Lot Note:
The leader of the New Hope School, Redfield’s winter scenes are amongst the most highly prized within his vast oeuvre. Redfield was not the only Pennsylvania Impressionist to paint en plein air but is known for taking the approach to painting directly out of doors to an almost extreme degree. He completed large-scale winter landscape such as the present lot "in one go"–without any underdrawing, painting from early morning until late afternoon, and all the while carrying 50 pounds of gear with his canvases strapped to a tree. In Homestead, Redfield employs vigorous brushwork to capture the effects of sunlight casting shadows through the barren trees across the landscape and the home, while a lone figure navigates a blanket of fresh snow.

Lot essay:

“I will run with the painting, like it’s a dog on a leash, chasing and almost falling behind it. That is also the space where I forget myself, where painting becomes something that I don’t control, neither emotionally nor intellectually” - Charline von Heyl (J. Farago, “An Interview with Charline von Heyl”, Even Magazine, no. 7, 2017, online).

Charline von Heyl’s painting practice occupies a crucial place in contemporary art for its rigorous investigation of what painting can be and do in the twenty-first century. Eschewing both pure abstraction and traditional figuration, von Heyl creates works that resist easy categorization. Her paintings unfold as nuanced visual events—layered, contradictory, and dynamic—challenging viewers to experience rather than interpret them. This resistance to fixity is central to her practice: von Heyl redefines painting as a process of continuous becoming rather than a static image.

A distinctive feature of von Heyl’s oeuvre is her steadfast engagement with the history of painting while refusing nostalgia. She draws upon the legacies of Cubism, Pop, Abstract Expressionism, and Op Art, yet transforms these influences into something distinctly her own. Her surfaces often contain traces of erasure, overpainting, and disruption, revealing the tension between intention and accident. In doing so, von Heyl exposes the act of painting as a form of thinking—an active dialogue between intuition, intellect, and the materiality of the work itself.

Von Heyl’s practice also expands the possibilities of abstraction. Rather than treating abstraction as a language of purity or transcendence, she treats it as a site of play, contradiction, and psychological charge. Her images—at once seductive and disorienting—invite viewers to navigate multiple registers of visual and emotional experience. This sense of instability and openness mirrors contemporary life, making her work both timely and timeless.

Ultimately, Charline von Heyl’s practice lies in her refusal to allow painting to settle into complacency. She reaffirms painting’s capacity to surprise, to question perception, and to sustain complexity in an age dominated by instant images and digital proliferation. Her work demonstrates that painting, far from obsolete, remains one of the most vital forms of critical and imaginative inquiry.

Lot essay:

“I like my women to be presented as very conscientious, very empowered, very charismatic – strong women who are aware of their environment and their experiences. I’m not making them do anything. It’s a collaborative effort because I’m taking the image, I’m photographing them, but they’re aware of me doing this with them. It’s not as though the artist is explaining the sitter.” - Mickalene Thomas 

Mickalene Thomas’ portraiture has had a transformative impact on contemporary art history by redefining how Black women are represented and celebrated in visual culture at large. Drawing from art history, pop culture, and personal narrative, Thomas fuses elements of painting, collage, photography, and rhinestone embellishment to create images that radiate confidence, sensuality, and power. Indeed, her portraits challenge the Eurocentric canon by reimagining classical poses and compositions through a distinctly Black, female lens. In doing so, Thomas not only inserts Black women into the history of art but also reframes beauty, glamour, and identity as sites of self-definition rather than external judgment. Her work has reshaped conversations about representation and visibility, asserting that portraiture can be both a political act and a deeply personal affirmation of presence and pride.

Thomas' work is included in myriad private and public collections in the United States and worldwide, including The Museum of Modern Art, the Whitney Museum of American Art, The Art Institute of Chicago, and the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum. A significant mid-career international retrospective was recently assembled for the artist, entitled All About Love, which explores themes of Black womanhood, identity, and empowerment through a multidisciplinary lens. The exhibition showcases over 90 works spanning two decades of Thomas' career, including paintings, collages, photographs, and installations. Co-organized by the Hayward Gallery, London, The Broad, Los Angeles, in partnership with the Barnes Foundation in Philadelphia and Les Abattoirs – Musée-Frac Occitanie Toulouse, the exhibition firmly underscores Thomas as one of the most relevant artists living today.

Fritz Scholder (Luiseño, 1937-2005) pushed boundaries and critically challenged existing traditions, working to shift Native American art from an overly idealized category plucked from nineteenth-century stereotypes to a thriving part of the contemporary art world. His paintings defy classification—transcending the categories of traditional, modern, Pop, Indian, not Indian—and continue to provoke intrigue through these contradictions. This is clear in Insane Indian no. 25, where a Native American illustrated in Pop aesthetics undermines preexisting expectations and is thus able to attain a greater degree of his own agency.

Scholder, of part Native American and part European ancestry, often said he was "not Indian" in the traditional sense, which gave him a unique, often controversial lens on Native identity. Inspired by his own experiences, he began painting Native Americans in ways that directly confronted and shattered long-standing depictions. As he explained, ‘“I vowed to myself that I would not paint Indians. Then I saw the numerous over-romanticized paintings of the ‘noble savage’ . . . and decided that someone should paint the Indian in a different context.” Rather than stoic warriors or mystical figures, his subjects were modern, complex, and often subversive: Native Americans awash in bright colors drinking beer, smoking cigarettes, eating ice cream cones, or draped in the American flag.

Insane Indian no. 25 (1972) illustrates a man in three quarter profile on a deep red ground balanced in simplified geometry. The composition emphasizes solidity—the man’s oval head, predominately in black, with white nose, feather, and highlights, mirrors the white arch of his chest. The alternating blacks and whites that define his chest and shoulders grounds his head, while accents of red, green, and peach weave through the figure in increasingly abstracted strokes. The title Insane Indian confuses.

The American West’s mythology of its relationship to indigenous cultures might anticipate an ‘insane Indian’ more in the realm of a berserker, a fierce opponent, a foil. Yet, Scholder’s depiction is the picture of equanimity. The expected cultural connotation is denied by the man’s apparent stability. Should the man be disturbed or in some way distressed, it is internal. But, his eyes, defined only in abstract swipes, negate a means for the viewer to truly interrogate this internality. The man’s complex inner life remains his alone, afforded a greater capacity of emotional depth than the Native American of American fiction.

This provocative painting by Scholder thus reflects the heart of his practice of depicting indigenous culture. While including some traditional trappings in some ways expected of Native Americans in painting such as feathered garments, Scholder digs deeper, resulting in a quiet yet captivating portrait of a man’s emotional life.

In Portrait of Al Held (1963), Alex Katz (American, b. 1927) balances familiarity and objectivity through his signature painting style and direct composition in order to create a striking portrait of his long-time friend and fellow artist Al Held (American, 1928-2005).

The subject of more than 200 solo exhibitions and international acclaim, Alex Katz applies a deliberately vibrant visual language between realism and abstraction, ambivalence and intimacy. Coming of age alongside the titans of New York’s Abstract Expressionism of the 1950s, Katz favored flatness of color and form rather than gestural primacy and raw emotion. His work is deceptively simple; his technique of painting wet on wet evokes a lustrous finish to his canvases, defying two-dimensionality even in their flatness. 

In terms of his thematic output, Katz is particular known for sharing his world, whether through hundreds of portraits of his wife of more than 60 years, Ada, his home in coastal Maine, or scenes and characters from downtown New York City among the cultural avant garde. This combination of immediacy and familiarity— flash-in-the-pan moments he captures in thick brushstrokes and meditatively stylized forms is clear in his depiction of Held.

Katz and Held met during in New York during the mid-century, when they were each in their 20s. For a time, both artists had studios in the same building, and saw each other’s work often. Katz has said of Held’s paintings then that “I think Al did some of the best artwork
on the planet at that time and I was very lucky to be near them.”[i] But, while Held focused primarily on abstraction, Katz continued to find the most meaning in figuration.

As Katz has said:
"Realist painting has to do with leaving out a lot of detail,” said Katz in an interview, “I think my painting can be a little shocking in all that it leaves out. But what happens is that the mind fills in what's missing. It's about being able to see something in a specific way. Painting is a way of making you see what I saw."[ii]
In this 1963 painting, Held, defined in surprisingly simplified forms in blues, browns, yellows, and whites. Without any tools of his trade, his blue-collared shirt, combed back hair, and direct eye contact, Katz illustrates Held not as a fellow artist but as an austere, stripped-back portrait of someone he knew well.

[i] Juan Manuel Bonet, “Alex Katz: A Great Figurative Voice,” Electra, Issue 17, 2022. https://electramagazine.fundacaoedp.pt/en/editions/issue-17/alex-katz-great-figurative-voice.
[ii] Aida Dunne, “I prefer Stan Getz to Sartre”, The Irish Times, March 3, 2007. https://www.irishtimes.com/news/i-prefer-stan-getz-to-sartre-1.1198117.

At the time the present portrait was executed, in 1936, Gertrude Abercrombie had been working on the New Deal government art projects for almost two years, initially for the Public Works of Art Project, followed in 1935 by the Illinois Art Project (IAP) of the Works Progress Administration (WPA). In contrast to Abercrombie’s later work, which is often small in scale and painted on Masonite panels, the works made for the project were paintings on canvas of a standard size, ranging from 24 x 20 inches to 30 x 40 inches. The WPA required one painting a month from each artist employed on the easel painting project, which left most artists with quite a bit of free time to produce other work. As Abercrombie was used to the format mandated by the projects, her independent work tended to be on canvas and of this size. She continued to paint on this scale, at least some of the time, into the mid 1940s.   

Abercrombie’s appointment to the PWAP and its regular monthly paycheck not only gave her the imprimatur of a legitimate artist, but it also allowed her to move out of her parents’ home and into an apartment of her own in the Weinstein Building in Hyde Park, which was home to many artists and writers. It was there that she met lifelong friends and made many connections with other artists and writers. Like many artists in the early stages of their careers, Abercrombie’s early work includes many portraits, both of herself and of these new friends and colleagues, who were willing subjects and offered her the opportunity to hone her skills. Her earliest work includes portraits of artists Tud Kempf, Macena Barton, Rudolph Weisenborn, Franklin Van Court Brown, Charles Sebree, and John Pratt. She also painted writer friends such as Thornton Wilder, Gertrude Stein, Wendell Wilcox, and James Purdy. Other portraits from this early period include art world figures like Cati Mount, Helen Mann, Inez Cunningham Stark, actors Grace Cornell and Davis Roberts, as well as family members Laura and Maurine Campbell and Elinor Porter Carlberg. This not only attests to the varied and noteworthy social connections she established in the first decade of her career, but from the beginning her portraits were distinctive, penetrating, and often idiosyncratic, usually offering an extremely intimate image of the sitter. Almost all of them include just the head or a small portion of the upper body of the sitter, sometimes with a disconnected arm or hand (see Thornton Wilder, for example, whose chin rests on a hand that emerges from the bottom of the painting and could be an inanimate object) which often have expressive purposes.   

By 1936, Edward (Eddie) Millman was already a well-established presence in the art world of Chicago. The year after designing murals for the 1933 Century of Progress World’s Fair, he traveled to Mexico to study with Diego Rivera. Upon his return, he became one of the most productive artists on the government supported projects, creating both easel paintings for the Illinois Art Project and murals for the competitive national Treasury Section for Painting and Sculpture. By the time Abercrombie painted his portrait, Millman had executed murals for the post offices in Moline (1935) and Decatur (1936). It’s possible that they became acquainted through their work on the IAP, or through other artist friends.   

While the present portrait is like that of other art world friends or acquaintances of Abercrombie’s, it is likely the only portrait image that includes the sitter’s entire body, in this case literally from head to foot. And while Eddie Millman’s entire form is visible, it is distorted in a way that may reveal several things: Abercrombie’s own difficulty with the human form; an effort to experiment with modernist distortion; and her interest in conveying something more than a strict likeness in her portrait. Although she excelled at the traditional techniques of chiaroscuro and perspective, which she learned through numerous art classes, she struggled with the human form. The artist avoids the complexities of anatomical accuracy in the many later paintings where she represents herself in a landscape or interior scene, by developing a simplified flattened form. In this painting, Millman seemingly sits sideways, his left arm draped over the back of the chair, his left leg crossed over his right. Abercrombie’s difficulty with creating a lap for the figure makes it look almost as if the upper body and the lower body have been pieced together without a midsection. This may also point to her interest in experimenting with modernist modes. This can be seen in her attempt to incorporate an avantgarde style in other work of the time, such as Self Portrait with Cat (She and I), c. 1934 in which she introduces an angularity reminiscent of Cubism; Nude with Guitar, c. 1934, an experiment in creating a full length nude; and her Self Portrait in Green, 1938 (Illinois State Museum), in which the large three quarter length figure shows some familiarity with a post-Cubist Picasso. Abercrombie, despite developing a recognizable mature style, had a curiosity that drove her to explore different modes of expression throughout her career. This may be another example of that experimentation. 

But the real achievement in the Portrait of Eddie Millman is in the creation of a figure who is complex, his body an abstracted combination of shapes, while his face displays a direct, open, honest gaze, that of a man with whom the viewer can connect. Whether intentional or not, the distortions of his body contrast with his straightforward countenance to project the competent, intelligent artist as a multifaceted, modern, complicated individual. and Portrait of Eddie Millman is an exceptional example of Abercrombie’s early proficiency to reveal multiple, even conflicting, ideas in the same work.

Lot Note:
While MacRae painted multiple still lifes and portraits over a long career, landscapes appear to be the most prominent category in her entire oeuvre. She painted scenes from her home city of New York and throughout the U.S., but her frequent visits to Switzerland, England, France, and Italy provided rich material for her brush. 

In this atmospheric landscape inspired by Emma Fordyce MacRae’s travels to Switzerland, the artist’s characteristic technical process is clearly evident. MacRae began by sketching her compositions over a gesso ground using soft pencil or black chalk. Traces of this underdrawing remain subtly visible beneath the surface, a hallmark of her style that adds structural clarity to the forms. She then applied blocks of color up to the outlines of the underdrawing, layering thick paint using a dry brush or palette knife to build up the scene.

In this work, her method of painting over a rough surface, namely Masonite, allows underlying colors and the white ground to peek through, particularly across the mountains and sky. This creates a chalky, mottled effect that lends the image an aged, fresco-like appearance—once described by a critic as evoking “the spots from which the color has fallen off” of old murals. This visual texture became a trademark of MacRae’s landscapes.

Lot Note:
Although modest in scale, this finely composed view of Annecy demonstrates Emma Fordyce MacRae’s signature approach to landscape, which rarely excludes human presence. Here, figures crossing a bridge animate the middle ground, yet their poses remain quiet and contained, embodying MacRae’s preference for stillness over narrative action. Even when in motion, her figures convey a timeless calm, and the overall composition is one of deliberate balance and quietude.

As the artist often did, MacRae uses both natural and architectural elements (namely the curve of the bridge, the clustered rooftops, and the vertical steeple) to create a taut spatial arrangement, as if artificially made from geometric shapes and blocks. Yet, the repetition of warm red and golden tones across the buildings and rooftops unifies the canvas, while the diffused light, likely painted with a dry brush or palette knife, softens the geometry. The result is a placid mood with luminous color, in the words of one critic.

Lot Note:
Emma Fordyce MacRae’s still lifes are marked by her distinctive compositional strategy, which often combined elements from different cultures and periods. Rather than merely depicting floral arrangements, MacRae thoughtfully selected vessels and objects from her personal collection to play an integral role in her compositions. These containers, ranging from simple ceramic pots to ornate Chinese vases, not only held the flowers but also contributed to the balance and visual harmony of the scene. Sometimes they offered relief from more complex floral patterns; other times, they served as compositional anchors.

In the present still life, MacRae places a cluster of foxgloves and lilies in a dual-handled Capodimonte ceramic vase, whose soft pastel tones and sturdy form provide a grounding counterpoint to the dark background and to the vertical rhythm of the blossoms. The vase itself, with its rounded curves and decorative banding, is characteristic of the types she reused across works. As in many of her floral pieces, MacRae creates a still and timeless atmosphere—what one critic described as “placid moods with luminous color.”

Lot Note:
Throughout her lengthy and prolific career, Jane Peterson remained free of dogmatic approaches to art, borrowing from various styles to piece together an aesthetic all her own. With its strong painterly quality, Street Scene is a remarkable example of her idiosyncratic manner. The work depicts a bustling moment captured through the use of two distinct methods. The blocks of bold color and simplified forms composing the lively scene are fiercely expressive, shifting the focus away from representational accuracy, instead distilling the dizzying emotions likely to be felt in the midst of this busy parade of horse-drawn carriages. On the other hand, the fast, broken brushwork that surrounds the ebullient tableau subtly conveys its transience. The painting, like a snapshot, insinuates how light and movement converged at this particular moment in time.

Lot Essay:
This rare and charming portrait depicts Federico Ubaldo della Rovere, the only son and heir of Francesco Maria II, Duke of Urbino. Born on May 16, 1605, Federico was raised in the splendor of the court, enjoying music, theater, and courtly life. At sixteen, he married Claudia de’ Medici, daughter of the Grand Duke of Tuscany. Around this time, his father effectively abdicated, handing him the reins of the Duchy.
Tragically, Federico died under mysterious circumstances just two years later, marking the end of the independent Duchy of Urbino, which then passed to the Papal States.

Claudio Ridolfi was a Venetian-trained painter who settled in Urbino by 1590. Though primarily known for religious works, Ridolfi produced several portraits at the della Rovere court, including at least three of Federico. This particular study, executed in oil on paper and likely a preparatory work for a formal portrait, displays the luminous palette and dynamic brushwork reminiscent of Federico Barocci. The life-like expression and vibrant rendering of the young boy reflect Ridolfi’s skill and the artistic influence of Barocci, who pioneered the use of oil sketches on paper.

Lot Essay:
Together with his Florentine contemporaries Jacopo Pontormo (1494-1557) and Rosso Fiorentino (1495-1540), Beccafumi ranks as one of the leading protagonists of early Italian Mannerism, and he is one of the most experimental and original masters of his time. During his career, he embraced a wide variety of artistic challenges (for instance providing the design and cartoons for the extraordinary marble floor in Siena Cathedral, 1519-29), applying his talent also to materials and media as varied as woodcuts, and the modelling and casting of bronze sculptures.

This handsome and rare work is part of a group of about twenty-five sketches, mostly head studies, executed by Beccafumi in oil on paper, which are directly or loosely connected to the master’s most prestigious commission, received on April 1529: the decorative cycle for the ceiling of the Sala del Concistorio, in the Palazzo Pubblico in Siena (c. 1530-35). (P. Torriti, Domenico Beccafumi, Milan 1998, pp. 153-163) The present vivid head, though not specifically connected to the above decoration, is generally similar in type to more than one head to be found in the fresco cycle, which suggests that it was indeed conceived for one of the figures represented in this series of compositions based on the classical theme of civic virtue (exemplum virtutis), an inconography derived from Cicero’s De officis ('On Duties').

Executed with broad and fluid strokes, with wonderful pinkish and red touches used to highlight some of the facial features, this handsome head of a youth – his gaze to the left – is a masterful example of Beccafumi’s studies of this type, characterized by freedom of execution which strongly appeals to our modern eye. The beautifully applied highlights in the present sheet determine the fall of light and construct planes to accentuate volumes. Beccafumi works from dark to light to emphasize the intensity of this lyrical image, which has the spontaneity and immediacy of an impressionist sketch. Despite their links with his painted compositions, it seems likely that Beccafumi produced these oil studies as finished works of art, though he clearly left them unfinished, especially in the background to focus solely on the features of the heads. It is perhaps no coincidence that his self-portrait, today in the Uffizi, is executed in this same medium. (Florence, Galleria degli Uffizi, Gabinetto Disegni e Stampe, inv. no. 1731; Torriti, op. cit., p. 272, no. D64, illus.)

Beccafumi's fascination with light and shade must have led him to this type of experimental work, a technique that would be embraced by several artists from the 17th century on, but was almost unprecedented in Beccafumi’s time. Through his great originality and technical accomplishment, Beccafumi succeeded in creating a ‘modern Sienese language,’ rooted in the artistic tradition of his native city.

Lot Essay:
Given its high degree of finish and coloring, as well as the fact that it is extensively heightened with both silver and gold, the present drawing is almost certainly a design for a tapestry, a suggestion further supported by the decorative motif drawn as a border around the composition. It was likely produced as a presentation modello, to be shown to a patron for approval before work on the actual tapestry cartoon was begun. While certain aspects of the drawing shows traces of a Northern hand, the overall effect is more in keeping with Florentine draftsmanship of the second half of the 16th century. As the patron saint of the city, Saint John the Baptist was a popular subject in Florentine art throughout the Cinquecento, and it is more than likely that the present sheet was intended not only as a modello for a tapestry commissioned by a Florentine patron but, in all probability, a tapestry woven in Florence itself.

The first tapestry workshops in Florence were established in 1545 by the Flemish weavers Nicolas Karcher and Jan Rost, both under the patronage of Duke Cosimo I de' Medici, who intended to establish Florence as a major center of tapestry production in ltaly. He not only encouraged Karcher and Rost to undertake freelance commissions, but also expected them to train local apprentices. Ducal commissions resulted in more than forty narrative tapestries woven in Florence between 1546 and 1553, for the most part intended for the Palazzo Vecchio.

In 1554, Cosimo established a new ducal tapestry factory in Florence, known as the Arazzeria Medicea, which was run by local Italian weavers and used less complex materials and techniques than their Flemish predecessors. The leading designer of this period was Jan van der Straet, known as Stradanus (1523-1605), who was to produce more than one hundred tapestry cartoons for the workshop, mainly intended for the various rooms of the Palazzo Vecchio and the Medici villas. After the death of Cosimo and the accession of Ferdinando I.

The present sheet may be tentatively associated with the work of Stradanus, Comparisons may be drawn between the leopard in the right foreground of the composition, as well as the trees and foliage, with a tapestry of The Meeting of Dante and Virgil, commissioned by a member of the Salviati family of Florence and today in the Minneapolis Institute of Arts. Woven by Jan Rost after a design by Francesco Salviati, probably assisted by Stradanus, the tapestry may be dated to between 1547 and 1549. Also comparable to the present sheet are the animals in a tapestry of A Stag Hunt with Traps, woven by Benedetto Squilli in 1568 after a design by Stradanus, in the collection of the Amministrazione Provinciale in Siena.

Lot Essay:
This rare preparatory drawing was likely created as a modello to present to a patron for the tomb of the renowned 15th-century humanist Niccolò Perotti. Identified by Dr. Paul Taylor, the sheet dates after Perotti’s death in 1480. Perotti, author of the first modern Latin grammar, was buried in Manfredonia Cathedral, Puglia. Sadly, the cathedral was destroyed in the 17th century, and no trace of the tomb remains. The drawing shows several design options for the tomb’s border and the cloth beneath the headrest. Perotti is depicted with hands crossed over a book, another at his feet. The inscription includes the date MCCCCLXXX and the opening line of Rudimenta Grammatices, printed in 1473 and widely distributed across Europe by century’s end.

Executed on green-primed paper, the artist used pen, ink, brush, and white highlights to evoke sculptural depth. The border includes six different possibilities for the its design, and two further options, embroidered or plain, for the pleated cloth below the tasseled pillow where the humanist's head rests. The capital letters inscribed on the base, before date of his death, MCCCCLXXX, correspond to the first line of his famed, 'Rudimenta Grammatices,' which by the end of the century was being distributed all over Europe and reprinted a momentous 117 times.

The style recalls Ferrarese master Cosmè Tura and Florentine sculptor Bernardo Rossellino. The careful rendering of drapery suggests influence from Ferrara’s sculptural traditions. In 15th-century Puglia, it was common to commission works from northern artists, especially from Ferrara and Venice, regions renowned for their artistic excellence. This drawing reflects that cultural and artistic exchange.

Lot Essay:
Until recently, this drawing was known only through an etching by Francesco Rosaspina (c. 1762-1841), part of a set of facsimiles after Parmigianino acquired by the British Museum in 1919. Eight etchings in the group, including this one, bear inscriptions indicating they reproduced works from the collection of Giovanni Antonio Armano, a late 18th century Venetian dealer. The Rosaspina print, in reverse to the actual drawing and showing slightly more of the right-hand figure, led scholar A.E. Popham to assert it depicted a genuine Parmigianino work from his Roman period.

Popham connected the drawing to Parmigianino’s Marriage of the Virgin in the École des Beaux-Arts, and to other pen-and-wash compositions with looping lines and atmospheric effects. These include the Pool of Bethesda in a private collection, Christ Healing the Sick (Musée des Beaux-Arts, Angers), and The Worship of Jupiter (British Museum). All are thought to be influenced by Raphael’s Vatican frescoes, particularly The School of Athens, and his tapestry designs for the Sistine Chapel.

The present drawing's dramatic light effects, enhanced with white heightening, suggest a nocturnal scene illuminated from within a nearby building—possibly a temple. One central figure gestures forward while looking back, hinting at a broader narrative or crowd, as seen in related works.

Popham’s belief that this piece was part of a larger composition is supported by parallels with the Art Institute of Chicago drawing, once also known only through prints. Both reflect Parmigianino’s imaginative engagement with Raphael’s elegant style during this lesser-understood, experimental phase of his career.

Lot Essay:
Cesare Dandini, a prominent Florentine painter of the 17th century, trained under Francesco Curradi, Cristofano Allori, and Domenico Cresti (Il Passignano). By 1621, he had established himself as an independent artist and quickly gained prestigious patrons, including Prince Don Lorenzo de’ Medici and Grand Duke Ferdinando II. Dandini became known for refined half-length allegorical and biblical figures, marked by rich color, graceful poses, and polished execution.

This painting of Saint John the Evangelist exemplifies Dandini’s mature style. The young saint, set against a plain background, is shown sharpening his quill while his Gospel lies open. His traditional symbol, the eagle, rests before him holding a large book. The cool tones of John’s skin and the vibrant sheen of his satin garments reflect Dandini’s fully developed technique and training.

A nearly identical version of this composition exists in the Guido Bruscoli collection in Florence. Dr. Sandro Bellesi dates that painting to the early 1630s and suggests the present work was completed later, with more refinement in the face and drapery. This painting may have been intended as part of a series of the Four Evangelists, a subject Dandini explored more than once during his career.

Lot Essay:
The present lot was once part of the large group of drawings which, on Guercino's death, were inherited by his nephews Benedetto (1633-1715) and Cesare (1637-1688) Gennari. By the middle of the eighteenth century, the drawings passed to Cesare's grandson, Carlo Gennari (1712-1790), by whom the group was dispersed. At this point, many drawings, including this sheet, were obtained by the Bolognese dealer, Francesco Forni, who then sold them to John Bouverie. (N. Turner and C. Plazzotta, Drawings by Guercino from British Collections, exhibition catalogue, London 1991, p. 8) According to an inventory of the Gennari family's property taken in 1719, prior to the dispersal of the drawings, 1,689 of them were placed in eight large albums, which were organized according to the medium and subject of the drawing. (D. Mahon and N. Turner, The Drawings of Guercino in the Collection of her Majesty the Queen at Windsor Castle, Cambridge 1989, pp.xx-xxi) One of these albums was entitled Dissegni di Penna, et Acquarella di diverse grandezze, rapresentanti diverse Teste, Figure, e Puttini; it contained 297 drawings, of which the present study was most probably one. (See Gainesville, et al., 1991-93, loc. cit.)

In Linda Wolk-Simon's entry on this drawing in the catalogue of the 1991-3 Horvitz Collection exhibition, she suggested that it has certain affinities with the kneeling St. Francis in Guercino's altarpiece of 1639-41, which depicts the Madonna and Child with Ss. Francis and Clare (Parma, Galleria Nazionale). (See D.M. Stone, Guercino: Catalogo completo dei dipinti, Florence 1991, cat. no. 165)  However, since the exhibition catalogue was published, an altarpiece by Guercino has come to light that may provide a stronger connection. The pala in question, which was documented but thought to have been lost, dates from 1663, and depicts the Madonna and Child appearing to Beato Marcolino Ammani di Forlí: it is to the latter figure that the present study appears to relate. The painting was discovered by Prisco Bagni, badly damaged and in storage at the Pinacoteca di Brera, Milan. It was subsequently cleaned, restored, and published by Bagni in 1991 as a late work, dating from 1663. Before the discovery of the painting, the composition was known, but only from a 1757 engraving by Bolzoni. (D. Mahon, P. Bagni et al, Giovanni Francesco Barbieri, il Guercino, 1591-1666, exh. cat., Bologna 1991, cat. no. 152; the engraving reproduced in P. Bagni's note on the painting in M. Foschi and G. Viroli (eds.), Il San Domenico di Forlí. La chiesa, il luogo, la città, exh. cat., Forlí, Oratorio di San Sebasiano, 1991, pp. 98, 101) Bagni also identified another drawing connected with the painting, a double-sided red chalk sheet, also in the Brera, which has a compositional study on the recto and a study for the kneeling friar on the verso. (P. Bagni in Il San Domenico di Forli, exh. cat., op. cit., pp. 99-100)

The present sheet is drawn in a notably different manner from the red chalk drawing, with broad, bold pen and brown ink, and wash, rather than the more tentative, loosely sculpted chalk of the double-sided study, which fits with what Nicholas Turner describes as the 'broken contours and lines of fluctuating intensity' of Guercino's late period. (Turner and Plazzotta, op.cit., p. 181) As Turner has also pointed out, the present study, on the other hand, can best be related stylistically to Guercino's drawings of the 1630s, and in particular to certain drawings of half- or bust-length single male figures that he made at this time, such as the Old Bearded Man (Royal Library, Windsor Castle), the Man Reading at a Table (Fogg Art Museum, Cambridge, Massachusetts), and the Bust of a Man, facing right (Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York). (Turner's observations cited by Wolk-Simon in the 1991-3 Horvitz exhibition catalogue, loc. cit.)

This difference in style between the two sheets may confirm Wolk-Simon's hypothesis that the present drawing was not drawn in preparation for a painting, but was instead an 'independent invention,' which accounts for the study's highly poetic nature, and the wonderfully broad, fluid manner in which it has been drawn. Indeed, considering it is thought that Guercino drew far less in the 1650s and 60s, and that his doctor had apparently forbidden him from drawing on account of chest pains, the idea that the artist might have used an earlier design, from one of his most intensive periods of draftsmanship, as inspiration for his last painting seems both appealing and plausible. (Turner and Plazzotta, op. cit., p.181)

Lot Essay:
In 1503, following the defeat of French forces at the Battle of Garigliano, Spain took control of the city of Naples, establishing it as an important center of their empire. This occupation created opportunities for painters living and working in the city to expand their markets and for increased artistic exchange between Italy and Spain.

One of the most successful artists in Naples to profit from the Spanish rule during the mid-17th century was Andrea Vaccaro. By the 1630s, Vaccaro, a native of the city, had become one of its leading painters, working frequently for Spanish patrons and regularly exporting his work to the Iberian Peninsula (as a result, the Museo del Prado in Madrid has a significant collection of his works). His paintings graced all of the major local collections of the day, including that of the Viceroy of Naples, Gaspar de Bracamonte (c. 1595-1676).

Vaccaro was drawn early on to the dramatic chiaroscuro of Caravaggio, whose Flagellation he copied (Museo di Capodimonte, Naples). The present Magdalene elegantly combines the drama and color of Naples and Rome with the restrained classicism of Guido Reni and Domenichino, who strongly influenced Vaccaro from around 1630, as seen in the Magdalene’s delicate, porcelain features and lyrical pose and expression. The stark tenebrism of the Spanish painter Jusepe de Ribera, who had moved to Naples in 1616, is also particularly evident in the present painting, in the still life at lower left and the somber simplicity of the background.

The evident popularity of the Magdalene as a subject during this period is attested to by the number of paintings Vaccaro produced of the saint. Vacarro's paintings of female figures for his Neapolitan patrons, usually on a more profane theme, were much demanded and have been described as presenting a female ideal combining latent sensuality with a classically derived composure. This figure of Mary Magdalen, as befits her historical character, occupies the territory between sensuousness and piety.

There are several autograph and studio versions of this composition, of varying quality, including paintings in the Museo del Capodimonte, Naples; the Galleria Nazionale di Palazzo Abatellis, Palermo; the State Hermitage Museum, St. Petersburg; the Palacio de Liria, Madrid; the Museu Nacional de Belas Artes, Rio de Janiero; and the Alte Pinakothek, Munich. The present canvas and one in a private collection in Naples are the only two to bear Vaccaro’s distinctively elegant monogram. Additionally, as Riccardo Lattuada has noted, with its qualities of refinement and noticeable delicacy, both in the execution and characterization of the saint, the present painting is one of the best extant versions.

Literature:

Lot Essay:
This exquisitely finished small copper, unpublished until now, dates to around 1630 and marks a significant early work by Carlo Dolci. Created when the artist was still a teenager, it reflects the formative influence of his master, Jacopo Vignali. Early paintings by Dolci are extremely rare, making the rediscovery of this piece an important addition to his oeuvre.

The subject is an unusual variation on the Sacra Conversazione, a long-standing Florentine theme. Here, the mature Christ is positioned between the Virgin and Saint Joseph, with the Holy Spirit above and God the Father above that, uniting both the Terrestrial and Celestial Trinities in a single composition. This highly theological interpretation reflects the intellectual seriousness that would define Dolci’s career, even at such a young age.

Stylistically, the painting relates closely to Dolci’s early works, such as The Adoration of the Shepherds (formerly Wengraf, Ltd., and Burghley House), with similar facial types, strong overhead lighting, and a restrained palette. Baldessari notes direct borrowings from Vignali’s Baptism of Christ (1627, Villa Strozzi), particularly in the figure of God the Father, setting a post-1627 date for the work. Influences from Matteo Rosselli are also seen in the simplicity of the composition and the Virgin’s delicate profile.

The painting may be identified with a sacra conversazione listed in the 1727 inventory of Gian Gualberto Guicciardini and later in the Antinori collection, both of whom owned works by Dolci (see Baldassari, Carlo Dolci, 1995, pp. 33–34, 168–169, 197).

Lot Essay:
Exceptionally refined amongst Ricci's surviving head studies, this beautifully painted and powerful work has been dated by Annalisa Scarpa Sonino to the late 1690s. Although the handling is typical of Ricci, the painting is rather unique amongst his identified works. A well-known series of head studies from the Consul Smith collection, purchased by George III and now at Hampton Court, all record figures from Veronese's painting now in the Gallerie dell' Accademia, The Feast in the House of Levi. Apart from these, an imposing self-portrait painted for the collection of the Medici Grand Dukes and an elegant, classicized profile study of a woman appear to be the only other works by Ricci done in a portrait format.

Dignified and profoundly thoughtful, the present figure is swathed in a blue coat with a brown silk stripe, the style of which is strongly reminiscent of the robes worn by Veronese's sitters. The long beard also gives the man a senatorial air, but his hair is tousled, creating an informal effect. It is tempting to believe that the work is a portrait of a fellow artist, friend, or relation. As a prototype, with its rich painterliness and strong contrasts of light and shade, the painting prefigures the splendid series of philosophers and Orientalists painted by Giovanni Battista Tiepolo, and his son and nephew.

Lot Essay:
Originally from Naples, where he first trained as an artist, Salvator Rosa moved to Rome in 1635. He joined the household of Cardinal Francesco Maria Brancaccio, a well-connected Neapolitan with literary and intellectual tastes. Rosa’s own poetic and theatrical talents attracted many patrons and supporters, and his friends and fellow artists delighted in his inventive, witty, and often outrageous conversation. Despite this seemingly light deportment, however, there was a disillusionment and darkness, partly connected to the uncertainty and violence in Neapolitan society and politics, but also indicative of his occasionally misanthropic character.

In 1639, Rosa made a series of landscape paintings peopled with ruffians and travelers, in part inspired by the work of the Bamboccianti painters, the rambunctious group of Dutch artists who lived nearby. As Michael Mahoney has kindly confirmed, the present work must be an early drawing, particularly Riberesque and
exceptional for being a fully realized composition from a period when most of Rosa’s surviving work is sketchy and fragmentary. The subject is particularly poignant, in light of the uncertain and dangerous society in which Rosa lived, and his habit of wandering the Naples countryside to sketch. A simply dressed man, perhaps robbed of his outer garments, is bound outstretched along the branches of a half-dead tree. A passerby points to the figure. The unusual event is particularly emphasized by the otherwise undisturbed landscape, with a sunlit plain and town in the distance. The elegant draftsmanship and the application of the wash in to convey the dappled light on the tree trunk and leaves, but an absence of any shading on the trousers of the hanging figure, adds starkness to the strange scene.

Lot Essay:
Baldassare Franceschini, known as Volterrano, was a preeminent fresco painting in Florence in the latter half of the 17th century. His first significant independent commission came in 1636, when he was entrusted by Don Lorenzo de' Medici with the fresco decoration of the courtyard of the villa of La Petraia, near Florence. Volterrano also painted frescoes and altarpieces for numerous churches and palaces in Florence, Volterra, and Rome. His large-scale, crowded fresco compositions reflect an adaptation into a Florentine idiom of the Roman Baroque style, derived from Pietro da Cortona's frescoes in the Palazzo Pitti. His work culminated in the cupola fresco of The Coronation of the Virgin. Commissioned by the Grand Duke Cosimo III, the fresco was the artist's last major project, as he suffered a stroke shortly after its completion.

The present work is a preparatory drawing for one of the lunettes of the chapel dedicated to Saint Auxanus (San Ansano) in the Church of the Sanissima Annunziata in Florence. The chapel was decorated in 1643, on the commission of Giovanni Grassi, who was a well-known musician in his youth. It shows the present cello-playing angel seated at the center of the composition. Another preparatory study includes a brisk and energetic sketch for the whole lunette that shows this angel flanked by two others (Castello Sforzesco, Milan), as well as an impressive and finished modello for the lunette in the Musée Bonnat-Helleu at Bayonne.

Lot Essay:
Alessandro Magnasco received his artistic training in Milan, where he spent much of his early career as a specialist in figure painting, often hired to depict staffage in the landscape and architectural paintings of other artists. However, it was only in the 1720s, when he was in his 50s, that the artist began to produce his own independent landscape paintings. These works are distinctive, characterized by rapid flickering brushwork, sepulchral lighting, and curiously dissolved, almost liquified forms, and often peopled with beggars, vagabonds, hermits, saints, monks, and torturers. Such figure types are indicative of the influence of the 17th century Dutch and Flemish genre paintings, which the artist would have seen in the collections of the Medici court in Florence while in their employ.

Only a relatively few compositional drawings by Magnasco are known today. Many of the extant drawings are studies of individual figures or small groups of figures, meant to be inserted into larger painted compositions. The present sheet relates to a bozzetto of the Nativity, now in the Philadelphia Museum of Art (inv. 50-4-11). In both, the composition is almost identical; the figure of Joseph emerges from the shadows, his knees bent, back arched, and gnarled hands gripping a staff. His pose leads to the central scene of Mary, her elegantly elongated features drawn in profile, gazing down at the baby Jesus. In each, intensely dramatic contrasts of light and dark define shape and form, with the actively applied brushwork recalling the energetic, flickering strokes and resplendent impasto of the artist's oil paintings.

This bozzetti is one of a series of four, previously in the Ildebrando Bossi Collection, Genoa. The three other bozzetti represent The Flight into Egypt (Cleveland, Museum of Art, inv. 48.13), The Visitation (present location unknown) and The Mystic Marriage of Saint Catherine (Kansas City, Nelson-Atkins Museum, inv. 47-93).

Lot Essay:
In 1807, Bartolomeo Pinelli was 26 years old and, after training in the studio of Felice Giani, had set up a studio of his own. At this date, the artist was involved in a number of different projects. He worked closely with Franz Kaisermann, painting staffage in some of his landscapes, and he was beginning to work on his famous prints of Roman costume, the first collection of which (Costumi romani) was published in 1809, with another (La nuova raccolta di cinquanta motivi pittoreschi e costumi di Roma) published the following year. The present drawing and the following lot clearly demonstrate that he was also absorbed with scenes from Classical literature and history, which would later come to fruition in illustrations for the Aeneid (1811) and on the subject of Greek history (1812).

The present work depicts the triumph of Marcus Furius Camillus over the Gauls in 387 BC. A Roman patrician, statesman, and Dictator of the Republic five times over, Furius Camillus was living in quiet retirement in Ardea when the Gauls marched south as far as Rome that year. Having conquered most of the city, except a stronghold on the Capitol, they let down their guard as they celebrated their spoils. Furius Camillus and a company of soldiers caught them unawares and won a dramatic victory, recovering Rome and destroying the Gauls' army. Later styled the Second Founder of the Republic, Furius Camillus was one of the greatest heroes of Classical Rome.

The scale and impact of this drawing and its companion, with their forceful execution, may suggest that Pinelli originally envisaged them as designs for paintings or frescoes in their own right. No finished picture is known, however; and when Pinelli did return to these subjects, between 1816 and 1821, it was to draw inspiration for another engraving project: his famous series of illustrations of Roman history. The engraving of Furius Camillus in that series, though slightly simplified, is clearly based upon the present work (B. Pinelli, Istoria romana, inventata ed incisa da Barolomeo Pinelli romano, Rome, 1821).

Lot Essay:
Unique within Le Moyne’s known oeuvre, the present pastel depicts an attractive young woman, her head turned to the right and in a loose chemise. It is a compelling addition to the very few pastels by the artist that survive today.

François Le Moyne, pupil of Louis Galloche (1670-1761), won the coveted Prix de Rome in 1711 but was not offered the traditional trip to Rome due to the economic climate in France at the time. Le Moyne only travelled to Italy in the early 1720s and stayed for a few short months. While there he was greatly influenced by Italian artists such as Correggio and Pietro da Cortona, and the Sienese painter Federico Barocci. 

Elected professor of the Académie de Peinture in 1733, Le Moyne's pupils included Charles Joseph Natoire and François Boucher. Le Moyne was held in high regard during his lifetime and produced magnificent ceiling decorations at Versailles, including for the famous Salond'Hercule. His drawings were collected by the most discerning connoisseurs of the century.

Throughout his short career, Le Moyne used three basic techniques when working on his drawings. His methods are concisely documented by Jean-Luc Bordeaux, in his 1984 monograph on the artist, as red chalk drawings on beige paper; black chalk studies heightened with white chalk on blue or grey paper; and finally trois crayons and/or pastels. (Jean-Luc Bordeaux, François Le Moyne and his Generation, 1688-1737, Neuilly-sur-Seine, 1984, p. 139) Bordeaux highlights the fact that works in both trois crayons and pastel are rare but remarks that Donat, one of Le Moyne’s first biographers, "reported that Le Moyne took great pains in making specific pastel studies of heads of the principal figures in his most important commissions…" (Ibid.) This revealing comment suggests that this was an important element in Le Moyne’s artistic endeavors, despite very few surviving pastels.

In a communication to a previous owner, Jean Luc Bordeaux supports the attribution of the present pastel to Le Moyne. While the head study does not relate directly to any known painting, Bordeaux identifies a number of painted figures by the artist to which she can be plausibly compared, on the basis of the facial type and tilt of the figure's head, as well as a variety of other nuances. He likens this beautiful head to the maiden in A maiden soaking a small piece of cloth in a fountain (known in two versions, in private collections), in which the facial features are similarly rendered in terms of the eyes and lips, and the manner in which the artist has handled the hair and ribbon is also comparable. Bordeaux also cites the figure of Andromeda in the Perseus and Andromeda in the Wallace Collection, where again facial features such as the chin and almond shaped eyes are very comparable, and the Venus in Venus and Adonis in the Nationalmuseum, Stockholm, in which once more the nose and lips, and handling of the hair, are all very similar.

Other stylistic elements identified by Bordeaux as typical of the artist's work include the rapid, rounded strokes made with a hard pastel stick to define the hair, and the light stumping around the corners of the figure's mouth, eyebrows, and eyelids. Also noted by Bordeaux is Le Moyne's overall preference for the consistency of softer pastel sticks and colors, often blended with cloth or brush, to convey the luminosity and smooth uninterrupted tonal textures of the sitter's skin. This softness is emphasized by the artist's more sculptural and angular treatment of the border of her negligée and the lively hair tendrils curling over the sitter's neck and along her shoulders. stands out against the more angular lines used to describe the borders of her garment. It is difficult to find close comparisons to the present pastel and others by the artist, as almost all of Le Moyne's known works in pastel or colored chalks are representations of men.

Le Moyne’s close relationship with his patron and friend François Berger has led Bordeaux tentatively to suggest that this beguiling and beautiful young woman may have been a member of the social circle of Berger and his wife. Her identity is, however, irrelevant to our appreciation of this refined image, or to the light that it sheds on our understanding of Le Moyne's work in this medium, a fascinating aspect of the artist's short but fruitful career.

Lot Essay:
Born in Geneva, Ferrière probably received his early training with Jean-Étienne Liotard before moving to Paris to study at the Académie des Beaux-Arts under Joseph-Marie Vien. By 1770, he had returned to his native city where he established himself as a painter and is documented ‘restoring’ paintings belonging to the city’s library. With the outbreak of the French Revolution and the ensuing unrest in Switzerland, Ferrière and his family emigrated to England, where the painter began specializing in miniatures. His portraits were successfully received in London, and he obtained commissions from members of the aristocracy and the Royal Family, and became a frequent exhibitor at the Royal Academy from 1793. After a period in Russia, the artist spent some time working in London before returning to Switzerland, where he once again became a prominent artistic figure and member of the Société des Arts.

This lively depiction of a young boy carrying a painting under his arm is a rare example for a painter that is best-known as a miniaturist. It demonstrates Ferrière's exceptional clarity and refinement of technique in oil, while at the same time bringing light and character to the portrayal. Comparable in tone and composition to pictures Ferrière would likely have seen in Paris, like Vien’s Portrait of Jacques-Louis David as a youth, c. 1765 (Angers, Musée des Beaux-Arts), the present portrait shows a remarkable sense of vivacious naturalism. The young boy's face is animated by the glinting reflections in his eyes, the deep shadow cast by the bucket hat, as well as as his ruddy cheeks and upturned mouth. With the frame tucked under his arm and one finger pointing, the appears poised for movement, as if just sent off on an errand.

Lot Essay:
In addition to his celebrated portraits of famous sitters such as Giuseppe Verdi, James Abbott McNeill Whistler, Consuelo Vanderbilt, the Duchess of Marlborough, and Count Robert de Montesquiou, in the mid-1880s Giovanni Boldini, began to turn to daily objects for inspiration. In these watercolors, scattered paint brushes, plaster busts, vases of flowers and pieces of furniture from his studio repeatedly appear, with the artist exploring their aesthetic possibilities.

In the present work, the arrangement is casual and artful, dominated by the overturned sugar bowl (which also appears in his The Corner of the Painter’s Table, c. 1897, Museo Boldini, Ferrara) and porcelain basket filled with shiny cherries. The repeated, curvilinear forms enhance the tactility of the subject, with movement given by the single spilled cherry cropped at the center right edge. The artist captures the precise details of the still life with broad strokes of watercolor and leaves areas of the white paper exposed to create the gleam of the silver sugar bowl and slatted design of the basket. Every element demonstrates the artist's brilliant confidence with the medium.

Lot Essay:
This striking work exemplifies Zandomeneghi’s skill with the delicate medium of pastel. The artist adopted in the 1890s, mainly using it for his portraits of women and children. Like many of his favorite subjects, Young Woman with a Bouquet of Flowers depicts the late nineteenth century life of the Parisienne. However, while fellow Italian expatriates like Giuseppe de Nittis and Giovanni Boldini favored painting fashionably dressed ladies, Zandomeneghi preferred portraying women and girls observed in the private moments of their everyday life. 

In the present work, the cropping of the composition and slight lean of the figure’s posture creates a sense of intimacy and connects subject and viewer. The artist suggests the softness of his model’s pale skin with the pastel, and leaves the exposed paper to create highlights along her forehead and cheek. A rich buildup of the medium creates thick, soft upswept strands of hair decorated with a finely carved wooden hairpin, perhaps an allusion to the contemporary trend of Japonisme­. Zandomeneghi’s subtly shifts the soft pinks and buttery yellows of casually arranged daisies with the vibrant blue of cornflowers, while white swirls and wavy vertical lines create abstract patterns of fabric and wallpaper. The complex intertwining of tone and texture is a hallmark of the artist’s best pastels.

A Venetian by birth, Federico Zandomeneghi associated with the Macchiaioli in Florence before moving to Paris in 1874. By the late 1870s he had become a habitué of the Café de la Nouvelle-Athènes on the Place Pigalle in Montmartre, where he met and befriended Edgar Degas. The two artists, both difficult, ill-tempered characters, were to remain lifelong friends. Degas persuaded Zandomeneghi to exhibit at the fourth Impressionist exhibition in 1879, and the Italian also took part in the Impressionist exhibitions of 1880, 1881, and 1886.
While the artist's working habits and compositional choices link him to Degas and Pierre-Auguste Renoir, as well as Mary Cassatt and Berthe Morisot, his compositions are specific to him and his Italian heritage. Works like Young Woman with a Bouquet of Flowers earned him the additional nickname of “Le vénitien,” stemming from his brilliant yet subtle use of color that recalls the work of the Macchiaioli.

Marguerite Phillips, Chicago, circa mid 1940s
Thence by descent
Acquired from the above by the present owner

Note
The Linden Glass Company of Chicago (1884-1934) represented the finest in leaded glass window craftsmanship and was the preferred stained-glass producer for Frank Lloyd Wright.  Opened in 1884 by Frank L. Linden (1859-1934) and Ernest J. Spierling (1856-1931) as the Spierling & Linden Decorating Co., the collaboration focused initially on murals, stained-glass and other fine interior decorating services and by 1906 became the largest stained-glass employer in Chicago, employing 50 workers. 

Linden created more glass for Frank Lloyd Wright than any other firm and was the major art glass fabricator for some of his best-known projects, including: Unity Temple (Chicago, Illinois); Frederick C. Robie House (Chicago, Illinois); Avery and Queene Ferry Coonley House (Chicago, Illinois); Susan Lawrence Dana House (Springfield, Illinois); and the Darwin D. Martin House (Buffalo, New York). The company closed in 1934 with the death of Frank Linden.

The eclectic collection offered here features a variety of colorations, lead weights and styles created by the Linden company through its manufacturing years. The intricacies of some of the leadwork in this collection are among the most complex and artistic in the medium. The designers of these windows are unknown.

This collection of windows belonged to Nels Ernest Johnson (1871-1954), who was named Vice President of Linden Co. in 1910. In the 1940s, when the Johnson Family moved from their home, the windows passed to the Phillips family, close friends and neighbors residing on North Magnolia Street in the Edgewater neighborhood of Chicago. The current owner purchased these from the Phillips family. Included in that purchase were several examples of Frank Lloyd Wright windows that sold at Sotheby's, Important Design, December 13, 2017, Lots 88, 89 and 92.

subject_matter: celadon fragments, lotus petal, lotus leaf, glaze texture, Southern Song Dynasty, ceramic, craquelure, blueish, greyish body, Imperial kilns
description_block:
Two Rare  Guanyao  Celadon    Fragments, Southern Song Dynasty 南宋 官窯粉青釉瓷片兩件 
 
 Southern Song Dynasty (1127-1279) 
 Comprising a fragment of a "lotus petal" bowl's rim, distinguished by its characteristic craquelure, and an exquisitely potted fragment from a lotus leaf-form cover. Both pieces display the quintessential finely potted greyish bodies and thick blueish-celadon glaze of the Imperial kilns of the Southern Song dynasty. Note: In 1086, the legendary finely-potted celadon-blue-glazed Ru ware was first commissioned by the Northern Song court, representing an unparalleled zenith in the history of Chinese ceramics. However, this golden age was tragically short-lived. Forty years later, the dynasty fell to the invading Jin armies, an event marked by the capture and humiliation of Emperors Huizong and Qinzong. Yet, the legacy of Ru ware endured. By 1149, its spirit was reborn in Lin’an (modern Hangzhou) in the form of Guan (Official) ware. As the Southern Song court's successor to Ru, Guan ware consciously emulated its revered predecessor in multiple aspects. As recorded in Ye Zhi's Southern Song text, Tanzhai Biheng: "After the imperial court moved south of the Yangtze River, Shao Chengzhang was put in charge of the rear garden establishment, known as the Shao Bureau. Following the old capital's traditions, a kiln was established within the Interior Department to produce celadons, named the 'Inner Kiln'." Serving exclusively as imperial ceramics, sacred objects such as altar stands were produced only by these official kilns. Guided by Daoist principles, both Ru and Guan ware pursued the ultimate celadon glaze, a color meant to embody the heavens. To compensate for the dark, iron-rich local clay, Guan artisans perfected a body of extraordinary fineness, often as thin as 0.3 cm. The delicate form was then enveloped in a thick, opulent glaze applied in multiple layers. Research from the Palace Museum in Beijing confirms that this glaze featured a high potassium and low calcium composition, which drastically reduced its fluidity during firing. This unique formula resulted in a glaze with a soft, dense texture and a warm, jade-like tactile quality—a triumph of artistry that came at the cost of an extremely low success rate. The Confucian dictum, "When sacrificial vessels become damaged, they are to be buried," was scrupulously followed. Excavations at the Guan kiln sites have revealed large caches of deliberately shattered and buried wares. This practice ensured that any piece failing to meet the exacting imperial standard would never enter the public domain, further cementing Guan ware's identity as the sole preserve of the court. Consequently, the finest Guan ware fragments are typically discovered in the vicinity of the old Southern Song palace grounds. The two fragments presented here are emblematic of this standard of palace quality. The larger fragment, originally part of a lotus-petal bowl, exhibits the most exquisite glaze texture. A network of long, dark crackles is interlaced with shorter, transparent fissures, creating a pattern reminiscent of multifold rose blossoms or crackled ice. For comparison, see a similarly glazed lobed bowl in the Tokyo National Museum (Ref. TG-1234) and a large round Guan washer in the collection of the Taipei Palace Museum (Ref. 故瓷016928).The smaller fragment is likely from a lotus-leaf-shaped cover. Its glaze is a lighter, clearer blue, yet the dark grey clay body beneath lends it a characteristic depth and serenity. The crackle pattern here is more understated, consisting of subtle, transparent lines. The glaze quality can be compared to a foliate rim dish in the British Museum from the Sir Percival David Collection (Museum No. PDF,A.46), and a Guan lobed dish formerly in the collections of Sir Harry M. Garner and the Ise collection, sold at Sotheby's Hong Kong in September 2025 (Lot 5022).For nearly a millennium, owning a piece of Southern Song Guan ware has been the dream of collectors. The Qianlong Emperor (r. 1735-1796) composed over seventy poems celebrating the Qing imperial collection, which numbered fewer than one hundred pieces.It is, therefore, more than an honor to present these precious fragments. It is a rare opportunity to glimpse the very peak of Song elegance—a beauty born from adversity and refined to perfection. ﻿公元1086年，傳世瑰寶汝瓷首度受命於北宋宮廷燒造，標誌著中國陶瓷史上無與倫比的巔峰。然而這黃金時代轉瞬即逝，僅四十年後王朝傾覆，金軍鐵蹄踏破山河，徽欽二帝蒙塵北狩的恥辱成為歷史烙印。汝瓷的香火卻未斷絕。至1149年，其美學精神在臨安（今杭州）以官窯之名重獲新生。作為南宋宮廷承繼汝窯的正統，官窯在多個層面刻意追摹前朝典範。據南宋葉寘《坦齋筆衡》所載：「中興渡江，有邵成章提舉後苑，號邵局。襲故京遺制，置窯於修內司，造青器，名內窯。」這些專屬御用的陶瓷中，祭壇供器等禮制重器僅由官窯燒造。秉承道家哲學，汝官二窯皆追求象徵天象的玄青釉色。為克服南方胎土含鐵量高的特性，官窯匠人將胚體修薄至僅0.3公分，再以多重施釉工藝覆以豐厚釉層。北京故宮研究院證實，其釉料獨特的高鉀低鈣配方大幅降低燒製流動性，形成溫潤致密、類玉質感的釉面——這般藝術成就的代價，是極低的成品率。《禮記》「祭器敝則埋之」的訓誡被嚴格遵循。官窯遺址考古發現大量刻意擊碎掩埋的殘器，此舉確保未達御準的器物永不流散民間，進一步強化官窯的宮廷專屬屬性。故最精粹的官瓷殘片，多見於南宋皇城舊址周邊。本次呈現的兩件殘片，正是這宮苑標準的典型體現。較大殘片原屬蓮瓣式碗，釉面呈現精妙絕倫的紋理：深色長開片與透明冰裂短線縱橫交織，形成層疊薔薇或春冰乍裂的意象。可參照東京國立博物館藏瓣口碗（編號TG-1234）及台北故宮藏官窯圓洗（編號故瓷016928）之釉色開片。較小殘片疑為荷葉式蓋器，釉色清透微藍，然因深灰胎骨映照而別具幽邃之境。開片紋理較為內斂，僅見隱約透明冰裂。其釉質可與大維德基金會藏葵口盤（編號PDF,A.46）及香港蘇富比2025年秋拍第5022號官窯葵口盤（原屬Garner爵士、伊勢收藏）相互參照。近千年來，典藏一片南宋官瓷始終是鑒藏家的終極夢想。乾隆皇帝（1735-1796年在位）曾為清宮不足百件的官窯珍藏題寫七十餘首御制詩。是次得以呈現此吉光片羽，非但與有榮焉，亦是窺見宋韻極致的難得機緣——這種於憂患中孕育、在淬煉裡臻至完美的美學境界，至今依然動人心魄。 
 Length of the larger 2 1/8 in., 5.4 cm. 
 
 This lot is located in Philadelphia.

Provenance:
Property from the Collection of George C.T. Wan, New York, thence by descent.

George Chien-Tze ("C.T.") Wan was born in Jiangxi province, of China. He became interested in Chinese porcelains when, in Shanghai, Mr. Wan worked as a representative for importers of Chinese porcelains to the United States. Through this work, he obtained sponsorship to immigrate to the United States in 1949. Within a year, C.T. Wan & Co., dealer in Chinese art and antiques, was inaugurated in New York City at 116 East 28th St. Thus began a dedication and passion for Asian art and collecting that was to fulfill Mr. Wan's excellent life until his passing in 2019. The store moved twice, first a few blocks away to 235 Fifth Avenue in the 1960's and then across the avenue in the 1980's to 242 Fifth Avenue. In the 2000’s, surrounded by his collection, Mr. Wan would smile and reflect on what great satisfaction and pride his life's work had brought to him.

萬寶古董行庫藏。該行由江西籍古董商萬氏創立，萬氏上世紀中葉在滬從事瓷器出口貿易，1949年移民紐約，于28街東116號經營瓷器，店名C.T. Wan & Co，后遷五大道235號，再遷242號。店址雖多次變動，都位於五大道與28街交匯處，這是當年紐約亞洲藝術交易的中心，如山中商會就在254號，與萬寶古董行一街之隔。千禧年后，萬氏年高，淡出經營，2019年下世，本次上拍子女繼承的部分庫存。

Literature:
Brian H. Peterson, The Cities, the Towns, the Crowds: The Paintings of Robert Spencer, Philadelphia, 2004, pg. 60, pl. 25 (illustrated).

Lot Note:
Robert Spencer held a prominent position among the Pennsylvania Impressionists working in Bucks County, where he rubbed elbows with fellow artists Charles Rosen, Daniel Garber, William Lathrop and others. A leading figure of the New Hope art colony, his aesthetic was nonetheless quite different from that of his peers, as it mostly eschewed the charming and picturesque qualities of the rural surroundings, focusing instead on the grit and tedium of early 20th century industrial subjects in and around New Hope. Through and through, Spencer was indeed a painter of the working people, whom he portrayed with both candor and compassion.

In Waterloo Row, Spencer used his distinctive muted palette and broken brushstrokes to depict a row of tenements in the town of New Hope. The scene, commonplace and rather unsentimental, is rendered through a plain composition of horizontal layers—the sky, roofs, facades, road and band of vegetation—intersected by the frail yet piercing vertical lines of three bare trees. Thus, the painting, in its grid-like structure, devoid of excessive flourishes, exudes an unnerving sense of penury, casting the tenement row in a dreary light, as if to reflect the harsh living and working conditions that are likely afflicting its inhabitants.

But beyond these geometric constraints, a certain spontaneity emerges. The lone figure and subtly warming sky suggest that the scene takes place shortly after dawn, just before the rising bustle. The white blotches of paint on the façades, the grasses dancing in the wind, and the curvy branches all contrast with the erect tree trunks and neatly rectangular windows and chimneys. They convey a gentle motion stirring in the stillness, the faint sounds of the early hours auguring the busy day of toiling to come, a budding liveliness at odds with the seemingly dull composition. 

Spencer’s ambition was to draw attention to the ordinary squalor that characterized tenements and industrial settings. Far from minimizing the indigence he witnessed, he sought to highlight the dignity and verve evident in the midst of destitution. Waterloo Row, an unvarnished rendition of working-class living quarters, was executed in 1917, at the heart of a pivotal decade for the advancement of workers’ rights in the United States.

Lot Note:
Like his well-known rival Edward Redfield, Walter Elmer Schofield was an exponent of an outstepping and hearty aesthetic, one that prioritized candor—he only painted what he saw—and energy. He had a particular flair for extracting the raw beauty of American landscapes in all kinds of weather, as if he relished a confrontation with the elements, and such bluster is now often understood as an attempt to equate virility with Americanism in art.

Winter was his season of choice to depict the wonders to be found out of doors. The more challenging a setting appeared, the more intense its rendition proved. Here, Schofield ventured to a snowy wooded exterior, and the act of capturing it on canvas amounted to stranding the viewer in its midst. With no path or recognizable landmarks in sight, we are enveloped in subtly gradated shades of blue, grey, brown and green, a multi-sensory moment allowing us to experience the frigid air and howling winds likely felt and heard by the painter himself.

Lot Note:
Quiet winter scenes were among Pennsylvania Impressionist Harry Leith-Ross’s most favored subjects, as he sought to capture in subtle and suggestive ways the serenity emanating from snow-covered rural landscapes. 12:24 (Emmy at Window), a gentle rendition of a winter night at once filled with chill and warmth, encapsulates Leith-Ross’s aesthetic, one that puts forth observations of nature through an eminently personal lens.

Here, we are let in on a rather intimate scene, even if from a distance. The view of the house is not frontal; we only get to see a side façade, unadorned, seemingly impenetrable, save for the one window in the top right corner that does not dwell in the dark, and where the gaze is immediately drawn. The red-clad figure in the window is Leith-Ross's wife, Emmy. She appears to be sitting atop the couple's bed or perhaps at a desk, possibly reading or writing. She is caught in a private moment–at a time of day usually quiet and deserted–but with a sensitivity that only her husband's brush can afford.

12:24 (Emmy at Window) is equally a depiction of a peaceful wintry Pennsylvania landscape as one might generally think of it, as it is about how it is personally experienced and, arguably, enjoyed. The main source of light in the painting, the window, seems to diffuse its warmth throughout, as it reverberates into the porch, the softly slumbering sky above, and even the bright glistening snow below. And quite poetically, it also defuses any lingering frictions, such as the tension between the frigid outdoors and the cozy interior. Like the diaphanous curtain draping the window, it soothes and softens, blending conflicting sensations into one welcoming and perfectly arranged whole.
